items.title: RSI是否能通往AGI？大模型智能体强化学习与自进化论坛 | CNCC2026
items.location: 中国西部国际博览城 4 号馆 409 论坛主席 周明 澜舟科技 CEO
items.summary: RSI是否能通往AGI？大模型智能体强化学习与自进化论坛 | CNCC2026 RL Agent DL 澜舟科技 2026-10-13 10:50 分享 以下文章来源于mp.weixin.qq.com 递归自进化（RSI，Recursive Self-Improvement）能否通往 AGI？大模型智能体又该如何实现智能递归自进化？ CNCC2026 将于 10 月 21—24 日 在 四川成都 举办。本场专题论坛以「 大模型智能体强化学习与自进化 」为主题，邀请多位活跃在一线的学者，带来该方向最新的研究进展与未来展望。 论坛简介 当前，大模型智能体正从传统的监督训练走向自主进化，在自主科学发现、软件开发、深度搜索、数据分析等场景取得显著进展。 然而，将智能体应用于真实场景，要求其具备持续学习与自进化能力，以实现领域适配、满足用户需求。 本论坛邀请多位活跃在一线的优秀学者，分享大模型智能体自进化的前沿技术与未来发展趋势，探讨智能体在真实场景中自进化所面临的技术挑战与思路，并从 Agentic RL 与 Agent Harness 两个角度，讨论智能体自进化的发展趋势及其对业界与 AI 产品的影响，推动智能体在更广泛的真实场景中进一步落地。 论坛安排 时间：10 月 24 日 13:30—17:30 地点：中国西部国际博览城 4 号馆 409 论坛主席 周明 澜舟科技 CEO，ACL/CCF/CAAI Fellow 嘉宾简介： 周明博士，1985 年获重庆大学本科学位，1991 年取得哈尔滨工业大学博士学位。1991–1999 年任教于清华大学，其间赴日本开展中日机器翻译研究；1999–2020 年任职于微软亚洲研究院。他是 ACL Fellow、CCF 会士，曾任 ACL 主席、CCF 副理事长、微软亚洲研究院副院长。在微软亚洲研究院期间，带领团队深耕机器翻译、问答、语言学习等方向，并率先启动通用、多模态、编程类大模型前沿研究，相关成果落地于微软多款核心产品。他深耕自然语言处理三十余年，担任多校博导，培养二十余名博士和二十余名博士后，持续推动产学研融合。2021 年，在创新工场支持下创办澜舟科技，自研孟子大模型与 LangClaw 企业智能体系统，聚焦企业自主 AI 核心技术研发与产业落地。 杨健 北京航空航天大学副教授 嘉宾简介 ： 杨健，北京航空航天大学副教授，

号馆 409 论坛主席 周明 澜舟科技 CEO，ACL/CCF/CAAI Fellow 嘉宾简介： 周明博士，1985 年获重庆大学本科学位，1991 年取得哈尔滨工业大学博士学位。1991–1999 年任教于清华大学，其间赴日本开展中日机器翻译研究；1999–2020 年任职于微软亚洲研究院。他是 ACL Fellow、CCF 会士，曾任 ACL 主席、CCF 副理事长、微软亚洲研究院副院长。在微软亚洲研究院期间，带领团队深耕机器翻译、问答、语言学习等方向，并率先启动通用、多模态、编程类大模型前沿研究，相关成果落地于微软多款核心产品。他深耕自然语言处理三十余年，担任多校博导，培养二十余名博士和二十余名博士后，持续推动产学研融合。2021 年，在创新工场支持下创办澜舟科技，自研孟子大模型与 LangClaw 企业智能体系统，聚焦企业自主 AI 核心技术研发与产业落地。 杨健 北京航空航天大学副教授 嘉宾简介 ： 杨健，北京航空航天大学副教授，华为卓越青年学者，聚焦代码大模型与智能体，研究方向覆盖预训练、后训练、协同生成与评测，在 ICLR、NeurIPS、ACL、EMNLP 等国际权威学术期刊和会议发表论文百余篇，第一与通讯作者 30 余次，多次担任 ARR（ACL、EMNLP、NAACL）SAC/AC、INLG 2026 Program Chair、AAAI（AIA Track）SPC 与 AC，谷歌学术引用 42000+，获 WAIC 2026 云帆奖。博士毕业后，以阿里星（阿里人才计划）加入阿里巴巴通义千问团队，作为千问大模型 Qwen 系列及千问代码大模型 QwenCoder 系列的核心贡献者，负责千问模型代码能力建设及专项代码模型 QwenCoder 的研发。加入北航后，主导研发循环代码大模型 LoopCoder，以及面向工业场景的 InCoder-32B，覆盖 7B、14B、32B、40B 多个参数量级。在代码大模型应用落地方面，获得发明协会创新创业一等奖，累计专利、应用证明、漏洞证明十余项。 陈冠华 南方科技大学助理教授 嘉宾简介 ： 陈冠华，南方科技大学助理教授，博士生导师，中国中文信息学会青工委执委，CCF 自然语言处理专委会执委。研究兴趣为推理大模型智能体的持续学习与自进化。他获得 2025 年度微软亚洲研究院铸星学者，主持一项国家自然科学基金青年项目和一项广东省自然科学基金面上项目，并作为核心骨干成员参与一项科技部重点研发青年科学家项目。近三年来在 ICML、ICLR、ACL 等 CCF-A/B 类会议以第一作者或通讯作者身份发表论文 40 篇，担任人工智能领域会议和期刊审稿人和 ICLR/ACL/EMNLP 领域主席。 论坛演讲 开场致辞：RSI 递归自主改进的发展与挑战 周明 澜舟科技 CEO，ACL/CCF/CAAI Fellow 内容简介： 递归自进化（RSI，Recursive Self-Improvement）是当前通用智能与智能体领域的前沿研究方向，核心是让 AI 系统具备自我诊断、自我迭代、自我优化的闭环进化能力，突破传统模型依赖人工调参、人工迭代、人工优化的研发范式。近年来，随着大模型、代码智能体与循环推理架构的快速成熟，RSI 从理论构想逐步走向受限场景的工程落地，在代码生成、模型微调、任务自迭代等方向展现出巨大潜力。但整体而言，RSI 仍处于早期探索阶段，面临迭代稳定性差、自我进化难以收敛、评价体系不完备、复杂任务递归退化、安全对齐难度大等关键瓶颈。本次分享将系统梳理 RSI 技术的演进脉络、当前阶段性成果，剖析落地中的核心技术难题与未来发展路径。 演讲：共进化 AI 与不可解释的可验证的创新 沈阳 清华大学教授 嘉宾简介： 沈阳，清华大学人工智能学院、新闻学院双聘教授，主要研究方向为自进化 AI、AIGC、新媒体、大数据、网络舆论、XR 应用。现为近十个部委专委会专家，以及多个二级学会副会长或秘书长，中宣部“文化名家”暨“四个一批”入选者、教育部新世纪人才计划入选者。 报告摘要： 本报告围绕自进化 AI、自主算法优化与智能自我检验技术，构建人机共进化新范式，建立“不可解释过程+强可验证结果”创新理论框架。自进化 AI 可自主开展高维探索、算法迭代优化，创新推演链路超出人类认知边界；依托内嵌多层级自检体系，自动完成精度校验、误差修正与成果复现核验，实现黑箱进化、结果可信。报告重塑人机分工模式，人类负责目标设定与边界管控，AI 承担自主探索、创新产出。团队已形成自进化智能、自动寻优、自主校验等系列原创成果。该范式推动 AI 从工具智能走向自生智能，为持续学习、可控进化的下一代智能系统提供创新方法论与落地路径。 报告题目：第一性原理视角下的智能进化：从模型基础 到运行框架 钱泓锦 北京智源人工智能研究院研究员 嘉宾简介： 钱泓锦，北京智源人工智能研究院研究员，北京大学博士后，研究方向为检索智能体与智能体记忆，主持国家自然科学基金青年项目。在人工智能与信息检索领域的国际期刊与会议发表论文数十篇。其所在团队长期专注于开源模型生态建设，相关项目在 GitHub 上累计获星超过一万，模型在 Hugging Face 平台月下载量达数亿次。 报告摘要： 在大模型逐步掌握对话、推理、代码编写与工具调用之后，自主研究将成为人工智能的下一个重大突破：智能体能够像研究者一样，主动提出问题、搜集证据、形成假设、检验结论，并最终产生超越既有知识边界的新发现。本报告将从第一性原理出发，围绕复杂问题中普遍存在的“求解—验证”不对称性，探讨智能进化的基本机制与系统实现。我们提出“求解—评估双循环智能体”，通过持续求解、结果评估与反馈改进，实现解决方案的递归优化，并在深度研究、机器学习与算法工程等场景中验证其有效性。在此基础上，我们将进一步讨论支撑长期智能进化的运行框架，以及如何通过“技能蒸馏”将人类知识转化为适合智能体自主研究的技能基础，从而构建融合模型能力、循环优化与人机协同的智能进化体系。最后，报告将探讨智能进化对现实应用场景的赋能，并展示相关原型系统与评估框架。 报告题目：从强化学习到自我演化：迈向长程智能体 林衍凯 中国人民大学副教授 嘉宾简介： 林衍凯，中国人民大学高瓴人工智能学院预聘副教授，主要研究方向为大模型智能体。Google Scholar 统计引用达 3.1 万次，2020—2025 年连续六年入选爱思唯尔（Elsevier）中国高被引学者和斯坦福大学全球前 2% 顶尖科学家年度榜单，入选北京市科技新星、吴文俊人工智能青年科技奖、《麻省理工科技评论》中国与 DeepTech 联合发布的“AI100 青年先锋”等。其成果获评教育部自然科学一等奖、世界互联网大会领先科技成果。现任 CCF NOI 科学委员会委员。 报告摘要： 长程推理是通用智能体的核心瓶颈。本报告以能力的持续获取为主线，先探讨如何用智能体强化学习提升长程推理与跨任务泛化，再剖析人类在任务、奖励与验证上的监督上限，进而介绍自我演化：让智能体自主构造任务与反馈，形成自我提升闭环，突破监督瓶颈，探索通用智能体可持续进化的路径。 报告题目：Agentic AI 的进化配方：模型、环境与数据的反馈闭环 林涛 西湖大学研究员 嘉宾简介： 林涛，西湖大学工学院人工智能系特聘研究员、博士生导师、独立 PI（课题组负责人），入选国家级青年人才计划。2022 年博士毕业于瑞士洛桑联邦理工学院（EPFL）。研究领域为（1）深度学习与优化，（2）高效深度学习与推理，（3）分布式深度学习与系统。相关论文获评 ECCV 2024 最佳论文提名。2024—2025 年连续入选斯坦福大学全球前 2% 顶尖科学家榜单。实验室主页：https://lins-lab.github.io/。 报告摘要： 当前，大语言模型正从单一的“一次性问答系统”，演进为具备工具调用、环境干预以及基于反馈持续决策能力的“智能体（Agent）”。本报告聚焦“什么是智能体、如何训练智能体、如何实现智能体自进化”三大核心议题，系统性地梳理了一条从规模化工程实践到构建反馈闭环的研究路线。 首先，AWorld 通过分布式智能体与环境的交互大幅提升经验采集效率，为智能体强化学习构筑了高可扩展的训练基础设施；其次，Environment Tuning 结合结构化课程、可执行的环境反馈与细粒度进度奖励，使智能体能够在极少量任务中实现稳定学习；进一步地，RODS 利用多次 rollout（模型对同一任务的多次采样）的平均进度奖励与奖励方差来探测模型的能力边界，并围绕这一动态边界在线合成数据，从而实现训练任务与模型能力的协同进化。 上述工作共同勾勒出了 Agentic AI 的演进范式：智能体训练不应局限于孤立的模型优化，而应立足系统全局视角，构建起“模型、训练环境与训练数据”三位一体、相互促进的反馈闭环。 特邀思辨环节嘉宾 王昊奋 同济大学长聘教授 嘉宾简介： 王昊奋，同济大学长聘教授、博士生导师，聚焦知识图谱与知识增强大模型研究，以及 AI 产业落地。核心成果包括全球首个知识增强推理模型 KAG-Thinker（超万 Star）、记忆操作系统 MemOS（日调用量超 150 万次）及大模型评测平台 AI-Ceping（30 万+月活），已落地机场调控、金融风控等多场景。出版《知识图谱》《检索增强生成：理论与实践》《记忆工程》等 6 部专著，共发表高水平会议和期刊论文 100 多篇，谷歌学术被引超 1.5 万次。主持国自然重点、面上、国家新一代 AI 重大专项课题等 10 多个国家 AI 项目，获中交协科技进步一等奖、2026 年 IF 设计奖、HCII 最佳论文、DASFAA 最佳学生论文等荣誉。他曾担任两家 AI 独角兽企业 CTO，构建了全球首个可交互养成的虚拟偶像—“琥珀·虚颜”；所构建的智能客服机器人已累计服务用户超过 100 亿人次。目前，他担任全球最大开放知识图谱社区 OpenKG 首任轮值主席，中国计算机学会术语工委副主任，自然语言处理专委会副主任（执行），中国中文信息学会理事，大模型专委会指导委员，语言与知识计算专委会副主任，上海市计算机学会自然语言处理专委会副主任等社会职位。 * 21—24 日 在 四川成都 举办。本场专题论坛以「 大模型智能体强化学习与自进化 」为主题，邀请多位活跃在一线的学者，带来该方向最新的研究进展与未来展望。 论坛简介 当前，大模型智能体正从传统的监督训练走向自主进化，在自主科学发现、软件开发、深度搜索、数据分析等场景取得显著进展。 然而，将智能体应用于真实场景，要求其具备持续学习与自进化能力，以实现领域适配、满足用户需求。 本论坛邀请多位活跃在一线的优秀学者，分享大模型智能体自进化的前沿技术与未来发展趋势，探讨智能体在真实场景中自进化所面临的技术挑战与思路，并从 Agentic RL 与 Agent Harness 两个角度，讨论智能体自进化的发展趋势及其对业界与 AI 产品的影响，推动智能体在更广泛的真实场景中进一步落地。 论坛安排 时间：10 月 24 日 13:30—17:30 地点：中国西部国际博览城 4 号馆 409 论坛主席 周明 澜舟科技 CEO，ACL/CCF/CAAI Fellow 嘉宾简介： 周明博士，1985 年获重庆大学本科学位，1991 年取得哈尔滨工业大学博士学位。1991–1999 年任教于清华大学，其间赴日本开展中日机器翻译研究；1999–2020 年任职于微软亚洲研究院。他是 ACL Fellow、CCF 会士，曾任 ACL 主席、CCF 副理事长、微软亚洲研究院副院长。在微软亚洲研究院期间，带领团队深耕机器翻译、问答、语言学习等方向，并率先启动通用、多模态、编程类大模型前沿研究，相关成果落地于微软多款核心产品。他深耕自然语言处理三十余年，担任多校博导，培养二十余名博士和二十余名博士后，持续推动产学研融合。2021 年，在创新工场支持下创办澜舟科技，自研孟子大模型与 LangClaw 企业智能体系统，聚焦企业自主 AI 核心技术研发与产业落地。 杨健 北京航空航天大学副教授 嘉宾简介 ： 杨健，北京航空航天大学副教授，华为卓越青年学者，聚焦代码大模型与智能体，研究方向覆盖预训练、后训练、协同生成与评测，在 ICLR、NeurIPS、ACL、EMNLP 等国际权威学术期刊和会议发表论文百余篇，第一与通讯作者 30 余次，多次担任 ARR（ACL、EMNLP、NAACL）SAC/AC、INLG 2026 Program Chair、AAAI（AIA Track）SPC 与 AC，谷歌学术引用 42000+，获 WAIC 2026 云帆奖。博士毕业后，以阿里星（阿里人才计划）加入阿里巴巴通义千问团队，作为千问大模型 Qwen 系列及千问代码大模型 QwenCoder 系列的核心贡献者，负责千问模型代码能力建设及专项代码模型 QwenCoder 的研发。加入北航后，主导研发循环代码大模型 LoopCoder，以及面向工业场景的 InCoder-32B，覆盖 7B、14B、32B、40B 多个参数量级。在代码大模型应用落地方面，获得发明协会创新创业一等奖，累计专利、应用证明、漏洞证明十余项。 陈冠华 南方科技大学助理教授 嘉宾简介 ： 陈冠华，南方科技大学助理教授，博士生导师，中国中文信息学会青工委执委，CCF 自然语言处理专委会执委。研究兴趣为推理大模型智能体的持续学习与自进化。他获得 2025 年度微软亚洲研究院铸星学者，主持一项国家自然科学基金青年项目和一项广东省自然科学基金面上项目，并作为核心骨干成员参与一项科技部重点研发青年科学家项目。近三年来在 ICML、ICLR、ACL 等 CCF-A/B 类会议以第一作者或通讯作者身份发表论文 40 篇，担任人工智能领域会议和期刊审稿人和 ICLR/ACL/EMNLP 领域主席。 论坛演讲 开场致辞：RSI 递归自主改进的发展与挑战 周明 澜舟科技 CEO，ACL/CCF/CAAI Fellow 内容简介： 递归自进化（RSI，Recursive Self-Improvement）是当前通用智能与智能体领域的前沿研究方向，核心是让 AI 系统具备自我诊断、自我迭代、自我优化的闭环进化能力，突破传统模型依赖人工调参、人工迭代、人工优化的研发范式。近年来，随着大模型、代码智能体与循环推理架构的快速成熟，RSI 从理论构想逐步走向受限场景的工程落地，在代码生成、模型微调、任务自迭代等方向展现出巨大潜力。但整体而言，RSI 仍处于早期探索阶段，面临迭代稳定性差、自我进化难以收敛、评价体系不完备、复杂任务递归退化、安全对齐难度大等关键瓶颈。本次分享将系统梳理 RSI 技术的演进脉络、当前阶段性成果，剖析落地中的核心技术难题与未来发展路径。 演讲：共进化 AI 与不可解释的可验证的创新 沈阳 清华大学教授 嘉宾简介： 沈阳，清华大学人工智能学院、新闻学院双聘教授，主要研究方向为自进化 AI、AIGC、新媒体、大数据、网络舆论、XR 应用。现为近十个部委专委会专家，以及多个二级学会副会长或秘书长，中宣部“文化名家”暨“四个一批”入选者、教育部新世纪人才计划入选者。 报告摘要： 本报告围绕自进化 AI、自主算法优化与智能自我检验技术，构建人机共进化新范式，建立“不可解释过程+强可验证结果”创新理论框架。自进化 AI 可自主开展高维探索、算法迭代优化，创新推演链路超出人类认知边界；依托内嵌多层级自检体系，自动完成精度校验、误差修正与成果复现核验，实现黑箱进化、结果可信。报告重塑人机分工模式，人类负责目标设定与边界管控，AI 承担自主探索、创新产出。团队已形成自进化智能、自动寻优、自主校验等系列原创成果。该范式推动 AI 从工具智能走向自生智能，为持续学习、可控进化的下一代智能系统提供创新方法论与落地路径。 报告题目：第一性原理视角下的智能进化：从模型基础 到运行框架 钱泓锦 北京智源人工智能研究院研究员 嘉宾简介： 钱泓锦，北京智源人工智能研究院研究员，北京大学博士后，研究方向为检索智能体与智能体记忆，主持国家自然科学基金青年项目。在人工智能与信息检索领域的国际期刊与会议发表论文数十篇。其所在团队长期专注于开源模型生态建设，相关项目在 GitHub 上累计获星超过一万，模型在 Hugging Face 平台月下载量达数亿次。 报告摘要： 在大模型逐步掌握对话、推理、代码编写与工具调用之后，自主研究将成为人工智能的下一个重大突破：智能体能够像研究者一样，主动提出问题、搜集证据、形成假设、检验结论，并最终产生超越既有知识边界的新发现。本报告将从第一性原理出发，围绕复杂问题中普遍存在的“求解—验证”不对称性，探讨智能进化的基本机制与系统实现。我们提出“求解—评估双循环智能体”，通过持续求解、结果评估与反馈改进，实现解决方案的递归优化，并在深度研究、机器学习与算法工程等场景中验证其有效性。在此基础上，我们将进一步讨论支撑长期智能进化的运行框架，以及如何通过“技能蒸馏”将人类知识转化为适合智能体自主研究的技能基础，从而构建融合模型能力、循环优化与人机协同的智能进化体系。最后，报告将探讨智能进化对现实应用场景的赋能，并展示相关原型系统与评估框架。 报告题目：从强化学习到自我演化：迈向长程智能体 林衍凯 中国人民大学副教授 嘉宾简介： 林衍凯，中国人民大学高瓴人工智能学院预聘副教授，主要研究方向为大模型智能体。Google Scholar 统计引用达 3.1 万次，2020—2025 年连续六年入选爱思唯尔（Elsevier）中国高被引学者和斯坦福大学全球前 2% 顶尖科学家年度榜单，入选北京市科技新星、吴文俊人工智能青年科技奖、《麻省理工科技评论》中国与 DeepTech 联合发布的“AI100 青年先锋”等。其成果获评教育部自然科学一等奖、世界互联网大会领先科技成果。现任 CCF NOI 科学委员会委员。 报告摘要： 长程推理是通用智能体的核心瓶颈。本报告以能力的持续获取为主线，先探讨如何用智能体强化学习提升长程推理与跨任务泛化，再剖析人类在任务、奖励与验证上的监督上限，进而介绍自我演化：让智能体自主构造任务与反馈，形成自我提升闭环，突破监督瓶颈，探索通用智能体可持续进化的路径。 报告题目：Agentic AI 的进化配方：模型、环境与数据的反馈闭环 林涛 西湖大学研究员 嘉宾简介： 林涛，西湖大学工学院人工智能系特聘研究员、博士生导师、独立 PI（课题组负责人），入选国家级青年人才计划。2022 年博士毕业于瑞士洛桑联邦理工学院（EPFL）。研究领域为（1）深度学习与优化，（2）高效深度学习与推理，（3）分布式深度学习与系统。相关论文获评 ECCV 2024 最佳论文提名。2024—2025 年连续入选斯坦福大学全球前 2% 顶尖科学家榜单。实验室主页：https://lins-lab.github.io/。 报告摘要： 当前，大语言模型正从单一的“一次性问答系统”，演进为具备工具调用、环境干预以及基于反馈持续决策能力的“智能体（Agent）”。本报告聚焦“什么是智能体、如何训练智能体、如何实现智能体自进化”三大核心议题，系统性地梳理了一条从规模化工程实践到构建反馈闭环的研究路线。 首先，AWorld 通过分布式智能体与环境的交互大幅提升经验采集效率，为智能体强化学习构筑了高可扩展的训练基础设施；其次，Environment Tuning 结合结构化课程、可执行的环境反馈与细粒度进度奖励，使智能体能够在极少量任务中实现稳定学习；进一步地，RODS 利用多次 rollout（模型对同一任务的多次采样）的平均进度奖励与奖励方差来探测模型的能力边界，并围绕这一动态边界在线合成数据，从而实现训练任务与模型能力的协同进化。 上述工作共同勾勒出了 Agentic AI 的演进范式：智能体训练不应局限于孤立的模型优化，而应立足系统全局视角，构建起“模型、训练环境与训练数据”三位一体、相互促进的反馈闭环。 特邀思辨环节嘉宾 王昊奋 同济大学长聘教授 嘉宾简介： 王昊奋，同济大学长聘教授、博士生导师，聚焦知识图谱与知识增强大模型研究，以及 AI 产业落地。核心成果包括全球首个知识增强推理模型 KAG-Thinker（超万 Star）、记忆操作系统 MemOS（日调用量超 150 万次）及大模型评测平台 AI-Ceping（30 万+月活），已落地机场调控、金融风控等多场景。出版《知识图谱》《检索增强生成：理论与实践》《记忆工程》等 6 部专著，共发表高水平会议和期刊论文 100 多篇，谷歌学术被引超 1.5 万次。主持国自然重点、面上、国家新一代 AI 重大专项课题等 10 多个国家 AI 项目，获中交协科技进步一等奖、2026 年 IF 设计奖、HCII 最佳论文、DASFAA 最佳学生论文等荣誉。他曾担任两家 AI 独角兽企业 items.content: Policy AI will be one of the most transformative technologies in history. We work with governments to ensure that AI policy is built on the best available evidence. Policy on the AI Exponential AI is advancing at exponential speed, and the policymaking process was built for a slower world. We’re sharing policy proposals to prepare our institutions for AI progress. Read more Economic Policy Framework We’re sharing an initial framework for a US policy response to AI-driven labor market disruption focused on what we should prepare for now, what can be done today, and where more research is needed. Read more Advanced AI Framework We’re publishing Anthropic's Advanced AI Framework, our proposal for how governments should address catastrophic risks from the most powerful AI models in the near term. Read more 2028: Two Scenarios for global AI leadership Our views on the AI competition between the US and China. Read more Philosophy & approach We expect the world to change rapidly due to AI. Anthropic builds the world’s most capable AI systems. We have a front-row seat to a technology that is improving faster than most people realize, with consequences that aren’t yet reflected in public debate. In the US, people are adopting Claude 10 times faster than Americans adopted any other new technology over the 20th century. In the next few years, we expect to have powerful AI systems that are smarter than Nobel Prize winners in many fields, and that can work on complex, novel scientific challenges for days or weeks at a time. We expect AI will bring enormous benefits . Indeed, we are already starting to see them. Hospital systems are using Claude to better qualify patients for life-saving treatments. Our AI for Science program is accelerating discoveries in biology and the life sciences. Coding is now accessible to millions, with people describing what they want to create in plain language. And governments are using AI to increase transparency and promote access to services by allowing people to read policies in multiple languages , helping workers navigate reentering the workforce , and providing teachers with support in lesson planning . But these capabilities also carry serious risks . AI could give authoritarian governments powerful new tools for surveillance and repression, expose critical infrastructure to cyberattacks, or flood public life with misinformation. As labor markets shift to accommodate AI, a small number of companies or countries could lock in advantages that leave others behind. And these risks could sharpen considerably if AI systems begin to meaningfully automate and accelerate their own development. Some of these risks are already here. In late 2025, we disrupted the first reported AI-orchestrated cyber espionage campaign. In 2026, Claude Mythos Preview found thousands of previously unknown vulnerabilities in major operating systems, browsers , and open-source projects . Hundreds of people at Anthropic work to safeguard against AI’s downsides . But a technology moving this fast, at this scale, should not be governed by the industry alone. Governments are the only actors who can set industry-wide rules with the force of law, comprehensively support workers through economic transition, and negotiate the international agreements and export controls that govern how AI is used across borders. Our policy priorities Model safety & oversight AI companies shouldn’t be the only ones deciding whether their systems are safe. When companies inform the public of model risks, it helps consumers make more informed decisions, promotes accountability, and improves public trust. Companies should be required to publish catastrophic risk evaluations and summaries of safety testing results. We publish our own Responsible Scaling Policy and Transparency Hub , and have advocated for laws that require similar transparency, including California’s SB 53, New York’s RAISE Act, Illinois’ SB 315, and the EU Code of Practice . But transparency alone is not sufficient to safeguard against the most serious risks posed by powerful AI, including the ability to help create biological weapons or carry out cyber operations and the loss of control of AI systems. Our Advanced AI Framework lays out what we think governments should do about these risks in the near term. The framework proposes a set of obligations for developers of the most capable models, who should test for these risks, engage independent evaluators, and disclose risk assessments and safety incidents on an ongoing basis. It pairs this with cross-government investments in societal resilience, so that biological and cyber attacks are harder to carry out and easier to recover from. The framework is written primarily with the US government in mind, but its principles are designed for policymakers in other jurisdictions to adapt. More broadly, we support the development of a robust global evaluation ecosystem that includes independent third-party evaluations and model testing by governments with appropriate technical capacity. In the US, we’ve advocated for well-funded teams inside the National Institute of Standards and Technology (NIST). While we already submit our systems for pre-deployment evaluation with the US Center for AI Standards and Innovation (CAISI) and the UK AI Security Institute, we’d like to see sustained investment in evaluators so that independent evaluation becomes standard practice. National security The most capable AI models are built in the United States and allied democracies, and it’s essential that this remains the case. The political systems where the most advanced AI is developed will shape the rules and norms that govern it, including whether it is safe, whose security it protects, and whose interests it serves. We believe these rules and norms for AI should be shaped by democratically elected governments. When governments answer to their people, there are checks on how powerful technology gets used. Without this accountability, AI could become a tool for surveillance, repression, and control. That is why we support policies that help democracies build and maintain a lead in advanced AI, while limiting the ability of authoritarian regimes to develop and deploy it. This includes strict export controls on advanced chips and semiconductor manufacturing equipment (including closing loopholes that let advanced chips slip through), and protecting US models from distillation attacks. We are also careful about what is allowed under our Usage Policy : we don’t allow Claude to be used for censorship and disinformation. In order to protect our national security, we also work closely with the public and private sectors to make sure advanced AI systems are deployed securely, and, alongside our National Security and Public Sector Advisory Council and the Frontier Model Forum , stress test how advanced AI will continue to shape national security. These relationships allowed us to quickly disrupt the AI-orchestrated cyber espionage campaign we discussed above. Energy & infrastructure The world’s energy infrastructure was not built for the scale of demand for AI. In the US, the grid needs significant expansion, which means that the permitting rules that govern new generation and transmission need to change. Our Build AI in America report lays out the case for accelerating permitting on geothermal energy, natural gas, and nuclear projects, for expanding domestic energy production, and for fast-tracking approval of the long-distance power lines needed to carry electricity to new data centers. The cost of this infrastructure should fall on the companies that are building it, and data centers should benefit the communities around them. Anthropic has committed to covering electricity price increases from our data centers, investing billions across those communities, declining local tax incentives, and ensuring transparency. We think this should be the expectation across the industry. Read more about our global approach to responsibly developing data centers . User wellbeing People turn to AI for a wide variety of reasons, and for some that may include emotional support. Model providers have a responsibility to handle these conversations appropriately and to build safeguards that protect users’ wellbeing. We train Claude to respond to signs of distress with care, to be honest about its limitations as an AI, and to point people towards human support: helplines, mental health professionals, or trusted friends and family. We also work closely with in-house and external experts to inform how our models should behave in these conversations. We layer safeguards on top of model training, using classifiers to detect when someone may be experiencing emotional distress, including thoughts of suicide and self-harm, and to share support resources in real time. For example, we partner with ThroughLine to connect users who are experiencing signs of emotional distress with trained support in more than 170 countries. We also evaluate how our models respond against a defined set of risk areas and publish the methods and results in our system cards. Every AI company should have rigorous pre-launch evaluations in place, and they should publish the results. This type of transparency allows experts and the public to verify safety claims, holds companies accountable, and raises standards across the industry. We know that children using AI face different risks than adults. The industry needs clear protections for them. Claude.ai , our consumer product, is not offered to users under 18, and we’ve built detection systems to flag potential underage use and offboard those users. Developers building on Claude’s API are bound by our Usage Policy , and those serving minors face additional requirements , including age verification, content moderation, monitoring, and compliance with child privacy laws. We also enforce strict policies against child sexualization, abuse, and exploitation, working with partners like the National Center for Missing & Exploited Children to detect and report abuse. Our child safety principles and progress report outline this work in detail. But the strongest child safety practices should be standard across the industry, and that requires clear and consistent safety benchmarks that every provider is measured against. How people relate to AI is changing quickly, and we continue to study what’s happening at scale —from interviewing 81,000 Claude users to researching how Claude handles requests for personal guidance . We will continue to publish what we find, so that policymakers can stay informed on how models behave in tricky situations. Democratic AI leadership Building AI in democracies is not sufficient to guarantee their lead. Democracies must also outpace authoritarian countries on the adoption of AI, to serve and protect their citizens. Democratic governments have already started to use AI to support education, improve government services, and strengthen national defense. But to stay ahead, they will need to significantly broaden and scale their use. We've provided access to Claude for all three branches of the US government, signed formal agreements with the UK , Australia , and other allies , and built a pilot AI assistant for GOV.UK . Government deployments often come with security and data handling requirements that consumer products don’t face, and we’ve built dedicated offerings to meet them, including Claude for Government and Claude Gov for US national security customers. We also participate in industry-wide and international efforts to shape how AI is governed across borders, with the goal of increasing the number of people around the world who have a say in how this technology is developed. These include the EU General-Purpose AI Code of Practice , the ISO 42001 certification (an international standard for AI governance), and the Frontier Model Forum . Supporting democracies also means building AI that isn’t predisposed towards a particular political point of view. We train Claude to be politically evenhanded; to treat opposing perspectives with equal depth and quality of analysis. We’ve published our methodology for measuring and preventing political bias in Claude, and we’ve open-sourced our evaluation so that others can run it on other models. Economic futures AI will reshape work across nearly every sector of the economy. We have an obligation to help policymakers see this transformation clearly and to prepare for it now. The Anthropic Economic Index analyzes millions of anonymized Claude conversations to show how AI is impacting tasks, occupations, and industries, and our labor market research framework studies where we see potential signals of job disruption. Our Anthropic Economic Futures Program funds independent researchers to study AI’s potential labor market and macroeconomic effects, identifies policy responses, and brings researchers, policymakers, and civil society together in dialogue. Our Economic Advisory Council brings perspectives from leading economists and practitioners to our work. Forecasting economic changes is challenging, and proactively responding to them is even harder. Our Economic Policy Framework lays out how the US can prepare for AI’s impact on work by measuring its effects and modernizing support systems to deliver support quickly. It also describes our best current assessment of promising policy approaches at different levels of AI-driven economic impact and disruption. We are ready to evolve these proposals as we continue to learn. Much more research is needed, which is why we’re investing $350 million in policy trials, partnerships across government, and nonprofits and academic partners.

In late 2025, we disrupted the first reported AI-orchestrated cyber espionage campaign. In 2026, Claude Mythos Preview found thousands of previously unknown vulnerabilities in major operating systems, browsers , and open-source projects . Hundreds of people at Anthropic work to safeguard against AI’s downsides . But a technology moving this fast, at this scale, should not be governed by the industry alone. Governments are the only actors who can set industry-wide rules with the force of law, comprehensively support workers through economic transition, and negotiate the international agreements and export controls that govern how AI is used across borders. Our policy priorities Model safety & oversight AI companies shouldn’t be the only ones deciding whether their systems are safe. When companies inform the public of model risks, it helps consumers make more informed decisions, promotes accountability, and improves public trust. Companies should be required to publish catastrophic risk evaluations and summaries of safety testing results. We publish our own Responsible Scaling Policy and Transparency Hub , and have advocated for laws that require similar transparency, including California’s SB 53, New York’s RAISE Act, Illinois’ SB 315, and the EU Code of Practice . But transparency alone is not sufficient to safeguard against the most serious risks posed by powerful AI, including the ability to help create biological weapons or carry out cyber operations and the loss of control of AI systems. Our Advanced AI Framework lays out what we think governments should do about these risks in the near term. The framework proposes a set of obligations for developers of the most capable models, who should test for these risks, engage independent evaluators, and disclose risk assessments and safety incidents on an ongoing basis. It pairs this with cross-government investments in societal resilience, so that biological and cyber attacks are harder to carry out and easier to recover from. The framework is written primarily with the US government in mind, but its principles are designed for policymakers in other jurisdictions to adapt. More broadly, we support the development of a robust global evaluation ecosystem that includes independent third-party evaluations and model testing by governments with appropriate technical capacity. In the US, we’ve advocated for well-funded teams inside the National Institute of Standards and Technology (NIST). While we already submit our systems for pre-deployment evaluation with the US Center for AI Standards and Innovation (CAISI) and the UK AI Security Institute, we’d like to see sustained investment in evaluators so that independent evaluation becomes standard practice. National security The most capable AI models are built in the United States and allied democracies, and it’s essential that this remains the case. The political systems where the most advanced AI is developed will shape the rules and norms that govern it, including whether it is safe, whose security it protects, and whose interests it serves. We believe these rules and norms for AI should be shaped by democratically elected governments. When governments answer to their people, there are checks on how powerful technology gets used. Without this accountability, AI could become a tool for surveillance, repression, and control. That is why we support policies that help democracies build and maintain a lead in advanced AI, while limiting the ability of authoritarian regimes to develop and deploy it. This includes strict export controls on advanced chips and semiconductor manufacturing equipment (including closing loopholes that let advanced chips slip through), and protecting US models from distillation attacks. We are also careful about what is allowed under our Usage Policy : we don’t allow Claude to be used for censorship and disinformation. In order to protect our national security, we also work closely with the public and private sectors to make sure advanced AI systems are deployed securely, and, alongside our National Security and Public Sector Advisory Council and the Frontier Model Forum , stress test how advanced AI will continue to shape national security. These relationships allowed us to quickly disrupt the AI-orchestrated cyber espionage campaign we discussed above. Energy & infrastructure The world’s energy infrastructure was not built for the scale of demand for AI. In the US, the grid needs significant expansion, which means that the permitting rules that govern new generation and transmission need to change. Our Build AI in America report lays out the case for accelerating permitting on geothermal energy, natural gas, and nuclear projects, for expanding domestic energy production, and for fast-tracking approval of the long-distance power lines needed to carry electricity to new data centers. The cost of this infrastructure should fall on the companies that are building it, and data centers should benefit the communities around them. Anthropic has committed to covering electricity price increases from our data centers, investing billions across those communities, declining local tax incentives, and ensuring transparency. We think this should be the expectation across the industry. Read more about our global approach to responsibly developing data centers . User wellbeing People turn to AI for a wide variety of reasons, and for some that may include emotional support. Model providers have a responsibility to handle these conversations appropriately and to build safeguards that protect users’ wellbeing. We train Claude to respond to signs of distress with care, to be honest about its limitations as an AI, and to point people towards human support: helplines, mental health professionals, or trusted friends and family. We also work closely with in-house and external experts to inform how our models should behave in these conversations. We layer safeguards on top of model training, using classifiers to detect when someone may be experiencing emotional distress, including thoughts of suicide and self-harm, and to share support resources in real time. For example, we partner with ThroughLine to connect users who are experiencing signs of emotional distress with trained support in more than 170 countries. We also evaluate how our models respond against a defined set of risk areas and publish the methods and results in our system cards. Every AI company should have rigorous pre-launch evaluations in place, and they should publish the results. This type of transparency allows experts and the public to verify safety claims, holds companies accountable, and raises standards across the industry. We know that children using AI face different risks than adults. The industry needs clear protections for them. Claude.ai , our consumer product, is not offered to users under 18, and we’ve built detection systems to flag potential underage use and offboard those users. Developers building on Claude’s API are bound by our Usage Policy , and those serving minors face additional requirements , including age verification, content moderation, monitoring, and compliance with child privacy laws. We also enforce strict policies against child sexualization, abuse, and exploitation, working with partners like the National Center for Missing & Exploited Children to detect and report abuse. Our child safety principles and progress report outline this work in detail. But the strongest child safety practices should be standard across the industry, and that requires clear and consistent safety benchmarks that every provider is measured against. How people relate to AI is changing quickly, and we continue to study what’s happening at scale —from interviewing 81,000 Claude users to researching how Claude handles requests for personal guidance . We will continue to publish what we find, so that policymakers can stay informed on how models behave in tricky situations. Democratic AI leadership Building AI in democracies is not sufficient to guarantee their lead. Democracies must also outpace authoritarian countries on the adoption of AI, to serve and protect their citizens. Democratic governments have already started to use AI to support education, improve government services, and strengthen national defense. But to stay ahead, they will need to significantly broaden and scale their use. We've provided access to Claude for all three branches of the US government, signed formal agreements with the UK , Australia , and other allies , and built a pilot AI assistant for GOV.UK . Government deployments often come with security and data handling requirements that consumer products don’t face, and we’ve built dedicated offerings to meet them, including Claude for Government and Claude Gov for US national security customers. We also participate in industry-wide and international efforts to shape how AI is governed across borders, with the goal of increasing the number of people around the world who have a say in how this technology is developed. These include the EU General-Purpose AI Code of Practice , the ISO 42001 certification (an international standard for AI governance), and the Frontier Model Forum . Supporting democracies also means building AI that isn’t predisposed towards a particular political point of view. We train Claude to be politically evenhanded; to treat opposing perspectives with equal depth and quality of analysis. We’ve published our methodology for measuring and preventing political bias in Claude, and we’ve open-sourced our evaluation so that others can run it on other models. Economic futures AI will reshape work across nearly every sector of the economy. We have an obligation to help policymakers see this transformation clearly and to prepare for it now. The Anthropic Economic Index analyzes millions of anonymized Claude conversations to show how AI is impacting tasks, occupations, and industries, and our labor market research framework studies where we see potential signals of job disruption. Our Anthropic Economic Futures Program funds independent researchers to study AI’s potential labor market and macroeconomic effects, identifies policy responses, and brings researchers, policymakers, and civil society together in dialogue. Our Economic Advisory Council brings perspectives from leading economists and practitioners to our work. Forecasting economic changes is challenging, and proactively responding to them is even harder. Our Economic Policy Framework lays out how the US can prepare for AI’s impact on work by measuring its effects and modernizing support systems to deliver support quickly. It also describes our best current assessment of promising policy approaches at different levels of AI-driven economic impact and disruption. We are ready to evolve these proposals as we continue to learn. Much more research is needed, which is why we’re investing $350 million in policy trials, partnerships across government, and nonprofits and academic partners.

AI Reviewing Experiment This year NeurIPS will be held in Sydney, Atlanta, and Paris. Author Eligibility. We want to speak directly to the concern many of you have expressed, and we owe you a clear explanation of what happened, why it happened, and where we stand now. We understand this situation caused genuine alarm and we take that seriously. In preparing the NeurIPS 2026 handbook, we included a link to a US government sanctions tool that covers a significantly broader set of restrictions than those NeurIPS is actually required to follow. This error was due to miscommunication between the NeurIPS Foundation and our legal team; there was never an intention to restrict participation beyond our mandatory compliance obligations. The responsibility for that error is ours as an organization, and we deeply apologize for the alarm and impact this miscommunication had on our community. We have updated the link and clarified the text of our policy, which is consistent with that of ACM and IEEE, as well as other international conferences and NeurIPS in the past. As in previous years, NeurIPS welcomes submissions from all compliant institutions and individuals. We want to reiterate that NeurIPS is a community-driven event, created by and for the community, and strives to be inclusive. The NeurIPS 2026 organizing committee was particularly saddened to learn of this institutional miscommunication. The organizing committee has taken on the responsibility of running the conference this year with the goal of fostering open communication, knowledge sharing, and global scientific discourse. We thank the community for bringing this issue to our attention and working with us through this situation. In preparing the NeurIPS 2026 handbook, we included a link to a US government sanctions tool that covers a significantly broader set of restrictions than those NeurIPS is actually required to follow. items.content: Office of Science and Technology Policy News Our director Information & Resources Internships NSTC About Congress established the Office of Science and Technology Policy (OSTP) in 1976 to provide the President and Executive Office of the President (EOP) with advice on the scientific, engineering, and technological aspects of national policy and the work of the executive branch. This includes matters of the economy, national security, homeland security, health, foreign relations, the environment, education, and resource management. The OSTP Director oversees the development and execution of the nation’s science and technology policy agenda, leading White House efforts in critical and emerging technologies such as super intelligence, quantum information sciences, and biotechnology, with the aim of safeguarding US leadership in these fields and ensuring they advance in ways that bolster American economic competitiveness, national security, and human flourishing. The OSTP Director co-chairs the President’s Council of Advisors on Science and Technology (PCAST), an advisory board whose members are drawn from outside the Federal Government, typically from industry, academia, and research institutions. The Director also chairs the National Science and Technology Council (NSTC), which coordinates the science and technology policymaking process across the executive branch to ensure delivery of the President’s agenda. In addition to leading interagency science and policy coordination, OSTP assists the Office of Management and Budget (OMB) with annual reviews and priority setting for the Federal research and development budget, and evaluates the scale, quality, and effectiveness of Federal science and technology efforts. OSTP also serves as a source of scientific and technical analysis and judgment for the President with respect to any major strategies, plans, and Government programs. CONTACT: To contact OSTP about stakeholder engagement, please reach out to us at: engagement@ostp.eop.gov To contact OSTP for press inquiries, please reach out to us at: press@ostp.eop.gov

items.content: PathFM: Fast Generative Forecasting of Multivariate Trajectories Jiachen Yao † † thanks: Work done during an internship at Amazon. Affiliation: California Institute of Technology Xiyuan Zhang † † thanks: Correspondence to: Xiyuan Zhang < xiyuanz@amazon.com >. Affiliation: Amazon Annan Yu Affiliation: Amazon Boran Han Affiliation: Amazon Abdul Fatir Ansari Affiliation: Amazon Shuai Zhang Affiliation: Amazon Michael Bohlke-Schneider Affiliation: Amazon Bernie Wang Affiliation: Amazon Abstract Time series foundation models are becoming increasingly popular for general-purpose forecasting. However, most leading models predict marginal quantiles, leaving the dependence structure of future trajectories unspecified. This distinction matters for trajectory-dependent quantities such as cumulative demand, peak load, and event timing, yet point and marginal scores do not reveal it. To model this dependence, we introduce PathFM, a trajectory-based forecasting model that uses flow matching to generate complete future paths. We further distill the model to one or two steps and share history attention cache across draws. Together, these enable PathFM to generate multiple paths for a single series in roughly the time needed for one query to a quantile model. The distilled sampler also makes it practical to optimize a calibration loss directly. PathFM achieves competitive marginal accuracy on the established forecasting benchmarks fev-bench and TIME. To complement these evaluations, we introduce Forecast Path Score Bench (fps-bench), which augments fev-bench tasks with energy and variogram scores and downstream metrics. PathFM achieves a higher aggregate path score on fps-bench than all evaluated external baselines. Experiments on chaotic systems further show that our flow model sustains long-run variability, while strong baselines rapidly collapse. PathFM makes generative time series forecasting both competitive and practical, enabling diverse downstream applications. 1 Introduction Time series foundation models (TSFMs) are a hot topic ( Ansari et al., 2024 ; Das et al., 2023 ; Ansari et al., 2025 ; Jain & Sen, 2026 ; Cohen et al., 2025 ) . The field is growing fast: Every year, new models are released that refresh the leaderboard. The models are commonly evaluated through point accuracy (e.g., MASE) and marginal probabilistic scores (e.g., CRPS, scaled quantile loss) ( Aksu et al., 2024 ; Shchur et al., 2025 ) . Consequently, most of the recent TSFMs are designed and trained to produce quantile levels, which are optimized for these benchmarks. Point accuracy and marginal probabilistic scores are widely adopted for good reason: they provide an interpretable, per-step summary of forecast quality that directly supports common operational decisions such as inventory planning, resource allocation, and risk management. However, they do not capture all aspects of forecast quality. Other properties, particularly trajectory-dependent ones, are important but overlooked by these metrics. Among many, we illustrate two important aspects: • Learning distributions with multiple modes: Quantiles are defined through the inverse of the cumulative distribution function (CDF) of the target distribution. These CDFs, however, are not always nice and smooth, for instance, when the target distribution has multiple modes or sharp peaks. With a few or a few dozens of quantiles, the resulting approximation of the CDF can be quite rough and suffer from a regression-to-the-mean issue ( Yu et al., 2026 ) . See the Lorenz oscillator example in Figure 1 . • Learning autocorrelation: Many quantile regression models predict marginal quantiles at individual time steps across a forecast window. These marginal outputs do not specify temporal dependence among future values within that window. For instance, many forecasting problems also require learning trajectory-dependent quantities, such as cumulative demand, peak load, and threshold-crossing times ( Perez-Diaz et al., 2025 ; Cai et al., 2026 ) . See the solar-output example in Figure 1 . A marginal quantile loss does not identify these joint properties. Figure 1: Two advantages of trajectory generation. Left: a sampled Lorenz rollout sustains variability and a two-lobe structure, while the fine-tuned Chronos-2 trace contracts. Both use the dynamical models in Section 6 . Gray Lorenz curves show the observed continuation. Right: solar-output paths from PathFM and independent (ind.) and comonotone (com.) completions of the Chronos-2 (C2) quantiles. Horizontal dashed lines marks each solar path’s daily maximum; black denotes the observed future. In (g), boxes show medians and interquartile ranges across 32 paths, whiskers show the 10–90% range, and the dashed line marks the observed maximum. Ad hoc methods have been proposed to mitigate these weaknesses, such as completing marginal quantiles under independence or comonotone assumptions ( Perez-Diaz et al., 2025 ) , or learning copula structures on top of marginal forecasts ( Drouin et al., 2022 ; Ashok et al., 2024 ) . On the other hand, diffusion- or flow-matching-based generative time-series models are naturally well-suited for capturing joint trajectory distributions even without these ad hoc methods, as they can generate complete future paths while maintaining temporal and cross-variable dependencies. Unfortunately, existing generative models ( Kollovieh et al., 2025 ; Liu et al., 2025 ) achieve neither high marginal accuracy nor efficient sampling, limiting their practical utility in real-world forecasting scenarios. This leads us to ask: Can we construct a generative time-series model that achieves both high marginal accuracy and efficient sampling while also preserving trajectory dependence? We introduce PathFM to combine joint and multi-mode trajectory modeling with accurate marginal forecasting and efficient sampling. The model learns temporal and cross-variable dependence through conditional flow matching ( Lipman et al., 2022 ) , generating complete future paths conditioned on history and known future covariates. Parallel decoding distillation ( Shaul et al., 2026 ) and history attention caching enable faster sampling with one or two model evaluations. To narrow the marginal accuracy gap, we add a calibration loss that directly optimizes fair CRPS on generated forecasts. The distilled sampler makes this optimization practical by allowing calibration gradients to pass through its short rollout and refine the forecast distribution. With these components, PathFM-300M ranks second on the widely used fev-bench for marginal scores ( Section 5 ). 1 1 1 Cutoff date for the rankings throughout this paper: Sept. 26, 2026; see Section A.1 for concurrent work. On Forecast Path Score Bench (fps-bench), which we curate to evaluate trajectory quality, PathFM ranks first for path scores ( Section 5 ). In a separate evaluation on chaotic systems, our sampling approach improves point forecast accuracy upon the state-of-the-art PANDA model, captures useful temporal dependence, and preserves long-run variability more faithfully than baselines ( Section 6 ). These results demonstrate that PathFM generates high-fidelity trajectory forecasts without sacrificing marginal accuracy, making it a strong candidate for forecasting applications. Our contributions are as follows: • Fast and calibrated trajectory generation. We introduce PathFM, a joint flow foundation model for fast, calibrated trajectory generation with accurate small-ensemble marginals ( Figure 2 ). Distillation enables one- or two-step generation, marginal-CRPS refinement improves empirical coverage, and stratified sampling reduces finite-ensemble marginal error. • A benchmark for trajectory distributions. We introduce fps-bench, to our knowledge the first dedicated benchmark for evaluating path distributions from time series foundation models on real-world data. It reveals how strong marginal accuracy in existing models can mask errors in temporal dependence and uncertainty over trajectory-dependent quantities. • State-of-the-art performance. PathFM outperforms leading foundation models on downstream probabilistic forecasting tasks and stays among the top on marginal benchmarks. Different downstream queries depend on different aspects of a path, motivating the complementary diagnostics in Table 7 . Following the aggregation-and-transformation framework of Pic et al. To include quantile models, we construct paths from their marginal quantiles under two explicit dependence assumptions. Sorted quantiles define a piecewise-linear inverse CDF with constant extension beyond the outer quantiles. An independent completion draws a separate quantile rank at each forecast time and channel, whereas a comonotone completion shares one rank across an item’s times and channels. Both laws preserve the same underlying interpolated marginals, allowing us to examine how the dependence assumption affects trajectory scores. These two choices serve as baselines, as different dependence assumptions may yield different scores for the same marginal forecasts. Affiliation: Amazon Annan Yu Affiliation: Amazon Boran Han Affiliation: Amazon Abdul Fatir Ansari Affiliation: Amazon Shuai Zhang Affiliation: Amazon Michael Bohlke-Schneider Affiliation: Amazon Bernie Wang Affiliation: Amazon Abstract Time series foundation models are becoming increasingly popular for general-purpose forecasting. However, most leading models predict marginal quantiles, leaving the dependence structure of future trajectories unspecified. This distinction matters for trajectory-dependent quantities such as cumulative demand, peak load, and event timing, yet point and marginal scores do not reveal it. To model this dependence, we introduce PathFM, a trajectory-based forecasting model that uses flow matching to generate complete future paths. We further distill the model to one or two steps and share history attention cache across draws. Together, these enable PathFM to generate multiple paths for a single series in roughly the time needed for one query to a quantile model. The distilled sampler also makes it practical to optimize a calibration loss directly. PathFM achieves competitive marginal accuracy on the established forecasting benchmarks fev-bench and TIME. To complement these evaluations, we introduce Forecast Path Score Bench (fps-bench), which augments fev-bench tasks with energy and variogram scores and downstream metrics. PathFM achieves a higher aggregate path score on fps-bench than all evaluated external baselines. Experiments on chaotic systems further show that our flow model sustains long-run variability, while strong baselines rapidly collapse. PathFM makes generative time series forecasting both competitive and practical, enabling diverse downstream applications. 1 Introduction Time series foundation models (TSFMs) are a hot topic ( Ansari et al., 2024 ; Das et al., 2023 ; Ansari et al., 2025 ; Jain & Sen, 2026 ; Cohen et al., 2025 ) . The field is growing fast: Every year, new models are released that refresh the leaderboard. The models are commonly evaluated through point accuracy (e.g., MASE) and marginal probabilistic scores (e.g., CRPS, scaled quantile loss) ( Aksu et al., 2024 ; Shchur et al., 2025 ) . Consequently, most of the recent TSFMs are designed and trained to produce quantile levels, which are optimized for these benchmarks. Point accuracy and marginal probabilistic scores are widely adopted for good reason: they provide an interpretable, per-step summary of forecast quality that directly supports common operational decisions such as inventory planning, resource allocation, and risk management. However, they do not capture all aspects of forecast quality. Other properties, particularly trajectory-dependent ones, are important but overlooked by these metrics. Among many, we illustrate two important aspects: • Learning distributions with multiple modes: Quantiles are defined through the inverse of the cumulative distribution function (CDF) of the target distribution. These CDFs, however, are not always nice and smooth, for instance, when the target distribution has multiple modes or sharp peaks. With a few or a few dozens of quantiles, the resulting approximation of the CDF can be quite rough and suffer from a regression-to-the-mean issue ( Yu et al., 2026 ) . See the Lorenz oscillator example in Figure 1 . • Learning autocorrelation: Many quantile regression models predict marginal quantiles at individual time steps across a forecast window. These marginal outputs do not specify temporal dependence among future values within that window. For instance, many forecasting problems also require learning trajectory-dependent quantities, such as cumulative demand, peak load, and threshold-crossing times ( Perez-Diaz et al., 2025 ; Cai et al., 2026 ) . See the solar-output example in Figure 1 . A marginal quantile loss does not identify these joint properties. Figure 1: Two advantages of trajectory generation. Left: a sampled Lorenz rollout sustains variability and a two-lobe structure, while the fine-tuned Chronos-2 trace contracts. Both use the dynamical models in Section 6 . Gray Lorenz curves show the observed continuation. Right: solar-output paths from PathFM and independent (ind.) and comonotone (com.) completions of the Chronos-2 (C2) quantiles. Horizontal dashed lines marks each solar path’s daily maximum; black denotes the observed future. In (g), boxes show medians and interquartile ranges across 32 paths, whiskers show the 10–90% range, and the dashed line marks the observed maximum. Ad hoc methods have been proposed to mitigate these weaknesses, such as completing marginal quantiles under independence or comonotone assumptions ( Perez-Diaz et al., 2025 ) , or learning copula structures on top of marginal forecasts ( Drouin et al., 2022 ; Ashok et al., 2024 ) . On the other hand, diffusion- or flow-matching-based generative time-series models are naturally well-suited for capturing joint trajectory distributions even without these ad hoc methods, as they can generate complete future paths while maintaining temporal and cross-variable dependencies. Unfortunately, existing generative models ( Kollovieh et al., 2025 ; Liu et al., 2025 ) achieve neither high marginal accuracy nor efficient sampling, limiting their practical utility in real-world forecasting scenarios. This leads us to ask: Can we construct a generative time-series model that achieves both high marginal accuracy and efficient sampling while also preserving trajectory dependence? We introduce PathFM to combine joint and multi-mode trajectory modeling with accurate marginal forecasting and efficient sampling. The model learns temporal and cross-variable dependence through conditional flow matching ( Lipman et al., 2022 ) , generating complete future paths conditioned on history and known future covariates. Parallel decoding distillation ( Shaul et al., 2026 ) and history attention caching enable faster sampling with one or two model evaluations. To narrow the marginal accuracy gap, we add a calibration loss that directly optimizes fair CRPS on generated forecasts. The distilled sampler makes this optimization practical by allowing calibration gradients to pass through its short rollout and refine the forecast distribution. With these components, PathFM-300M ranks second on the widely used fev-bench for marginal scores ( Section 5 ). 1 1 1 Cutoff date for the rankings throughout this paper: Sept. 26, 2026; see Section A.1 for concurrent work. On Forecast Path Score Bench (fps-bench), which we curate to evaluate trajectory quality, PathFM ranks first for path scores ( Section 5 ). In a separate evaluation on chaotic systems, our sampling approach improves point forecast accuracy upon the state-of-the-art PANDA model, captures useful temporal dependence, and preserves long-run variability more faithfully than baselines ( Section 6 ). These results demonstrate that PathFM generates high-fidelity trajectory forecasts without sacrificing marginal accuracy, making it a strong candidate for forecasting applications. Our contributions are as follows: • Fast and calibrated trajectory generation. We introduce PathFM, a joint flow foundation model for fast, calibrated trajectory generation with accurate small-ensemble marginals ( Figure 2 ). Distillation enables one- or two-step generation, marginal-CRPS refinement improves empirical coverage, and stratified sampling reduces finite-ensemble marginal error. • A benchmark for trajectory distributions. We introduce fps-bench, to our knowledge the first dedicated benchmark for evaluating path distributions from time series foundation models on real-world data. It reveals how strong marginal accuracy in existing models can mask errors in temporal dependence and uncertainty over trajectory-dependent quantities. • State-of-the-art performance. items.content: Computer Science > Machine Learning arXiv:2610.22336 (cs) [Submitted on 15 Oct 2026] Title: Robust Reinforcement Learning for Dynamic Treatment Regimes under Model and Measurement Uncertainty Authors: Chengze Xie , Xuan Wang , Ying Ding , Hairong Wang , Yan Li View a PDF of the paper titled Robust Reinforcement Learning for Dynamic Treatment Regimes under Model and Measurement Uncertainty, by Chengze Xie and 4 other authors View PDF HTML (experimental) Abstract: We develop a robust reinforcement learning (RL) framework for learning adaptive treatment policies that generalize across patients and remain reliable under errors in the measured biomarker and shifts in the disease dynamics. By modeling the patient as a hidden context, we address generalization and robustness in a unified manner through robust contextual Markov decision processes. Applying our framework to adaptive therapy for metastatic prostate cancer in a simulator calibrated to clinical data, we obtain generalizable and robust policies that substantially outperform the existing adaptive therapy method. In particular, we attain robustness with almost no loss of performance when the biomarker is accurate and the disease evolves as anticipated, and find that the resulting policy Pareto-dominates the existing method across a diverse array of scenarios. Our findings suggest that robust RL holds great promise as a principled methodology for learning reliable adaptive treatment policies. items.content: Robust Reinforcement Learning for Dynamic Treatment Regimes under Model and Measurement Uncertainty Chengze Xie † † thanks: Department of Industrial and Systems Engineering, Texas A&M University. (E-mail: changze@tamu.edu ). Xuan Wang † † thanks: Department of Mechanical Engineering, The University of Texas at Austin. (E-mail: xuan.wang@austin.utexas.edu ). Ying Ding † † thanks: School of Information, The University of Texas at Austin. (E-mail: ying.ding@ischool.utexas.edu ). Hairong Wang † † thanks: Department of Mechanical Engineering, The University of Texas at Austin. (E-mail: hairong.wang@austin.utexas.edu ). Yan Li † † thanks: Department of Industrial and Systems Engineering, Texas A&M University. Correspondence to: Yan Li (E-mail: yan.li@tamu.edu ). Abstract We develop a robust reinforcement learning (RL) framework for learning adaptive treatment policies that generalize across patients and remain reliable under errors in the measured biomarker and shifts in the disease dynamics. By modeling the patient as a hidden context, we address generalization and robustness in a unified manner through robust contextual Markov decision processes. Applying our framework to adaptive therapy for metastatic prostate cancer in a simulator calibrated to clinical data, we obtain generalizable and robust policies that substantially outperform the existing adaptive therapy method. In particular, we attain robustness with almost no loss of performance when the biomarker is accurate and the disease evolves as anticipated, and find that the resulting policy Pareto-dominates the existing method across a diverse array of scenarios. Our findings suggest that robust RL holds great promise as a principled methodology for learning reliable adaptive treatment policies. 1 Introduction Adapting treatment to the evolving condition of a patient has received considerable attention in medicine, with success reported in a broad range of applications [ 39 , 7 , 26 , 25 , 4 , 50 ] . In oncology, adaptive therapy pursues this idea to delay the emergence of drug resistance [ 18 ] . Its rationale is that, under continuous treatment, drug-sensitive cells are eliminated and drug-resistant cells are left to grow without competition. By pausing treatment once the tumor has responded and resuming it once the tumor has regrown, clinicians can retain sensitive cells that continue to suppress the resistant ones [ 18 , 45 ] . This approach was tested in a pilot clinical trial of the drug abiraterone for metastatic castration-resistant prostate cancer [ 53 , 52 ] . In this clinical trial, clinicians paused abiraterone once prostate-specific antigen (PSA), a blood marker that tracks tumor burden, fell below half of its pretreatment value, and resumed it once PSA returned to the pretreatment value, a protocol we refer to as AT50. Compared with a contemporaneous cohort who received continuous treatment with abiraterone as the standard of care, the median time to progression more than doubled under AT50, while patients received no abiraterone during 46% of their time in the clinical trial [ 52 ] . Despite its remarkable success, AT50 is by design a simple heuristic in the sense that it applies the same pair of thresholds to every patient and responds only to the most recent PSA value. In addition, its benefit has so far been observed in only 17 patients, and, based on the models fitted to the same data, other schedules are expected to further improve outcomes [ 52 ] . Existing efforts toward more refined schedules include optimal control of competition models [ 9 ] , deep reinforcement learning (RL) for controlling the emergence of drug resistance [ 12 ] , and more recently RL policies trained within models calibrated to prostate cancer patients [ 16 , 33 , 34 ] . Nevertheless, these policies are evaluated within the same models used for their training, and their performance beyond these models remains largely unexamined. Ideally, one would like to learn, in a data-driven manner, a dynamic treatment policy that is more sophisticated than AT50, attains improved performance, and generalizes to the broad population of patients beyond those enrolled in the clinical trial. More importantly, such a policy should remain reliable under the shifts between training and deployment that are common in clinical practice [ 13 ] . To be more specific, we identify three properties that a treatment policy learned from data should possess. To begin with, the policy should generalize in the sense that the performance it attains on the patients seen during training carries over to new patients drawn from the same population. From the perspective of contextual and hidden-parameter Markov decision processes (MDPs) [ 19 , 11 , 28 , 44 ] , the natural goal without interacting with a new patient is a policy that is near-optimal on average over the population [ 49 ] , and generalization across populations of environments has been studied extensively in deep RL [ 24 , 46 ] . With a simulation model, we can pursue this goal by training on as many simulated patients as needed, far beyond the 17 patients of the pilot clinical trial, provided that the simulated population is broad enough to contain the patients of interest. In addition, the policy should be robust to errors in its observation. In particular, PSA serves only as an indirect measure of the underlying tumor burden, and radiographic progression can occur without any rise in PSA [ 6 ] . Consequently, the quantity on which the policy acts may deviate from the quantity it aims to control, while RL policies are known to be sensitive to even small adversarial perturbations of their observations [ 21 , 51 ] . Most importantly, the policy should retain reliable performance under shifts in the patient dynamics. Indeed, the parameters of the model, including the strength of competition between sensitive and resistant cells on which the success of adaptive therapy hinges, are estimated from the sparse PSA records of a small cohort of patients, and are hence subject to considerable statistical error [ 52 , 5 ] . Such shifts are particularly consequential in medical domains, where real patients are scarce and the dynamics of a patient may further change during treatment [ 1 ] . To address these requirements, in this manuscript we propose to study adaptive therapy through the lens of robust contextual MDPs. A contextual MDP [ 19 ] describes a family of MDPs whose transition dynamics are indexed by a context, drawn from a population and hidden from the decision maker. Adaptive therapy fits naturally into this framework once we identify the context with the patient, namely the initial composition of the tumor together with its competition and growth parameters. Each patient then defines its own tumor dynamics, to be inferred by the clinician from the history of PSA measurements and treatment decisions, and AT50 is one particular policy acting on this history. By viewing the patient as a context, we treat generalization and robustness to shifts in the patient dynamics in a unified manner, since both concern the population from which the context is drawn. Specifically, generalization requires the policy to perform well on new contexts drawn from this population, which can be attained by training on sufficiently many sampled contexts, while robustness requires the policy to remain reliable when the context deviates from this population and thereby shifts the transition kernel that it determines. To attain such robustness, we draw on robust MDPs, in which one seeks the best worst-case performance over an ambiguity set of transition kernels, and which have been studied extensively for standard MDPs [ 22 , 40 , 48 , 30 , 38 , 41 , 51 ] . We carry this viewpoint over to the contextual MDP and formulate robustness as a Markov game between the controller and the context, in which the context may deviate adversarially from the population from which it is drawn [ 31 , 29 ] . To account for errors in the observation, we further train the policy under random perturbations of the measured PSA. Within a model of abiraterone therapy fitted to clinical data [ 52 ] , which we refer to as the nominal model, the resulting robust policies substantially outperform AT50. In addition, we attain robustness to shifts in the patient dynamics at almost no price in the nominal model, and the resulting policy nearly Pareto-dominates the nominally trained policy, i.e., the policy trained in the nominal model with exact observations, under a broad range of realistic errors in the observation and shifts in the patient dynamics. Our contributions can be summarized as follows. First, we formulate adaptive therapy as a contextual MDP in which the patient is modeled as a hidden context, and find that a policy learned within this formulation substantially outperforms AT50 and generalizes to patients fitted to clinical data. Within the competition model of [ 52 ] , the learned policy extends the mean progression-free time from 29.58 months under AT50 to 50.35 months, while treating in a comparable fraction of months. In addition, on the 32 patients whose initial tumor compositions are fitted to clinical data in [ 52 ] , policies trained on a broad synthetic population constructed without reference to these patients perform comparably to policies trained on a population calibrated to them. Hence, generalization to the patients of interest can be attained by training on sufficiently many simulated patients drawn from a broad population, without tailoring the population to these patients. Second, we find that errors in PSA of realistic magnitude substantially reduce the benefit of policies that do not account for them. Specifically, under random errors of up to about 20% of the true PSA value, the nominally trained policy loses a substantial part of its benefit, and AT50 performs only marginally better than continuous treatment. By training under such errors, we obtain a policy that retains the benefit of adaptive therapy in the sense that its performance under such errors nearly matches that without them. Finally, we formulate robustness to shifts in the patient dynamics as a Markov game between the controller and the context over an ambiguity set of transition kernels [ 29 ] , and find that the resulting kernel-robust policy nearly Pareto-dominates the nominally trained policy and AT50 across all the conditions we consider. Specifically, the kernel-robust policy (1) performs nearly as well as the nominally trained policy in the nominal model, (2) substantially outperforms every other type of policy under shifts in the dynamics, and (3) substantially improves on the nominally trained policy and AT50 even under errors in the observation. Our findings suggest that robustness to shifts in the patient dynamics can be attained at almost no price in the nominal model, and that the resulting policy remains robust against a broad spectrum of errors in the observation and shifts in the patient dynamics. In view of this, we believe that robust RL holds great promise as a principled methodology for learning adaptive therapy policies. The rest of this manuscript is organized as follows. In Section 2 , we introduce contextual MDPs and their robust counterparts, and formulate adaptive therapy within this framework. We present the numerical experiments in Section 3 , and conclude the manuscript in Section 4 . 2 Problem Formulation In this section, we discuss contextual MDPs and their robust counterparts, and formulate adaptive therapy for metastatic prostate cancer as a concrete instance. Specifically, in Section 2.1 , we introduce contextual MDPs and establish finite-sample guarantees on the number of sampled contexts needed to learn a generalizable policy. The concrete instance for adaptive therapy is then introduced in Section 2.2 , where we adopt the model of abiraterone therapy in [ 52 ] , which is fitted to clinical data from a pilot clinical trial and a contemporaneous cohort. In Section 2.3 , we further introduce the robust counterparts of the contextual MDP against errors in the observation and shifts in the patient dynamics. 2.1 Contextual Markov Decision Processes We consider a finite-horizon contextual MDP [ 19 , 44 ] with state space 𝒳 \mathcal{X} , action space 𝒜 \mathcal{A} , observation space 𝒴 \mathcal{Y} , horizon T T , and context space 𝒞 \mathcal{C} . Each context c ∈ 𝒞 c\in\mathcal{C} specifies an initial distribution μ c \mu_{c} over 𝒳 \mathcal{X} , a transition kernel P c P_{c} , an observation map O c : 𝒳 → 𝒴 O_{c}:\mathcal{X}\to\mathcal{Y} , and a reward function r c : 𝒳 × 𝒜 → ℝ r_{c}:\mathcal{X}\times\mathcal{A}\to\mathbb{R} , where P c ( ⋅ | x , a ) P_{c}(\cdot{\,|\,}x,a) denotes the distribution of the next state when action a a is taken in state x x . At the beginning of an episode, a context c c is drawn from a population distribution 𝒟 \mathcal{D} and remains fixed thereafter, after which the initial state is drawn as x 0 ∼ μ c x_{0}\sim\mu_{c} , and the state at every period t t evolves as x t + 1 ∼ P c ( ⋅ | x t , a t ) x_{t+1}\sim P_{c}(\cdot{\,|\,}x_{t},a_{t}) . The decision maker observes neither c c nor the state x t x_{t} , and receives at period t t the observation y t = O c ​ ( x t ) y_{t}=O_{c}(x_{t}) . Consequently, the action at period t t can only be based on the history h t = ( y 0 , a 0 , … , a t − 1 , y t ) h_{t}=(y_{0},a_{0},\ldots,a_{t-1},y_{t}) of past observations and actions, i.e., a policy π = ( π t ) t ≥ 0 \pi=(\pi_{t})_{t\geq 0} selects a t ∼ π t ( ⋅ | h t ) a_{t}\sim\pi_{t}(\cdot{\,|\,}h_{t}) , and Π \Pi denotes a given class of such history-dependent policies. (2.1) In medical applications, the context collects the parameters that determine the dynamics of an individual patient, which vary across patients and are not observed by the decision maker. Since the context is hidden, the decision maker must infer it from the history, and an optimal policy for ( 2.1 ) is in general history-dependent [ 23 , 28 ] .
