Abstract We develop a robust reinforcement learning (RL) framework for learning adaptive treatment policies that generalize across patients and remain reliable under errors in the measured biomarker and shifts in the disease dynamics. By modeling the patient as a hidden context, we address generalization and robustness in a unified manner through robust contextual Markov decision processes. Applying our framework to adaptive therapy for metastatic prostate cancer in a simulator calibrated to clinical data, we obtain generalizable and robust policies that substantially outperform the existing adaptive therapy method. In particular, we attain robustness with almost no loss of performance when the biomarker is accurate and the disease evolves as anticipated, and find that the resulting policy Pareto-dominates the existing method across a diverse array of scenarios. Our findings suggest that robust RL holds great promise as a principled methodology for learning reliable adaptive treatment policies. 1 Introduction Adapting treatment to the evolving condition of a patient has received considerable attention in medicine, with success reported in a broad range of applications [ 39 , 7 , 26 , 25 , 4 , 50 ] . In oncology, adaptive therapy pursues this idea to delay the emergence of drug resistance [ 18 ] . Its rationale is that, under continuous treatment, drug-sensitive cells are eliminated and drug-resistant cells are left to grow without competition. By pausing treatment once the tumor has responded and resuming it once the tumor has regrown, clinicians can retain sensitive cells that continue to suppress the resistant ones [ 18 , 45 ] . This approach was tested in a pilot clinical trial of the drug abiraterone for metastatic castration-resistant prostate cancer [ 53 , 52 ] . In this clinical trial, clinicians paused abiraterone once prostate-specific antigen (PSA), a blood marker that tracks tumor burden, fell below half of its pretreatment value, and resumed it once PSA returned to the pretreatment value, a protocol we refer to as AT50. Compared with a contemporaneous cohort who received continuous treatment with abiraterone as the standard of care, the median time to progression more than doubled under AT50, while patients received no abiraterone during 46% of their time in the clinical trial [ 52 ] . Despite its remarkable success, AT50 is by design a simple heuristic in the sense that it applies the same pair of thresholds to every patient and responds only to the most recent PSA value. In addition, its benefit has so far been observed in only 17 patients, and, based on the models fitted to the same data, other schedules are expected to further improve outcomes [ 52 ] . Existing efforts toward more refined schedules include optimal control of competition models [ 9 ] , deep reinforcement learning (RL) for controlling the emergence of drug resistance [ 12 ] , and more recently RL policies trained within models calibrated to prostate cancer patients [ 16 , 33 , 34 ] . Nevertheless, these policies are evaluated within the same models used for their training, and their performance beyond these models remains largely unexamined. Ideally, one would like to learn, in a data-driven manner, a dynamic treatment policy that is more sophisticated than AT50, attains improved performance, and generalizes to the broad population of patients beyond those enrolled in the clinical trial. More importantly, such a policy should remain reliable under the shifts between training and deployment that are common in clinical practice [ 13 ] . To be more specific, we identify three properties that a treatment policy learned from data should possess. To begin with, the policy should generalize in the sense that the performance it attains on the patients seen during training carries over to new patients drawn from the same population. From the perspective of contextual and hidden-parameter Markov decision processes (MDPs) [ 19 , 11 , 28 , 44 ] , the natural goal without interacting with a new patient is a policy that is near-optimal on average over the population [ 49 ] , and generalization across populations of environments has been studied extensively in deep RL [ 24 , 46 ] . With a simulation model, we can pursue this goal by training on as many simulated patients as needed, far beyond the 17 patients of the pilot clinical trial, provided that the simulated population is broad enough to contain the patients of interest. In addition, the policy should be robust to errors in its observation. In particular, PSA serves only as an indirect measure of the underlying tumor burden, and radiographic progression can occur without any rise in PSA [ 6 ] . Consequently, the quantity on which the policy acts may deviate from the quantity it aims to control, while RL policies are known to be sensitive to even small adversarial perturbations of their observations [ 21 , 51 ] . Most importantly, the policy should retain reliable performance under shifts in the patient dynamics. Indeed, the parameters of the model, including the strength of competition between sensitive and resistant cells on which the success of adaptive therapy hinges, are estimated from the sparse PSA records of a small cohort of patients, and are hence subject to considerable statistical error [ 52 , 5 ] . Such shifts are particularly consequential in medical domains, where real patients are scarce and the dynamics of a patient may further change during treatment [ 1 ] . To address these requirements, in this manuscript we propose to study adaptive therapy through the lens of robust contextual MDPs. A contextual MDP [ 19 ] describes a family of MDPs whose transition dynamics are indexed by a context, drawn from a population and hidden from the decision maker. Adaptive therapy fits naturally into this framework once we identify the context with the patient, namely the initial composition of the tumor together with its competition and growth parameters. Each patient then defines its own tumor dynamics, to be inferred by the clinician from the history of PSA measurements and treatment decisions, and AT50 is one particular policy acting on this history. By viewing the patient as a context, we treat generalization and robustness to shifts in the patient dynamics in a unified manner, since both concern the population from which the context is drawn. Specifically, generalization requires the policy to perform well on new contexts drawn from this population, which can be attained by training on sufficiently many sampled contexts, while robustness requires the policy to remain reliable when the context deviates from this population and thereby shifts the transition kernel that it determines. To attain such robustness, we draw on robust MDPs, in which one seeks the best worst-case performance over an ambiguity set of transition kernels, and which have been studied extensively for standard MDPs [ 22 , 40 , 48 , 30 , 38 , 41 , 51 ] . We carry this viewpoint over to the contextual MDP and formulate robustness as a Markov game between the controller and the context, in which the context may deviate adversarially from the population from which it is drawn [ 31 , 29 ] . To account for errors in the observation, we further train the policy under random perturbations of the measured PSA. Within a model of abiraterone therapy fitted to clinical data [ 52 ] , which we refer to as the nominal model, the resulting robust policies substantially outperform AT50. In addition, we attain robustness to shifts in the patient dynamics at almost no price in the nominal model, and the resulting policy nearly Pareto-dominates the nominally trained policy, i.e., the policy trained in the nominal model with exact observations, under a broad range of realistic errors in the observation and shifts in the patient dynamics. Our contributions can be summarized as follows. First, we formulate adaptive therapy as a contextual MDP in which the patient is modeled as a hidden context, and find that a policy learned within this formulation substantially outperforms AT50 and generalizes to patients fitted to clinical data. Within the competition model of [ 52 ] , the learned policy extends the mean progression-free time from 29.58 months under AT50 to 50.35 months, while treating in a comparable fraction of months. In addition, on the 32 patients whose initial tumor compositions are fitted to clinical data in [ 52 ] , policies trained on a broad synthetic population constructed without reference to these patients perform comparably to policies trained on a population calibrated to them. Hence, generalization to the patients of interest can be attained by training on sufficiently many simulated patients drawn from a broad population, without tailoring the population to these patients. Second, we find that errors in PSA of realistic magnitude substantially reduce the benefit of policies that do not account for them. Specifically, under random errors of up to about 20% of the true PSA value, the nominally trained policy loses a substantial part of its benefit, and AT50 performs only marginally better than continuous treatment. By training under such errors, we obtain a policy that retains the benefit of adaptive therapy in the sense that its performance under such errors nearly matches that without them. Finally, we formulate robustness to shifts in the patient dynamics as a Markov game between the controller and the context over an ambiguity set of transition kernels [ 29 ] , and find that the resulting kernel-robust policy nearly Pareto-dominates the nominally trained policy and AT50 across all the conditions we consider. Specifically, the kernel-robust policy (1) performs nearly as well as the nominally trained policy in the nominal model, (2) substantially outperforms every other type of policy under shifts in the dynamics, and (3) substantially improves on the nominally trained policy and AT50 even under errors in the observation. Our findings suggest that robustness to shifts in the patient dynamics can be attained at almost no price in the nominal model, and that the resulting policy remains robust against a broad spectrum of errors in the observation and shifts in the patient dynamics. In view of this, we believe that robust RL holds great promise as a principled methodology for learning adaptive therapy policies. The rest of this manuscript is organized as follows. In adaptive therapy, treatment is instead paused before such depletion occurs, which allows the sensitive cells to recover during the treatment break and to continue suppressing the resistant ones. items.title: Make America Healthy Again
items.summary: Make america healthy again President Trump launched the Make America Healthy Again initiative to confront chronic disease, improve nutrition, and lower healthcare costs. This year, the administration advanced reforms targeting childhood health, food quality, and preventive care while increasing transparency and accountability in healthcare systems. These actions are laying the foundation for a healthier, stronger America. By prioritizing prevention over treatment and empowering families with better information and choices, the administration is addressing the root causes of poor health outcomes. These efforts are improving quality of life, strengthening communities, and ensuring a healthier future for the next generation of Americans. more : Establishment of a Committee of Inquiry to Investigate Allegations of False Statements by Lisa DeNell Cook promises made, promises kept 01 The Trump administration made incredible strides in its effort to Make America Healthy Again, with roughly 35% of the American food industry — including major corporations like Walmart, Hershey and Nestlé — agreeing to eliminate artificial dyes from their products. 02 At President Trump’s direction, the Department of Health and Human Services revised its childhood vaccine recommendations from 72 shots for 11 diseases to 10 “consensus vaccines.” 03 President Trump established the Make America Healthy Again Commission, tasked with investigating and addressing the root causes of America’s escalating health crisis, with an initial focus on childhood chronic diseases. 04 Agriculture Secretary Brooke Rollins signed a slew of waivers allowing states to remove junk food from SNAP. 05 The Department of Health and Human Services removed COVID-19 vaccines from the list of shots recommended for healthy children and pregnant women. 06 Following negotiations with the Trump Administration, a variety of major pharmaceutical companies have agreed to bring American drug prices in line with the lowest paid by other developed nations, ending decades of Big Pharma exploiting U.S. consumers. 07 President Trump secured $50 billion in funding for rural hospitals. 08 President Trump signed the Whole Milk for Health Kids Act into law, restoring nutritious whole and 2% milk in American schools. 09 The Trump Administration Rollins released new dietary guidelines that prioritize whole, nutrient-dense foods over processed junk. items.title: Volvo Cars and NVIDIA Expand Partnership to Advance Safe Automated Driving
items.summary: Volvo Cars and NVIDIA Expand Partnership to Advance Safe Automated Driving October 15, 2026 Volvo Cars today announced it is expanding its partnership with NVIDIA to unlock new levels of safety in automated driving technology in future cars from Volvo, building on the companies’ decade-long collaboration. items.content: Volvo Cars and NVIDIA Expand Partnership to Advance Safe Automated Driving October 15, 2026 Volvo Cars today announced it is expanding its partnership with NVIDIA to unlock new levels of safety in automated driving technology in future cars from Volvo, building on the companies’ decade-long collaboration. Guided by Volvo Cars’ pioneering safety knowledge and powered by the NVIDIA Hyperion sensor and compute architecture, the technology will enable future Volvo cars to safely navigate complex real-world environments from door to door. This includes everything from highways and busy urban streets to parking scenarios. The technology will make its debut in a next-generation Volvo car as part of the company’s recently announced largest-ever product push. Volvo Cars will combine its industry-leading vehicle safety systems and engineering expertise with NVIDIA’s AI and accelerated computing technologies. These include the Hyperion sensor and compute architecture, Halos OS, and Alpamayo Stack driving software. Together, the companies will raise the bar for AI-enabled car safety while making driving feel easier and more effortless for customers, with a gradual introduction of eyes-off and mind-off driving. Volvo Cars brings nearly a century of real-world safety research and its human-centric approach to this development. The ambition is to set a new benchmark for automated driving that is safe, convenient and worthy of customer trust. “Volvo has been synonymous with car safety for almost 100 years,” said Håkan Samuelsson, president and CEO of Volvo Cars. “By working with NVIDIA, we bring together two distinct strengths: industry-leading safety knowledge and world-class AI technology. That combination gives us a unique opportunity to create safer and more attractive cars for our customers.” “Accelerated computing has transformed the car into an intelligent machine that can understand the world around it,” said Jensen Huang, founder and CEO of NVIDIA. “Volvo has spent nearly a century protecting people on the road. Together, we’re combining Volvo’s extraordinary vehicle safety systems with NVIDIA Hyperion and Halos to build a new generation of cars that make driving safer and more effortless.” This expanded partnership marks another milestone in the companies’ long-standing collaboration, which began in 2017. Volvo Cars is bringing the industry’s most advanced computing capabilities into its next generation of electric cars, establishing it as a leader in software-defined cars. About NVIDIA NVIDIA (NASDAQ: NVDA) is the world leader in AI and accelerated computing. About Volvo Car Group Volvo Cars was founded in 1927. Today, it is one of the most well-known and respected car brands in the world with sales to customers in more than 100 countries. Volvo Cars is listed on the Nasdaq Stockholm exchange, where it is traded under the ticker “VOLCAR B”. "For life. To provide freedom to move in a personal, sustainable and safe way." This purpose is reflected in Volvo Cars' ambition to become a fully electric car maker and in its commitment to an ongoing reduction of its carbon footprint, with the ambition to achieve net-zero greenhouse gas emissions by 2040. In 2025, Volvo Cars sold over 710 thousand cars, with an electrified share of 46%. Volvo Cars on average employed 42,600 full-time employees. Volvo Cars' head office, product development, marketing and administration functions are mainly located in Gothenburg, Sweden. Volvo Cars' production plants are located in Gothenburg, Ghent (Belgium), South Carolina (US), Chengdu, Daqing and Taizhou (China). The company also has R&D and design centres in Gothenburg and Shanghai (China). items.content: Featured projects Today, Meta is releasing the weights for Muse Spark Open , the most capable US open-weights model to date. It’s available today on Hugging Face under the Muse Model License. Muse Spark Open runs optimized on the SGLang and vLLM inference engines, with optimization for NVIDIA, AMD, and Intel. Building on our August release of Muse Spark, this open weights version has additional safety post-training to make it more robust against misuse as a standalone model without system guardrails. The result is a model that is a top open source choice for safety. Muse Spark Open is an 816B total/42B active parameter model with a context window of 1M tokens. Built for coding and agentic work, Muse Spark Open is natively multimodal and shares the same base model as Muse Spark 1.3. Meta loves open source, and as the creators of PyTorch, we’re committed to giving back to ensure the entire ecosystem fully supports Muse Spark Open. First, we’ve integrated Helion , our exciting new PyTorch-native high-level DSL for performant and portable ML kernels, to ship high-performance operations. Additionally, TorchTitan already supports Muse Spark out of the box for supervised fine-tuning and RL in the open, and we’re excited to see how far the PyTorch community can take it! Muse Spark Open Muse Spark Open is a coding-optimized open-weight model. Trained specifically for agentic coding workflows, it delivers higher first-attempt accuracy, reliable tool calling, and deep codebase understanding across the repos developers actually work in. You can read more in our previous model release blog here . Enhanced Coding Capabilities Strong at code generation, debugging, and codebase understanding. Trained on real developer workflows — multi-file refactors, debugging sessions, and long-running tasks — so the model keeps up with how you actually work. 1M context window means it handles your entire project including complex dependencies, legacy code, and thousands of files without needing to break your task into pieces Multimodal Understanding Muse Spark Open has audio and audio-video perception — alongside image and document understanding. As a reasoning model, it processes image, audio, and text inputs — natively and reliably. Agentic Muse Spark Open is built from the ground up as an agentic model. It maps out steps, acts, observes, and self-corrects over long horizons — not just single-shot tool calls. It’s trained to browse the web (including multimodal browsing), and use an agentic harness to: spawn and coordinate subagents for decomposable work; and leverage computer use capabilities unified across desktop, mobile, and browser. It’s trained on long-horizon, multi-site tasks, and generates separate commentary that lets the model state intent before acting—so you can always know what it’s doing and why. Why Helion kernels? Helion is a PyTorch native kernel authoring language designed for writing high-performance kernels across heterogeneous hardware platforms. Following early adoption from the open-source ecosystem, Helion became a part of the PyTorch Foundation in April 2026. Muse Spark Open ships with Helion implementations of operations such as RoPE, RMSNorm, quantization, etc., delivering 1.03 – 3.95x speedups compared to custom kernels written in hardware specific languages (e.g. NVIDIA CUDA and CuTe DSL) on NVIDIA GB300. These same kernels were directly portable for AMD, scoring similar performance improvements on AMD Mi350 with an overall 3% improvement in end-to-end throughput. In addition, we also launched Helion megakernels for Muse Spark Open in SGLang. Written entirely in Helion, these kernels fuse multiple operations into a single persistent kernel to improve low latency inference, and can likewise be autotuned for different shapes and hardware. Helion kernels can be further autotuned by users for broader hardware platforms and workloads – including different accelerator architectures (NVIDIA, AMD, Google TPU, etc.), quantization formats, tensor shapes, and parallelism strategies – without maintaining separate hand-tuned implementations for every configuration. Together, these capabilities make it easier to achieve portable performance while reducing the cost of developing and maintaining specialized kernels. Post-training with TorchTitan TorchTitan is a PyTorch native platform designed for rapid experimentation and large-scale training of generative AI models. Starting today, TorchTitan adds a model definition for Meta’s Muse Spark Open , so developers can tune it to their needs. TorchTitan features native support for multi-turn SFT and LoRA out-of-the-box, as well as reinforcement learning capabilities (TitanRL) that allow users to fine-tune Muse Spark Open. Get Started We’re sharing this work because we want everyone to have access to the best AI models. Muse Spark Open ships with custom, auto-tunable Helion GPU kernels in SGLang, delivering 1.03–3.95× kernel-level speedups on NVIDIA and AMD GPUs and a 3% end-to-end speedup on AMD MI350. You can also customize it for your use case by leveraging PyTorch’s TorchTitan to further tune the model. Start Building Today: https://huggingface.co/meta-models/Muse-Spark-open-816B-A42B Muse Spark is the full size model from our model family. We previously released Muse Glimmer, a small dense model. Start using it today, with ExecuTorch .

items.content: Featured projects TL;DR Deploying PyTorch models on microcontrollers has historically required converting to other framework formats, maintaining separate toolchains, and debugging cross-framework numerical mismatches. ExecuTorch eliminates this conversion step entirely. The Cortex-M backend enables PyTorch models to run directly on Arm Cortex-M CPUs with Arm CMSIS-NN acceleration. It supports all capability tiers (Scalar, DSP, and MVE/Helium) from a single workflow. We benchmark four of the five models from the MLPerf Tiny suite on the Alif Ensemble E8. Each model runs in 21.5 ms or less and uses under 90 KiB of RAM on a single Cortex-M55 core. For heterogeneous SoCs, the Cortex-M backend also provides the CPU execution path alongside Ethos-U NPU delegation. Minimal binary footprint. The ExecuTorch core runtime is under 20 KiB of flash, and operator selective build links only the operators your model needs, so total code size scales with the model rather than the framework. Background Microcontrollers power billions of always-on devices: wearables, industrial sensors, voice interfaces, and smart home appliances. These devices operate under extreme constraints: often less than 1 MB of SRAM, single-digit megabytes of flash, and power budgets measured in milliwatts. Despite these limitations, there’s growing demand to run meaningful ML workloads on these platforms and the hardware is evolving to meet it. Modern Cortex-M based microcontroller units (MCUs) now include DSP & vector ISAs, large tightly-coupled memories (TCMs), and power-efficient NPUs such as the Arm Ethos-U NPU that make ML inference more practical in resource constrained devices. Until now, deploying ML on Cortex-M meant leaving the PyTorch ecosystem. Developers had to convert models to alternative formats, maintain separate toolchains for training and deployment, and debug numerical mismatches introduced during conversion. For teams that train in PyTorch, which accounts for over 90% of the research code published at top ML conferences, this translation step adds friction to every iteration cycle. ExecuTorch was designed to eliminate this gap. Arm MCU support has been available through the Ethos-U NPU, and the Cortex-M backend extends it to Cortex-M CPUs, so a model can run on parts with or without an accelerator. The trained PyTorch model is exported, quantized and lowered for the device within the same stack that serves models on mobile, desktop and server. The Cortex-M Backend The ExecuTorch Cortex-M backend replaces standard PyTorch operators with CMSIS-NN-backed custom operators through ahead-of-time compiler passes. At inference time, these operators call directly into Arm’s CMSIS-NN library , an open source collection of optimized neural network kernels for Cortex-M processors. Key properties: CMSIS-NN accelerated. Quantized operations (linear, conv, add, mul, softmax, activations, etc.) are replaced with optimized implementations that call CMSIS-NN functions and additional optimized Cortex-M implementations directly. Target-aware compilation. The CPU variant (M0 through M85) and ISA tier are specified at compile time, so the correct CMSIS-NN backend is selected, eliminating runtime dispatch overhead. Purpose-built quantizer. Produces INT8 quantized graphs matching the data layout requirements of CMSIS-NN kernels, using PyTorch’s PT2E quantization framework. Single compiler toolchain. The Cortex-M lowering path operates directly on the ExecuTorch edge dialect, keeping the compilation pipeline simple and debuggable. Cortex-M Capability Tiers The backend targets the full Cortex-M spectrum: Tier Cores Key Feature Use Case Scalar M0, M0+, M3, M23 Standard ARM instructions Ultra-low-cost, minimal silicon DSP M4, M7, M33, M35P SIMD multiply-accumulate Mid-range MCUs, signal processing MVE (aka Helium) M55, M85 128-bit vector ops, beat-based execution High-performance MCU ML inference Arm Helium technology is where the biggest performance gains are. CMSIS-NN leverages Helium’s beat-based execution model to pipeline data movement and compute, providing significant throughput gains for the depthwise and pointwise convolutions common in edge ML architectures. That said, the same workflow targets all variants. The target configuration selects the appropriate backend automatically. ExecuTorch is Embedded Friendly Unlike mobile or cloud environments that must accommodate varied hardware at runtime, microcontroller deployments target a fixed hardware profile. Embedded developers possess precise knowledge of their deployment target, including the exact CPU core, available ISA extensions, SRAM allocation, and flash capacity. ExecuTorch’s ahead-of-time stack is designed to exploit this. ExecuTorch makes target-specific decisions at compile time: graph-level optimizations, memory planning, weight packing, and kernel selection are all target-aware at compile time. Concretely, for Cortex-M this means: Graph-level compute elimination. Redundant dtype conversions, quantize/dequantize pairs, and memory format transposes are removed during lowering, so only necessary compute reaches the device. Quantization parameter folding. Scale and zero-point arithmetic is precomputed into integer multiplier/shift form at export, so quantized kernel inference stays entirely in fixed-point. AOT weight layout transposition. Convolution weights are transposed from PyTorch’s native layout (OIHW) to CMSIS-NN’s expected format (OHWI) at export time. The permute cost is paid once during compilation and never at inference. Static memory planning across heterogeneous memories. All tensor and scratch buffers are allocated and laid out ahead of time, with support for spanning multiple memory regions (e.g., TCM and SRAM). Developers can also customize placement to put latency-critical buffers in fast local memory. No heap allocator, no fragmentation, and no runtime memory management required. Target-specific operator replacement. The CortexMPassManager selects CMSIS-NN kernel variants matched to your core’s ISA tier (Scalar, DSP, or MVE) at compile time, not at runtime. Developer Workflow import torch from torchao.quantization.pt2e.quantize_pt2e import convert_pt2e, prepare_pt2e from executorch.backends.cortex_m.edge_compile_config import cortex_m_edge_compile_config from executorch.backends.cortex_m.passes.cortex_m_pass_manager import CortexMPassManager from executorch.backends.cortex_m.quantizer.quantizer import CortexMQuantizer from executorch.backends.cortex_m.target_config import CortexM, CortexMTargetConfig from executorch.exir import to_edge_transform_and_lower # 1. Export model = MyModel().eval() example_inputs = (torch.randn(1, 1, 49, 10),) exported = torch.export.export(model, example_inputs) # 2. Quantize and calibrate quantizer = CortexMQuantizer(use_explicit_layout=True) prepared = prepare_pt2e(exported.module(), quantizer) for sample in calibration_data: prepared(sample) quantized = convert_pt2e(prepared) # 3. Re-export the quantized model quantized_exported = torch.export.export(quantized, example_inputs) # 4. Lower to Edge and apply the Cortex-M passes pass_manager = CortexMPassManager( target_config=CortexMTargetConfig(cpu=CortexM.M55), use_explicit_layout=True, ) edge = to_edge_transform_and_lower( quantized_exported, compile_config=cortex_m_edge_compile_config(), transform_passes=pass_manager, ) # 5. Serialize for integration into firmware et_program = edge.to_executorch() with open("model.pte", "wb") as f: f.write(et_program.buffer) The resulting .pte binary is linked into firmware alongside the ExecuTorch runtime and CMSIS-NN library, then flashed to the device. At runtime, inference executes the precompiled graph with minimal runtime overhead and no dynamic memory allocation for tensors. Using the Cortex-M Backend Alongside Ethos-U Many Cortex-M MCUs pair the CPU with an Arm Ethos-U NPU such as the U55, U65, or U85. ExecuTorch’s EthosUPartitioner delegates supported operations to the NPU via the Vela compiler, and operations left outside the partition run on the Cortex-M CPU within the same graph. The Cortex-M passes run after Ethos-U partitioning and reuse the quantization parameters already in the graph. This allows a model quantized with EthosUQuantizer to use CMSIS-NN for CPU operations whose quantization, layout and shape constraints meet the Cortex-M backend requirements. Otherwise they fall back to ExecuTorch’s portable kernels, which are functional but not accelerated. The practical benefit is that NPU operator coverage is not an all-or-nothing gate. A model with a handful of undelegated operations can ship today on mixed CPU/NPU execution, and move more of the graph onto the NPU as coverage grows. MLPerf Tiny Benchmark Suite We measured inference latency and memory usage across four of the five MLPerf Tiny Inference benchmark models on the Alif Ensemble E8 . These benchmark models represent a set of common deep neural networks representative of TinyML workloads. The Alif E8 integrates multiple Cortex-M55 cores alongside Ethos-U55 and U85 NPUs; we measured on a single M55 high performance core running at 400 MHz, with the Ethos-U NPUs unused. ExecuTorch’s ahead-of-time memory planning means RAM usage is deterministic and bounded, with no fragmentation risk under sustained workloads. items.raw_text: Featured projects TL;DR Deploying PyTorch models on microcontrollers has historically required converting to other framework formats, maintaining separate toolchains, and debugging cross-framework numerical mismatches. ExecuTorch eliminates this conversion step entirely. The Cortex-M backend enables PyTorch models to run directly on Arm Cortex-M CPUs with Arm CMSIS-NN acceleration. It supports all capability tiers (Scalar, DSP, and MVE/Helium) from a single workflow. We benchmark four of the five models from the MLPerf Tiny suite on the Alif Ensemble E8. Each model runs in 21.5 ms or less and uses under 90 KiB of RAM on a single Cortex-M55 core. For heterogeneous SoCs, the Cortex-M backend also provides the CPU execution path alongside Ethos-U NPU delegation. Minimal binary footprint. The ExecuTorch core runtime is under 20 KiB of flash, and operator selective build links only the operators your model needs, so total code size scales with the model rather than the framework. Background Microcontrollers power billions of always-on devices: wearables, industrial sensors, voice interfaces, and smart home appliances. These devices operate under extreme constraints: often less than 1 MB of SRAM, single-digit megabytes of flash, and power budgets measured in milliwatts. Despite these limitations, there’s growing demand to run meaningful ML workloads on these platforms and the hardware is evolving to meet it. Modern Cortex-M based microcontroller units (MCUs) now include DSP & vector ISAs, large tightly-coupled memories (TCMs), and power-efficient NPUs such as the Arm Ethos-U NPU that make ML inference more practical in resource constrained devices. Until now, deploying ML on Cortex-M meant leaving the PyTorch ecosystem. Developers had to convert models to alternative formats, maintain separate toolchains for training and deployment, and debug numerical mismatches introduced during conversion. For teams that train in PyTorch, which accounts for over 90% of the research code published at top ML conferences, this translation step adds friction to every iteration cycle. ExecuTorch was designed to eliminate this gap. Arm MCU support has been available through the Ethos-U NPU, and the Cortex-M backend extends it to Cortex-M CPUs, so a model can run on parts with or without an accelerator. The trained PyTorch model is exported, quantized and lowered for the device within the same stack that serves models on mobile, desktop and server. The Cortex-M Backend The ExecuTorch Cortex-M backend replaces standard PyTorch operators with CMSIS-NN-backed custom operators through ahead-of-time compiler passes. At inference time, these operators call directly into Arm’s CMSIS-NN library , an open source collection of optimized neural network kernels for Cortex-M processors. Key properties: CMSIS-NN accelerated. Quantized operations (linear, conv, add, mul, softmax, activations, etc.) are replaced with optimized implementations that call CMSIS-NN functions and additional optimized Cortex-M implementations directly. Target-aware compilation. The CPU variant (M0 through M85) and ISA tier are specified at compile time, so the correct CMSIS-NN backend is selected, eliminating runtime dispatch overhead. Purpose-built quantizer. Produces INT8 quantized graphs matching the data layout requirements of CMSIS-NN kernels, using PyTorch’s PT2E quantization framework. Single compiler toolchain. The Cortex-M lowering path operates directly on the ExecuTorch edge dialect, keeping the compilation pipeline simple and debuggable. Cortex-M Capability Tiers The backend targets the full Cortex-M spectrum: Tier Cores Key Feature Use Case Scalar M0, M0+, M3, M23 Standard ARM instructions Ultra-low-cost, minimal silicon DSP M4, M7, M33, M35P SIMD multiply-accumulate Mid-range MCUs, signal processing MVE (aka Helium) M55, M85 128-bit vector ops, beat-based execution High-performance MCU ML inference Arm Helium technology is where the biggest performance gains are. CMSIS-NN leverages Helium’s beat-based execution model to pipeline data movement and compute, providing significant throughput gains for the depthwise and pointwise convolutions common in edge ML architectures. That said, the same workflow targets all variants. The target configuration selects the appropriate backend automatically. ExecuTorch is Embedded Friendly Unlike mobile or cloud environments that must accommodate varied hardware at runtime, microcontroller deployments target a fixed hardware profile. Embedded developers possess precise knowledge of their deployment target, including the exact CPU core, available ISA extensions, SRAM allocation, and flash capacity. ExecuTorch’s ahead-of-time stack is designed to exploit this. ExecuTorch makes target-specific decisions at compile time: graph-level optimizations, memory planning, weight packing, and kernel selection are all target-aware at compile time. Concretely, for Cortex-M this means: Graph-level compute elimination. Redundant dtype conversions, quantize/dequantize pairs, and memory format transposes are removed during lowering, so only necessary compute reaches the device. Quantization parameter folding. Scale and zero-point arithmetic is precomputed into integer multiplier/shift form at export, so quantized kernel inference stays entirely in fixed-point. AOT weight layout transposition. Convolution weights are transposed from PyTorch’s native layout (OIHW) to CMSIS-NN’s expected format (OHWI) at export time. The permute cost is paid once during compilation and never at inference. Static memory planning across heterogeneous memories. All tensor and scratch buffers are allocated and laid out ahead of time, with support for spanning multiple memory regions (e.g., TCM and SRAM). Developers can also customize placement to put latency-critical buffers in fast local memory. No heap allocator, no fragmentation, and no runtime memory management required. Target-specific operator replacement. The CortexMPassManager selects CMSIS-NN kernel variants matched to your core’s ISA tier (Scalar, DSP, or MVE) at compile time, not at runtime. Developer Workflow import torch from torchao.quantization.pt2e.quantize_pt2e import convert_pt2e, prepare_pt2e from executorch.backends.cortex_m.edge_compile_config import cortex_m_edge_compile_config from executorch.backends.cortex_m.passes.cortex_m_pass_manager import CortexMPassManager from executorch.backends.cortex_m.quantizer.quantizer import CortexMQuantizer from executorch.backends.cortex_m.target_config import CortexM, CortexMTargetConfig from executorch.exir import to_edge_transform_and_lower # 1. Export model = MyModel().eval() example_inputs = (torch.randn(1, 1, 49, 10),) exported = torch.export.export(model, example_inputs) # 2. Quantize and calibrate quantizer = CortexMQuantizer(use_explicit_layout=True) prepared = prepare_pt2e(exported.module(), quantizer) for sample in calibration_data: prepared(sample) quantized = convert_pt2e(prepared) # 3. Re-export the quantized model quantized_exported = torch.export.export(quantized, example_inputs) # 4. Lower to Edge and apply the Cortex-M passes pass_manager = CortexMPassManager( target_config=CortexMTargetConfig(cpu=CortexM.M55), use_explicit_layout=True, ) edge = to_edge_transform_and_lower( quantized_exported, compile_config=cortex_m_edge_compile_config(), transform_passes=pass_manager, ) # 5. Serialize for integration into firmware et_program = edge.to_executorch() with open("model.pte", "wb") as f: f.write(et_program.buffer) The resulting .pte binary is linked into firmware alongside the ExecuTorch runtime and CMSIS-NN library, then flashed to the device. At runtime, inference executes the precompiled graph with minimal runtime overhead and no dynamic memory allocation for tensors. The Cortex-M passes run after Ethos-U partitioning and reuse the quantization parameters already in the graph. This allows a model quantized with EthosUQuantizer to use CMSIS-NN for CPU operations whose quantization, layout and shape constraints meet the Cortex-M backend requirements. Otherwise they fall back to ExecuTorch’s portable kernels, which are functional but not accelerated. The practical benefit is that NPU operator coverage is not an all-or-nothing gate. A model with a handful of undelegated operations can ship today on mixed CPU/NPU execution, and move more of the graph onto the NPU as coverage grows. items.content: At a glance Challenges a core assumption in robotics AI: Our research shows that running physical AI inference exclusively on onboard GPUs can limit robot performance, battery life, and scalability, and that offloading inference to edge or cloud GPUs can offer significant advantages. Demonstrates measurable benefits of inference offloading: Across representative mobile manipulation workloads, offloading improved task success rates, enabled larger AI models, and helped robots respond more effectively in dynamic, real-world environments. Extends robot operating time: Replacing power-hungry onboard AI compute with lightweight onboard hardware and remote inference can substantially improve battery life, enabling robots to operate longer between charges. Introduces a new capability in the Physical AI Toolchain: Developers can now containerize, deploy, and orchestrate robotics AI workloads across robots, edge infrastructure, and the cloud using Kubernetes-based tooling for distributed inference. Readily-available physical AI, with robotics assisting users in manufacturing, home, and warehouses scenarios, holds immense potential to improve safety, productivity, and assistance across a wide range of tasks. In many ways, AI for the physical world represents a major frontier for AI . Physical AI must operate in open, unpredictable environments, interact with both other robots and people, and work with a diversity of embodiments. Realizing this vision requires advances along three dimensions: robot hardware, embodied AI models, and systems infrastructure for training and inference. While robot hardware and the AI models have advanced rapidly in recent years, we turn our focus on a relatively under-addressed aspect: inference infrastructure of physical AI . Enabling robots to effectively and safely operate in the physical world will require sophisticated systems to handle large volumes of distributed inference compute. Today, the prevailing approach to physical AI is to provision a GPU onboard the robot, e.g., by wiring a GPU to the robot. In this model, the robot’s inference will be confined to the onboard GPU, and provide the robot with the necessary chunks and sequence of actions for the execution of its tasks. While higher-level planning may be performed in the cloud, task execution typically remains tied to the robot itself. We challenge this assumption. As physical AI models grow in size and sophistication, the constraints of onboard compute become increasingly apparent. GPUs consume significant power, reduce battery life, add cost and weight, and can limit the ability to run the latest generation of AI models. To better understand the systems implications of physical AI, we conducted the first systematic study of robotics workloads. We focused on mobile robotic manipulation , with the canonical task such as “check for rubbish in the kitchen and put it in the trash.” Such a task involves planning the path to the kitchen, perceiving the environment to find rubbish, navigating to the rubbish, picking up the rubbish, and navigating back to the trash can for disposal. We evaluated representative models across three core capabilities: semantic mapping and planning, navigation, and manipulation, as summarized in Figure 2. Figure 2: Details of the models used for the different components of mobile manipulation. Offloading physical AI inference out of the robot improved its response time and accuracy, along with battery lifetime and cost. We evaluated the inference models across a range of onboard, edge, and cloud compute configurations. Details of the specific test hardware are available in our technical report . Benefits in task performance : Our evaluation shows offloading inference can significantly improve robot performance across mapping, planning, navigation, and manipulation workloads. Some smaller GPUs could not accommodate the mobile manipulation stack. On GPUs with sufficient memory, mapping and planning slowed by up to 383% compared to an A100, thus limiting the robot’s abilities in dynamic spaces. Navigation showed a 30% drop in its timely detection of obstacles with lighter GPUs. While the VLA models did not dramatically slow down with smaller GPUs, the slowdown was still sufficient to drop their accuracies by 50%. In other words, onboard GPUs limited the performance of the robots while offloading their inference to an on-premise or cloud GPU boosts their operations, as shown in the videos below and quantified in the graphs. As physical AI models continue to grow in size and complexity, the benefits of offloading are likely to become even more pronounced. Figure 3a: The video shows the handover task with onboard GPUs. Figure 3b: The video shows the handover task when the inference is offloaded. Figure 4: Success rates of robot arms handing over objects to each other when inference is performed with different GPUs (some onboard, and some offloaded). Offloading improves success rates. Benefits in battery lifetime : Beyond performance, onboard GPUs also significantly drained the battery life of the robot. We compared the increase in battery lifetime by replacing an onboard GPU with a Raspberry Pi-5 board and shipping all the data to the offloaded GPU. The larger onboard GPUs, such as Jetson Thor, drained robot batteries by up to 160% (or a few hours) for even the larger robots. Figure 5: Impact of offloading GPU inference on the battery life of the robots; the above numbers are for the Stretch-3 robot. The above results show that offloading GPU inference out of the robot is critical for functioning in the open world with large models and long battery lifetimes. Nonetheless, offloading inference out of the robot involves a complex tradeoff involving performance, network latency and bandwidth, and available GPU resources. We believe that our measurement study will inform the design of physical AI inference systems. Microsoft Research StorY OptiMind: When the system meets the floor A three‑month pilot in a Midwestern bottling plant shows what happens when AI moves beyond chat and into decision-making, where constraints shift, stakes are real, and answers must hold. Learn more Opens in a new tab Toolset for automatic offload We have built a toolset for easy inference offloading out of the robot and distributing inference between the edge GPU and cloud. Kubernetes is a natural platform to provide a uniform abstraction to distribute robotic AI between the robot’s compute, edge GPU, and overflowing to the cloud. The toolset allows automatic containerization and offloading of robotics workloads using declarative specifications, distributes physical AI containers with smart policies using Kubernetes, and integrates with robotic simulators, LeRobot, and ROS2 for easy development. The sequence of steps below shows how the toolset can be prompted with what to offload, and how it creates a separate container for GPU inference and offloads the same. Figure 6: Steps in the offloading toolset with containerization and deployment. Microsoft has recently released the Physical AI Toolchain (opens in new tab) for operationalizing physical intelligence at scale. Physical AI Toolchain is an open-source, production-ready framework that integrates Microsoft Azure (opens in new tab) cloud services with NVIDIA’s (opens in new tab) physical AI stack, accelerating robotics and physical AI developers to automate and scale data curation, augmentation, and evaluation across perception, mobility, imitation learning, and reinforcement learning pipelines. We are announcing the addition of an industry-first capability for offloaded physical AI inference for robots as part of the Physical AI Toolchain. This release includes example projects for offloading inference of a SO-101 and a UR10e. The videos below show the offloading of the inference of Microsoft’s Rho model , targeted at dual-arm robots, to a Jetson Thor GPU, which controls the actions of the Mobile Aloha robot (opens in new tab) . Figure 7a: Offloading of GPU inference of Microsoft’s Rho model controlling the Mobile Aloha robot for interactions with the BusyBox to press the blue button. Figure 7b: Offloading of GPU inference of Microsoft’s Rho model controlling the Mobile Aloha robot for interactions with the BusyBox to turn the knob to position 4. Check out the inference offload feature, look into the source code, and let us know your feedback. We have already tested it with many real-world use cases, and look forward to hearing about your deployment experiences. items.raw_text: At a glance Challenges a core assumption in robotics AI: Our research shows that running physical AI inference exclusively on onboard GPUs can limit robot performance, battery life, and scalability, and that offloading inference to edge or cloud GPUs can offer significant advantages. Demonstrates measurable benefits of inference offloading: Across representative mobile manipulation workloads, offloading improved task success rates, enabled larger AI models, and helped robots respond more effectively in dynamic, real-world environments. Extends robot operating time: Replacing power-hungry onboard AI compute with lightweight onboard hardware and remote inference can substantially improve battery life, enabling robots to operate longer between charges. Introduces a new capability in the Physical AI Toolchain: Developers can now containerize, deploy, and orchestrate robotics AI workloads across robots, edge infrastructure, and the cloud using Kubernetes-based tooling for distributed inference. Readily-available physical AI, with robotics assisting users in manufacturing, home, and warehouses scenarios, holds immense potential to improve safety, productivity, and assistance across a wide range of tasks. In many ways, AI for the physical world represents a major frontier for AI . Physical AI must operate in open, unpredictable environments, interact with both other robots and people, and work with a diversity of embodiments. Realizing this vision requires advances along three dimensions: robot hardware, embodied AI models, and systems infrastructure for training and inference. While robot hardware and the AI models have advanced rapidly in recent years, we turn our focus on a relatively under-addressed aspect: inference infrastructure of physical AI . Enabling robots to effectively and safely operate in the physical world will require sophisticated systems to handle large volumes of distributed inference compute. Today, the prevailing approach to physical AI is to provision a GPU onboard the robot, e.g., by wiring a GPU to the robot. In this model, the robot’s inference will be confined to the onboard GPU, and provide the robot with the necessary chunks and sequence of actions for the execution of its tasks. While higher-level planning may be performed in the cloud, task execution typically remains tied to the robot itself. We challenge this assumption. As physical AI models grow in size and sophistication, the constraints of onboard compute become increasingly apparent. GPUs consume significant power, reduce battery life, add cost and weight, and can limit the ability to run the latest generation of AI models. To better understand the systems implications of physical AI, we conducted the first systematic study of robotics workloads. We focused on mobile robotic manipulation , with the canonical task such as “check for rubbish in the kitchen and put it in the trash.” Such a task involves planning the path to the kitchen, perceiving the environment to find rubbish, navigating to the rubbish, picking up the rubbish, and navigating back to the trash can for disposal. We evaluated representative models across three core capabilities: semantic mapping and planning, navigation, and manipulation, as summarized in Figure 2. Figure 2: Details of the models used for the different components of mobile manipulation. Offloading physical AI inference out of the robot improved its response time and accuracy, along with battery lifetime and cost. We evaluated the inference models across a range of onboard, edge, and cloud compute configurations. Details of the specific test hardware are available in our technical report . Benefits in task performance : Our evaluation shows offloading inference can significantly improve robot performance across mapping, planning, navigation, and manipulation workloads. Some smaller GPUs could not accommodate the mobile manipulation stack. On GPUs with sufficient memory, mapping and planning slowed by up to 383% compared to an A100, thus limiting the robot’s abilities in dynamic spaces. Navigation showed a 30% drop in its timely detection of obstacles with lighter GPUs. While the VLA models did not dramatically slow down with smaller GPUs, the slowdown was still sufficient to drop their accuracies by 50%. In other words, onboard GPUs limited the performance of the robots while offloading their inference to an on-premise or cloud GPU boosts their operations, as shown in the videos below and quantified in the graphs. As physical AI models continue to grow in size and complexity, the benefits of offloading are likely to become even more pronounced. Figure 3a: The video shows the handover task with onboard GPUs. Figure 3b: The video shows the handover task when the inference is offloaded. Figure 4: Success rates of robot arms handing over objects to each other when inference is performed with different GPUs (some onboard, and some offloaded). Offloading improves success rates. Benefits in battery lifetime : Beyond performance, onboard GPUs also significantly drained the battery life of the robot. We compared the increase in battery lifetime by replacing an onboard GPU with a Raspberry Pi-5 board and shipping all the data to the offloaded GPU. The larger onboard GPUs, such as Jetson Thor, drained robot batteries by up to 160% (or a few hours) for even the larger robots. Figure 5: Impact of offloading GPU inference on the battery life of the robots; the above numbers are for the Stretch-3 robot. The above results show that offloading GPU inference out of the robot is critical for functioning in the open world with large models and long battery lifetimes. Nonetheless, offloading inference out of the robot involves a complex tradeoff involving performance, network latency and bandwidth, and available GPU resources. We believe that our measurement study will inform the design of physical AI inference systems. Microsoft Research StorY OptiMind: When the system meets the floor A three‑month pilot in a Midwestern bottling plant shows what happens when AI moves beyond chat and into decision-making, where constraints shift, stakes are real, and answers must hold. Learn more Opens in a new tab Toolset for automatic offload We have built a toolset for easy inference offloading out of the robot and distributing inference between the edge GPU and cloud. Kubernetes is a natural platform to provide a uniform abstraction to distribute robotic AI between the robot’s compute, edge GPU, and overflowing to the cloud. The toolset allows automatic containerization and offloading of robotics workloads using declarative specifications, distributes physical AI containers with smart policies using Kubernetes, and integrates with robotic simulators, LeRobot, and ROS2 for easy development. The sequence of steps below shows how the toolset can be prompted with what to offload, and how it creates a separate container for GPU inference and offloads the same. Figure 6: Steps in the offloading toolset with containerization and deployment. Microsoft has recently released the Physical AI Toolchain (opens in new tab) for operationalizing physical intelligence at scale. Physical AI Toolchain is an open-source, production-ready framework that integrates Microsoft Azure (opens in new tab) cloud services with NVIDIA’s (opens in new tab) physical AI stack, accelerating robotics and physical AI developers to automate and scale data curation, augmentation, and evaluation across perception, mobility, imitation learning, and reinforcement learning pipelines. We are announcing the addition of an industry-first capability for offloaded physical AI inference for robots as part of the Physical AI Toolchain. This release includes example projects for offloading inference of a SO-101 and a UR10e. The videos below show the offloading of the inference of Microsoft’s Rho model , targeted at dual-arm robots, to a Jetson Thor GPU, which controls the actions of the Mobile Aloha robot (opens in new tab) . Figure 7a: Offloading of GPU inference of Microsoft’s Rho model controlling the Mobile Aloha robot for interactions with the BusyBox to press the blue button. Figure 7b: Offloading of GPU inference of Microsoft’s Rho model controlling the Mobile Aloha robot for interactions with the BusyBox to turn the knob to position 4. Check out the inference offload feature, look into the source code, and let us know your feedback. We have already tested it with many real-world use cases, and look forward to hearing about your deployment experiences. items.content: At a glance A new form of computing . Zero-knowledge proofs let you run a workload and receive, alongside the result, a short proof that the program ran correctly. Anyone can check the proof in milliseconds, without rerunning the program, without trusting whoever ran it, and without needing data on which the program was run. Three grand challenges have stood in the way of broad adoption : making proofs fast enough to produce, making them available to normal programs without cryptographic expertise, and resting them on cryptography that will still be trusted many decades from now. Magnetar makes major progress on all three challenges. It proves programs written in Rust, Go, or C, runs 10 to 39 times faster on average than the prior fastest comparable systems, and rests its security only on standard hash functions. It is the latest result of more than a decade of research at Microsoft Research on making zero-knowledge proofs practical. A new form of computing Every result a computer produces comes with an implicit question: did the program run as claimed and produce correct outputs? Today, answering that question often requires a degree of trust alongside verification. We trust the operator, the vendor, the counterparty, or the agent, and we rely on contracts, audits, and logs to establish that trust. Zero-knowledge proofs offer a fundamentally different approach to establishing trust. A program runs, and along with its output it produces a short proof, a cryptographic certificate that this program, on these inputs, produced this output. The proof is small and fast to check. Whoever receives it can confirm the result in milliseconds without rerunning the program, and can pass the proof on to anyone else who needs the same assurance. With the zero-knowledge property, the proof also reveals nothing about inputs that should stay private. This changes what correctness means in the real world. A result no longer has to be trusted because of who produced it. It can be checked because of what accompanies it. An AI agent acting on someone’s behalf could attach a proof that each action complied with the policy it was given. Regulated financial institutions could prove that transactions were processed correctly without making their transactions public. These become possible once producing a proof is as routine as running the program. Three grand challenges Zero-knowledge proofs were invented in the 1980s, and the ideas behind proving program execution have been around nearly as long. What has kept them from becoming a general tool is three challenges that have resisted being solved at the same time. Efficiency . Producing a proof has historically taken millions of times more computation than running the program itself. Years of research have brought that overhead down, but the fastest systems have achieved their speed by making compromises elsewhere. Generality and usability. Many proof systems require developers to manually rewrite their program as a cryptographic circuit, which is a fixed arithmetic description of that exact computation. This takes months. Every change to the application means a new circuit, and the translation is itself a frequent source of security bugs. A general-purpose alternative is to prove the execution of an ordinary processor, so that any compiled program can be proven as written. Until recently, that generality came at a steep cost in speed or security. Security. A proof is only as strong as the cryptography beneath it. Many proof systems rest on elliptic curves, which can be broken by a sufficiently powerful quantum computer. Microsoft is addressing this problem with its Quantum Safe Program, which will move its products and services to post-quantum cryptography, a goal it recently accelerated to 2029 . Post-quantum proof systems already exist, but some rest on lattice assumptions, and most rest on new cryptographic functions invented to reduce the cost of proving. These new cryptographic functions have not faced the decades of scrutiny given to the cryptography protecting today’s internet, and some rest on mathematical conjectures about error-correcting codes that have not been proven. They have bought their speed with strong assumptions. PODCAST SERIES The Shape of Things to Come Join Microsoft’s Doug Burger and guests as they dig into the fundamental truths about AI and how it will reshape the future. Listen now Opens in a new tab More than a decade of work For more than a decade, Microsoft Research has worked on making zero-knowledge proofs and verifiable computing practical. Early research followed two approaches, both practical only for small programs. The first (opens in new tab) (opens in new tab) lets a verifier check a long computation through a short conversation with the prover using a technique called the sum-check protocol (opens in new tab) , but this applied only to computations with a particular layered structure. The second (opens in new tab) (opens in new tab) used elliptic-curve cryptography to create very small proofs for almost any computation. But this requires a one-time trusted setup involving secret information which, if leaked, could allow anyone to forge proofs. This approach is also vulnerable to quantum computers. In 2019, a new zero-knowledge proof system called Spartan returned to the sum-check approach and made it work for general-purpose programs without a trusted setup. Spartan can also be instantiated with different cryptographic building blocks. That flexibility is what later allowed the proof system to be built on hash functions alone. A sequence of results then filled in the remaining pieces: Phalanx (opens in new tab) , in 2021, showed how to exploit repetition, such as a processor running the same instruction cycle on every step, to prove computations an order of magnitude faster than Spartan. Magnetar’s processor description is built on this idea. Nova (opens in new tab) , HyperNova (opens in new tab) , NeutronNova (opens in new tab) , Neo and SuperNeo (opens in new tab) showed that stopping Spartan’s proving early, and folding the partial results together, makes it practical to prove computations of any size at far lower cost. Brakedown (opens in new tab) , in 2021, introduced a fast hash-based commitment scheme and combined it with Spartan, giving the first Spartan variant whose security rests on standard hash functions. Spice (opens in new tab) , Lasso (opens in new tab) , Nebula (opens in new tab) , and then Twist and Shout (opens in new tab) made the memory operations at the heart of a general-purpose processor inexpensive to prove, and Jolt (opens in new tab) showed that combining them with Spartan can efficiently prove the execution of a complete processor. Earlier this year, Vega (opens in new tab) applied this line of work to digital identity, proving facts from a government credential in under a tenth of a second . More recently, BinarySpartan (opens in new tab) brought Spartan to binary fields, where a processor’s logic and standard hash functions can be efficiently expressed. BinarySpartan also relies on Ligerito (opens in new tab) , a Brakedown-style commitment scheme with much shorter proofs, and on ring switching (opens in new tab) , which makes it efficient to commit to vectors of bits. Each of these solved a piece of the problem. Magnetar is where the pieces come together. Magnetar Magnetar is a zero-knowledge virtual machine, or zkVM, and it makes major progress on all three challenges at once. Figure 1. Magnetar proves a program’s execution and returns a small proof that anyone can check, with security resting only on standard hash functions. It is general-purpose. Magnetar proves the execution of RISC-V, an open processor architecture with mature compilers for every mainstream language. A developer writes a program in Rust, Go, or C, compiles it as usual, and Magnetar proves it as written. Consider what this means in practice. A business policy, a data pipeline, or an interpreter for the Ethereum Virtual Machine (EVM) is just a program, and the engineers who already maintain it can prove their executions exactly as written. As a result, proving stops being a specialist activity. It is faster than prior systems in the same class. Magnetar proves 7.2 to 8.7 million processor instructions per second on a laptop. Across 15 benchmark programs, from cryptographic hashing to token transfers inside a small EVM interpreter, it is 10 to 39 times faster on average than the fastest existing zkVMs on the same machine, and more than 300 times faster than two others on a token-transfer benchmark. An optimized Magnetar proves 9.5–12.8 million cycles per second, which increases each speedup reported here by about 1.3×. Its proofs verify in about 12 milliseconds. Its security rests on standard cryptography. Magnetar depends on a standard hash function such as SHA-256 or SHA-3, the same primitives that already protect every organization’s systems. It requires no elliptic curves, no lattices, no special-purpose hash functions, no trusted setup, and no unproven conjecture about error-correcting codes. Hash functions are the most thoroughly studied primitives in the cryptographic toolkit, and they are the basis of the stateless hash-based signatures that NIST standardized as its own conservative post-quantum option. For a system that must still be trustworthy in many decades to come, relying only on standard hash functions removes a cryptographic migration from the roadmap. The same design decision pays a second dividend. Checking a Magnetar proof consists mostly of evaluating standard hash functions and binary-field arithmetic, which are exactly the operations Magnetar proves efficiently. Verifying a proof is therefore an ordinary workload for it. This is what allows Magnetar to prove computations of any size, by proving them in pieces and then combining the pieces. This also allows Magnetar to prove a long-running system such as a ledger or a blockchain. The technical paper gives the full design, security analysis, and measurements. Looking ahead Magnetar advances zero-knowledge proofs and verifiable computing to a stage where they can be built on the cryptography that organizations already trust, at speeds that make it usable, by engineers who write normal code. Magnetar enables a future where cryptographic proofs are a routine output of computation. We expect that technology leaders will stop asking whether proofs of execution are practical and focus instead on which results would they prefer to verify rather than taking on trust . If you’re interested in exploring how zero-knowledge proofs can support your use case, we’d love to hear from you (opens in new tab) . items.content: Agentic AI / Generative AI How to Rewrite Apache Spark UDFs for GPU Acceleration with AI Agents Oct 13, 2026 By Rishi Chandra and Erik Ordentlich Like Discuss (0) L T F R E AI-Generated Summary NVIDIA cuDF plugin for Apache Spark leverages GPU parallelism to accelerate data analytics workloads and improve total cost of ownership. User-defined functions in Spark break the declarative abstraction, forcing GPU-accelerated pipelines to fall back to CPU execution and incur data transfer overhead. UDFs can be rewritten using Spark SQL expressions, the RapidsUDF interface with the Java API for cuDF , or custom CUDA kernels via JNI to eliminate fallback and achieve over 20x speedups. The cuDF skills for Apache Spark provide agent-driven workflows that guide testing, conversion, benchmarking, and optimization with verification-driven feedback loops. A major consumer technology company converted more than 30 production UDFs using this workflow, with one rewrite reducing operator time from 274.55 to 12.78 hours across a 600-billion-row workload. Next Steps Install the cuDF skills for Apache Spark to begin rewriting UDFs with agent assistance. Watch the Data + AI Summit session on coding AI agents for Spark UDF GPU acceleration for a deeper walkthrough. Follow the cuDF plugin for Apache Spark getting-started guide to enable GPU acceleration in Spark pipelines. Powered by NVIDIA Nemotron. AI-generated content may summarize information incompletely. Verify important information. Learn more Enterprise applications have become increasingly demanding. Agentic AI has compounded the need for vast amounts of enterprise data with frequent, complex queries across increasingly large datasets. Meeting that demand requires greater data throughput without a proportional increase in cost. NVIDIA cuDF addresses this challenge by leveraging the massive parallelism and high-bandwidth memory of GPUs for data analytics. Particularly, the NVIDIA cuDF plugin for Apache Spark brings this acceleration to Apache Spark , the industry-leading platform for big data processing and analytics, to achieve better TCO performance in major workloads. User-defined functions (UDFs) have long been problematic for accelerated query engines, introducing runtime overheads due to their opaque nature. While UDFs can often be replaced with more performant code, rewriting UDFs has long been a laborious process requiring careful validation. This post describes how to use agents to rewrite UDFs into GPU-accelerated equivalents within minutes, achieving 22x+ speedups in Apache Spark jobs . We’ll introduce the cuDF skills for Apache Spark , a set of skills to quickly break through the UDF bottleneck for end-to-end development, from testing, to benchmarking, through integration. The UDF challenge cuDF achieves seamless GPU acceleration in part due to Apache Spark’s declarative programming interface. The SQL / Dataframe abstractions are powerful because they separate what a query should produce from how the system should execute it. This enables the cuDF plugin to transparently parallelize row-wise operations using the massive SIMD capabilities of GPUs, without any change in user code. Apache Spark, however, also supports UDFs: custom routines to extend built-in functionality. While useful for implementing bespoke business logic, UDFs break the declarative abstraction—they contain arbitrary user code which the system cannot reason about or parallelize in any general sense. During execution, the GPU accelerator must convert the data from a columnar to row-wise format, and fall back to the CPU to execute the UDF row-by-row: Figure 1.A CPU UDF forces an otherwise GPU-resident pipeline to convert columnar batches to rows, execute on the CPU, and convert back to columnar format Thus in an otherwise accelerated query, UDFs have the following drawbacks: The UDF incurs a round-trip data transfer overhead due to fallback. The UDF forgoes potential compute speedup, had it been written using GPU-accelerated primitives. Accelerating UDFs With a small, targeted code change, many UDFs can be rewritten into a GPU-accelerable form by using the right primitives. Rewriting UDFs eliminates the overhead associated with accelerator fallback, and can yield speedups of over 20x . We outline three approaches to rewrite UDFs: Approach Complexity Best For SQL Low, highest level of abstraction Simple relational logic, e.g. small or inlined functions cuDF Medium, more flexibility and control over execution Most cases, e.g. moderately complex logic like string parsing, nested types CUDA High, maximum flexibility and kernel-level control Most complex or performance critical logic Table 1. Comparison of SQL, cuDF, and CUDA approaches for rewriting Spark UDFs, organized by complexity and best-fit use case To make these approaches concrete, consider a simple Scala UDF that converts temperature from Celsius to Fahrenheit: final class ToFahrenheit extends Function1[java.lang.Double, java.lang.Double] with Serializable { override def apply(celsius: java.lang.Double): java.lang.Double = { if (celsius == null) null else celsius * 9.0 / 5.0 + 32.0 } } spark.udf.register("to_fahrenheit", new ToFahrenheit) spark.sql(""" SELECT *, to_fahrenheit(celsius) AS fahrenheit FROM temperatures """) Rewriting the UDF with SQL The most direct solution for simple UDFs is to replace the UDF with an equivalent Spark SQL expression: spark.sql(""" SELECT *, celsius * 9.0 / 5.0 + 32.0 AS fahrenheit FROM temperatures """) This makes the function visible in Spark’s expression tree. During query planning, the cuDF plugin will replace these expressions with their corresponding GPU implementations, keeping the data and execution fully on the GPU. Rewriting the UDF with cuDF When SQL primitives are insufficient or undesirable, the UDF can instead operate directly on GPU columns using the RapidsUDF interface, a contract provided by the cuDF plugin. The contract requires a single method, evaluateColumnar : import ai.rapids.cudf.{ColumnVector, Scalar} import com.nvidia.spark.RapidsUDF import scala.util.Using final class ToFahrenheit extends Function1[java.lang.Double, java.lang.Double] with Serializable with RapidsUDF { override def apply(celsius: java.lang.Double): java.lang.Double = { if (celsius == null) null else celsius * 9.0 / 5.0 + 32.0 } override def evaluateColumnar( numRows: Int, args: ColumnVector*): ColumnVector = { Using.Manager { use => val scale = use(Scalar.fromDouble(9.0 / 5.0)) val offset = use(Scalar.fromDouble(32.0)) val scaled = use(args.head.mul(scale)) scaled.add(offset) }.get } } The cuDF plugin recognizes instances of the RapidsUDF interface and passes a GPU-resident ColumnVector to the evaluateColumnar function. The function then composes operations from the Java API for cuDF operations to process the column in parallel. This approach provides a richer API for more complex processing. Rewriting the UDF with CUDA For highly complex logic that cannot be efficiently composed from existing cuDF operations, a RapidsUDF can invoke a custom CUDA kernel through the Java Native Interface (JNI) . We’ve elided the code for brevity, but examples of CUDA conversions can be found in the cuDF examples for Spark UDFs . Efficient rewrites with AI agents Despite the performance benefits, UDF rewrites can require significant engineering effort. They demand careful API selection, semantic validation, and performance measurement, while columnar APIs can be unfamiliar to practitioners with less experience in vectorized programming. Fortunately, much of this work is well suited to coding agents. With proper guardrails, an agent can search unfamiliar APIs, implement candidate rewrites, and iterate quickly while executable tests and performance measurements determine whether each change is acceptable. Available skills The cuDF skills for Apache Spark decompose the rewrite into four focused feedback loops. Each skill defines both the work to perform and the evidence required before proceeding to the next stage: Figure 2. Four skills guide agents through testing, conversion, benchmarking, and optimization, with verification-driven feedback loops at each stage Scaffolding and design Reliable agent execution begins with a reliable development environment. The skills provide a complete project template containing the cuDF- and Spark-specific scaffolding required for end-to-end development. This includes test and benchmark harnesses, encoded routines for output verification, and build configuration. By encoding this knowledge into code, the agent can focus on the UDF rather than repeatedly reconstructing specialized infrastructure. The skills also provide best practices for GPU programming with cuDF, including memory management and configuration. This serves as an advisory tips and tricks reference. To best leverage the power of frontier models, the agent remains free to explore different implementations based on surrounding context and select an approach based on measured correctness and performance. Performance results A major consumer technology company used this workflow to convert 30+ UDFs used in production data pipelines into GPU-accelerated implementations. The rewrites preserved the behavior of the original CPU UDFs while removing costly fallbacks from otherwise GPU-accelerated workloads. As an example, the following benchmark shows the resulting before-and-after performance for a UDF in one such workload: Figure 3. Rewriting a production CPU-based UDF with cuDF reduced operator time from 274.55 to 12.78 hours, a 22x speedup across a 600-billion-row workload This particular UDF was affecting more than 3,000+ jobs , and in this job, saw a 22x speedup when implemented as a cuDF-enabled RapidsUDF. With the help of agents, these performance gains are much more attainable, enabling practitioners to iterate on rewrites on the order of hours rather than days or weeks, without compromising correctness. Get started Converting UDFs to GPU implementations can unlock major speedups and contribute to overall cost savings in GPU-accelerated pipelines. With agent skills, the rewrite process can be made both easy and reliable. To get started, install the cuDF skills for Apache Spark on GitHub , either directly or using the npx skill installer: npx skills add NVIDIA/cudf-spark --skill ‘*’ For a deeper walkthrough of the workflow and practical lessons from building it, see the Data + AI Summit session, Coding with AI Agents to Supercharge Your Spark UDFs with GPU Acceleration . To learn more about GPU acceleration for Apache Spark, follow the cuDF plugin for Apache Spark getting-started guide to unlock better performance and TCO across your Spark pipelines. Visit our webpage to learn more about NVIDIA cuDF: GPU-Accelerated Structured Data Processing , or you can read the docs for more information on NVIDIA cuDF plugin for Apache Spark . He holds a bachelor’s degree in Computer Science from Johns Hopkins University. He holds a PhD in electrical engineering from Stanford University. View all posts by Erik Ordentlich Comments
