Figure 5: The sandbox loop from panel A in Figure 1 above: isolated tool session, terminal database state, side effects, executable judges. Each task defines a starting backend state, a user goal, the available MCP tools, the domain policy, and executable checks over the terminal state. A simulated user holds private context (a booking reference, a preference, or a date of birth) and releases it only when asked. Every attempt gets an isolated MCP session with freshly initialized state. Two attempts of the same task never share a database row or cached tool state, which is what makes 20-trial comparison meaningful. At the end, a side-effect extractor derives what actually changed, and deterministic judges compare it against the required end state, accepting any trajectory that produces the right outcome while rejecting wrong, missing or extra effects. For requirements with no clean database value ("did the agent disclose this is not guaranteed?"), a narrow binary rubric question handles the semantics. 477 of the 507 tasks are graded on state alone; 30 add response rubrics. The trust boundary: the model sees tasks, dialogue and tool schemas. Golden state, assertions, grading internals and credentials stay on the evaluator side. Run it yourself ThinkingBox is now on Hugging Face, both the harness and the dataset . ThinkingBox-Bench now sits behind the OpenEnv interface, and each finished episode returns a binary pass/fail reward. The released adapter is designed for evaluation; separate, non-benchmark scenarios can use the same interface in training workflows. Before you start Tested on Linux and WSL, with Python 3.11+, uv and Docker. You also need a thinkingbox-data checkout at the pinned release and model endpoints for the agent, simulated user and judge. OpenEnv + the ThinkingBox environment git clone https://github.com/huggingface/OpenEnv cd OpenEnv uv sync --project envs/thinkingbox_env --frozen # 2. The executable benchmark, at the pinned release git clone https://github.com/microsoft/thinkingbox-data git -C thinkingbox-data checkout thinkingbox-bench-v1.0 # 3. The ThinkingBox CLI, which provides `tb` uv tool install "thinkingbox @ git+https://github.com/microsoft/thinkingbox" Start Typesense In a second terminal , start Typesense 30.1 and wait for its health check: mkdir -p .typesense-data docker run -- rm -d --name thinkingbox-typesense \ -p 8108:8108 \ -v " $PWD /.typesense-data:/data" \ typesense/typesense:30.1 \ --data-dir /data --api-key=Fake --enable-cors until curl -fsS http://127.0.0.1:8108/health; do sleep 1; done Start the MCP servers In a third terminal , start the Session Proxy and MCP servers. cd OpenEnv tb mcp-start --host 127.0.0.1 --port 7111 \ --servers " $PWD /thinkingbox-data/servers/servers.yaml" curl -fsS http://127.0.0.1:7111/health Start the OpenEnv server Back in the first terminal, start the OpenEnv server against a ThinkingBox YAML config naming your three models ( config guide ): OPENENV_TB_CONFIG= " $PWD /thinkingbox.yaml" \ uv run --project envs/thinkingbox_env --frozen server Check readiness Gate on readiness before running anything. It returns 503 until its observable data, configuration and Session Proxy checks pass. Whatever k your use case justifies; say whether you are reporting best-of-k or every-of-k, and how you computed it. Enterprise Article Published October 3, 2026 Upvote 81 +75 Tuhin Kundu tuhink Follow microsoft Microsoft ThinkingBox grades AI agents on the records they leave behind, not the sentences they generate, and then asks whether they can do it twenty times in a row. It is now available through Hugging Face. Figure 1: ThinkingBox runs an agent against isolated MCP tool sessions, then grades the terminal backend state and side effects it leaves behind. From our ThinkingBox paper . This is a joint blog by Microsoft and Hugging Face, special thanks to Tommy Guy (founder at Enderis AI, previously Microsoft), Sergio Paniego from Hugging Face and our former interns Zhuochun Li (University of Pittsburgh), Ali Keramati (UC Irvine), Youngmin Ko (Northwestern) for co-authoring/reviewing efforts. A customer writes in. Her $745 kitchen appliance has been stuck in a courier "exception" at a Nashville distribution center, fifteen days past its estimated delivery date. The AI agent does careful work. Nine tool calls: it pulls the order, checks tracking, looks up her customer profile, searches the refund policy twice, confirms no ticket exists, opens one, documents the timeline, and reads the policy correctly; her account segment genuinely does not qualify for late-delivery compensation. Then it closes the ticket as resolved and replies “ Since your query is resolved, is there anything I may assist you with? ” Two things are wrong. The carrier exception is still open, so the required end state was on hold , pending resolution. And the customer never got a real answer to what she actually asked. An AI grader checking tool calls would see nine well-formed ones. The grader checking whether the agent wrote to the database would see that too. The database is what disagrees . That gap is what ThinkingBox measures. Across 507 stateful business workflows, each run 20 times against various LLM models, it grades agents on terminal backend state and side effects. This post covers what we found, what consistency costs, and how to run the benchmark yourself through OpenEnv . You can run this one yourself: the example above is adapted from a benchmark task sandbox_external_retail_group1.py:test_case_ST003_006 , and the executable check that fails is a single field: the ticket's status is solved where the required end state is hold. The full trace is in Appendix D.4, Case 3 of our paper . Contents A tool call is not an outcome One success is not reliability Can you depend on the model behind your agent? What consistency costs Failure signatures How it works Run it yourself Where this goes next Want to try it before reading the results? Skip to section Run it yourself . A tool call is not an outcome Final responses and valid tool calls are only proxies. An agent can sound correct while leaving the wrong value, changing the wrong record, or creating an extra side effect. Only the records it leaves behind settle the question. The gap is substantial. In a common-set ablation covering 121,680 valid trials across 12 LLM models, 79,853 attempts failed the executable checks. Of those failures, 67.24% still terminated cleanly, invoked a state-changing tool, and reported no final tool error. Executable checks nevertheless found wrong field values in 77.61% of them, unintended extra effects in 43.30%, and missing required effects in 25.36%. Those state-check findings overlap. A trajectory is a claim. Database state is the evidence. Repetition is the trust test. One success is not reliability An agent that processes a refund correctly once and mishandles it the next four times is not a working refund agent. So every task runs 20 independent times , each from an identical clean backend, and we report three different things: Table 1: The three numbers we report, and the question each one answers. Metric What it measures What it answers pass@1 Share of all attempts that succeeded How does it usually do? pass@20 Share of tasks solved at least once in 20 tries Can it ever do this? Breadth. Observed 20/20 Tasks that actually passed all 20 recorded attempts Can it always be correct? We use observed 20/20 in this blog post as the literal count of how many of the 507 tasks passed 20 out of 20. No estimator, no smoothing. Starting with the familiar view. items.content: Back to Articles The model that didn't exist, so you made it yourself Published October 8, 2026 Update on GitHub Upvote 55 +49 yuvraj sharma ysharma Follow Abubakar Abid abidlabs Follow Last week, I wanted a small version of the prompt rewriter that ships with Qwen-Image 2.1. The official one is a 9B model that needs about 20 GB of memory and thinks for thousands of tokens before writing a single paragraph. On the Hub, I found only compressed copies of that same 9B model. So I described what I wanted to ML Intern , and the next day I had a 0.8B version that runs on a CPU. It returns valid output 99.7% of the time and uses about a quarter of the teacher's tokens. The compute for the whole project, including having the 9B model label 8,797 example requests, came to USD 16. Over the course of the next few days, I made five more models the same way. Each one started as a message in HuggingChat with ML-intern switched on, and each one ended as a public model on the Hub with its evaluation in the model card. ML-intern plans the work, asks me for a budget before it spends anything, runs a small test before the real job, then trains, evaluates and publishes on Hugging Face hardware. How I prompt ML Intern The first message is where I spend my effort. My first prompt, for the citrus model shared below, was about 450 words. By my 6th project it was closer to 2,000, because each project taught me something I wanted in the next one. All seven prompts are on GitHub at yvrjsharma/ml-intern-prompts , exactly as I wrote them. A prompt starts with the idea in one line and why I want it. Then it names the exact pieces: the dataset, the base model, the training script. Anything I have already checked goes under a heading that literally says "Verified facts, do not re-derive", so the agent spends its budget on the work instead of rediscovering what I know. For the camera-angle LoRA that section listed which trainer had just added transparent-image support, and which open GitHub issues made the fallback trainer risky. Two lines in the prompt are critical . The first asks for a baseline before any training. For example, the citrus prompt says: "Also report the base model's zero-shot score on the same metric before training so we can see the gain." Without it you get a trained model and no idea whether it is better than what you started with. The second is a smoke test with a check attached. For the image LoRAs I asked for 50 training steps, then a check that the saved weights had actually changed, before paying for the full run. At the end of the prompt, I lay out the expected deliverables and limit the cost. I define what belongs in the model card and include a instruction like: "Cap total spend at USD 12 and ask me before exceeding it." Because ML-intern begins every task with zero dollar budget and needs permission before executing paid jobs, this spending limit stays strictly enforced. When you leave out a budget, the agent suggests a couple of paths depending on project size and asks which one you prefer. You don't necessarily need all of that on your first attempt. For example, I didn't have the verified-facts section in my citrus brief and ML Intern still produced a model that more than tripled the accuracy of the Qwen3.5-2B model. Let me walk you through 6 things I built with Ml-Intern in just a couple of days. 1. A model that knows your field A general vision model can describe a yellowing citrus leaf. However, telling you whether it is a mite problem or a magnesium deficiency, and the bio and non-bio remedies to treat the plant is very hard. Using Claude, I put together a training dataset merged from three sources hosted by the Project-AgML organization on the Hub. The resulting citrus-disease-vlm-instruct is a dataset containing 3,017 annotated images across 21 distinct pests, illnesses, nutritional gaps, and treatment approaches. ML-intern handled the fine-tuning of Qwen3.5-2B using these examples, making sure to benchmark the foundation model beforehand. On the 335 test photos, the base model named the right problem 14.9% of the time. After two epochs on one A10G, the fine-tuned model got 52.8%. Compute cost, about USD 1.90. Check out: Model · Dataset · Citrus Doctor App 2. A model that draws your character Image models know plenty of characters. Huggy, drawn in the flat style of the Hugging Face brand assets, was not one of them. I asked ML-Intern for a LoRA on FLUX.2 klein base 4B , trained on 84 captioned drawings from Chunte/huggy_for_training dataset. The agent saved a checkpoint every 100 steps and drew the same set of prompts with each one, which made choosing easy. Step 200 was the first where Huggy was fully on-model . From step 500 on, Huggy's style started bleeding into prompts that had nothing to do with Huggy! The trained LoRA also works on the distilled klein model at 4 steps. Compute cost, about USD 7.60. Check out: Model · Dataset · Huggy Generator App 3. A model that does a new trick Camera-angle LoRAs are among the most-liked community add-ons for earlier Qwen-Image models. You can give the model a picture of an object and ask to see it 45 degrees from the left. When I checked a few days after the Qwen-Image 2.1 model release, nobody had made one, so I tasked ML-intern to build it. ML-intern rendered 1,030 scanned household objects from Google Scanned Objects at 24 angles each, 24,722 transparent images, on a CPU job that cost a few cents. It later finalised 461 objects for training and 40 held out for testing, and 1,844 before-and-after training pairs spread evenly over 23 camera instructions. Training ran 2,000 steps in about 90 minutes on one A100 (~USD 3.75). The whole project took about half a day and 48 jobs, counting the ones that failed on missing packages or wrong paths and had to be resubmitted by ML-Intern. Total compute cost, about USD 16. Check out: Model · Dataset · Viewpoint Orbit App Doodle-in LoRA is another cool idea. Upload a photo with a magenta scribble on it and add a short prompt naming an object. The LoRA replaces the scribble with that object while keeping the original lighting and composition consistent. No dataset existed for this, so my prompt described how to make one. Start from a real photo in Open Images, remove one object with the LaMa inpainting model, and draw a scribble where the object used to be. The untouched photo is the target. ML-intern wrote and tested the pair-building scripts in a CPU sandbox, then ran them as GPU jobs, recording the author and license of every source photo along the way. It built 6,042 training pairs and a 160-pair test set, where 40 of the test pairs come from 23 object classes kept out of training entirely. Before training, it measured the base model on its own and with the Viggle turbo LoRA, and checked that running edits in batches produced identical images, which made the evaluation cheaper. Training ran 2,000 steps in 1 hour 38 minutes on one A100 (~USD 4), and a comparison of the saved checkpoints on 48 test pairs picked step 500. Paired with the Viggle turbo LoRA at 6 steps the LoRA performed really well. 67.5% of objects detected where they were drawn, at 4.7 seconds per edit. Objects from the 23 unseen classes landed as reliably as the rest (65.0% versus 64.2%). The project took a little over a day and 59 jobs. Total compute cost, about USD 24. Check out: Model · Dataset · Doodle-in App 4. A model that fits your device The Pocket Rewriter from the top of this post is the first one. ML-intern started by generating 8,797 short image requests with a small instruct model through Inference Providers, following a mix set in my prompt: photos, posters, logos, infographics and more, about a third of them asking for exact text in quotes, and many in languages other than English. The 9B teacher then rewrote all of them on one A100 in 2 hours 37 minutes (~USD 6.50). After filtering for quality, 1,840 examples were selected for training dataset. Training the 0.8B and 2B students took 12 and 18 minutes on an A10G (USD 0.75 for both). The 0.8B also ships as an 812 MB GGUF file for running on a CPU. The project took about 11 hours and 24 jobs. Total compute cost, about USD 16. Check out: Pocket rewriter 0.8B Student · 2B Student · Dataset · Pocket Studio App · Compare the teacher-student in Rewriter Arena Agate-Preview-002-4step is the second. Logolabs' Agate Preview 002 is a 260M-parameter text-to-image model, small enough for a browser, but it needs 50 steps with guidance, which is 100 network passes per image. I asked ML-intern to distill it down to just 4 passes! It took two runs. The first cached 155,000 training images as latents, baked the guidance into the model, then cut the step count in stages from 16 to 8 to 4, all on A100s. The 4-step student beat the teacher run at the same 4 steps on GenEval and FID, after that ML-intern exported it to ONNX for the browser. This run took about 13 hours and USD 22. I did a second training run by asking ML-Intern to improve the 4-step student a bit more. It then made 24,000 more image pairs with the teacher at 16 steps and fine-tuned the 4-step student against them for about an hour. GenEval went from 0.509 to 0.536, against the teacher's 0.563 at 50 steps, with just 4 steps (one-fourth the compute). ML-intern re-exported the browser version. The second run took about 8 hours. Total compute cost across both runs, about USD 37. Check out: Agate 4-step model · Dataset · Run Agate in your browser · Agate 4-step LIVE What it cost Model Base model Compute Citrus Doctor Qwen3.5-2B USD 1.90 Huggy LoRA FLUX.2 klein base 4B USD 7.60 Pocket rewriter (0.8B and 2B) Qwen3.5-0.8B and 2B USD 16.05 Viewpoint Orbit LoRA Qwen-Image 2.1 USD 16 Doodle-in LoRA Qwen-Image 2.1 USD 24.30 Agate 4-step (two runs) Agate Preview 002 USD 37 Total about USD 103 These are the GPU and CPU job charges reported for each session. Make yours ML-intern is in HuggingChat . Switch on ML-intern mode and paste a prompt. If you want a starting point, my example prompts are free to copy. Start from a model you wish existed and a dataset you have, or one you can describe. Give it a small budget, ask for a baseline and a smoke test, and read what comes back before you raise the cap. If you make something with it, share it on X and tag @Gradio and @HuggingFace . We would love to see the models you make that nobody else would think to build for you. items.content: Back to Articles Run fast, private agents on-device with LFM2.5-24B-A2B Team Article Published October 13, 2026 Upvote 59 +53 Raahul Vignesh Raahul26 Follow LiquidAI Song Duong sduong Follow LiquidAI Akhilesh Deepak Gotmare akhileshdeepakgotmare Follow LiquidAI Fernando Fernandes Neto fernandofernandes Follow LiquidAI Jiahui Wang WWWjiahui Follow LiquidAI Mayank Agarwal mayankagarwal Follow LiquidAI nathan ranchin nathanrchn Follow LiquidAI Sergei Tilga tilgasergey Follow LiquidAI Sinoué GAD GAD-cell Follow LiquidAI Tim Seyde tseyde Follow LiquidAI Zetian Li zetianli Follow LiquidAI changyi yang changyiyang Follow LiquidAI Simon Lee yungisimon Follow LiquidAI Leonie Monigatti iamleonie Follow LiquidAI Maxime Labonne mlabonne Follow LiquidAI Karthik Macherla karthikrmacherla Follow LiquidAI Alfred Eng alfredeng Follow LiquidAI Khoi Nguyen KTLK Follow LiquidAI Paul Pak paulpak58 Follow LiquidAI xx tugot17 Follow LiquidAI Tarek Dakhran tdakhran Follow LiquidAI Anthony Maltsev amaltsev Follow LiquidAI Aldo Gael Carranza agcarranza Follow LiquidAI Tyler Murray undfined Follow LiquidAI Aditya Tadimeti adityatadimeti Follow LiquidAI Jimmy T.H. Smith jimmysmith1919 Follow LiquidAI Yuri Khrustalev ykhrustalev Follow LiquidAI LFM2.5-24B-A2B is a 24B-parameter reasoning model with just 2B active parameters, built for fast, private agents on-device. It thinks before it answers, calls tools, and works through multi-step tasks inside popular agent harnesses. Because only 2B parameters are active per token, each reasoning token is cheap, so you can run agents continuously on your own hardware. Best-in-class agent: Competitive with Qwen3.6-35B-A3B, a model with ~50% more total and active parameters, on agentic and tool-use tasks, scoring 48.09 on LiveClaw versus 38.19. Reasoning at MoE speed: Always thinks before it answers. With only 2B active parameters per token, each reasoning token is cheap. Efficient inference: 184 tok/s on an Apple M5 Max and up to 21K output tok/s on a single NVIDIA B300 GPU. How we built a reasoning agent with 2B active parameters LFM2.5-24B-A2B builds on LFM2-24B-A2B and keeps its architecture: 40 layers, 64 experts per MoE block with top-4 routing, and the same hybrid of gated short convolutions and GQA. The context window grows from 32K to 131K tokens, and an in-place tokenizer expansion doubles the vocabulary from 65K to 128K tokens for better non-Latin tokenization. Unlike its predecessor, it is a reasoning-only model that produces an explicit chain of thought before its final answer. Pre-training was scaled up from ~17T to ~33T tokens. Mid-training then adds 2T tokens at 32K context, weighted toward reasoning, math, code, instruction following, and multilingual text, and 300B tokens at 131K context, weighted toward long-context data. Tool calls and multi-turn trajectories appear throughout both phases. Post-training turns the base model into an agent in five stages: Supervised fine-tuning (SFT) Teacher specialization Multi-domain on-policy distillation (MOPD), non-agentic: distill the specialist teachers on non-agentic tasks. MOPD, agentic: a second distillation stage focused on agentic tasks. Agentic reinforcement learning (Agentic RL): train the model inside agent harnesses, such as OpenClaw , Hermes Agent , Pi , and OpenCode . Benchmark results We evaluated LFM2.5-24B-A2B against Qwen3.6-35B-A3B, Gemma-4-26B-A4B-it, and Nemotron-3.5-Lightning on 16 benchmarks covering tool use and agentic workflows, knowledge, instruction following, math, and coding. It is the smallest model in the group, yet it is competitive with MoEs with ~50% more total and active parameters. Benchmark LFM2.5-24B-A2B Qwen3.6-35B-A3B Gemma-4-26B-A4B-it Nemotron-3.5-Lightning (30B-A3B) AutomationBench 27.69 8.72 5.46 2.61 BFCLv4 65.01 65.00 57.09 53.78 ToolSandbox 80.71 75.02 72.09 75.13 LiveClaw 48.09 38.19 41.25 37.72 PinchBench 83.18 89.93 77.12 84.20 τ³-Bench Banking 8.04 7.63 4.54 7.01 WebArena Verified 26.75 37.62 25.62 28.69 GPQA Diamond 74.42 83.69 74.90 72.42 AA-Omniscience -24.90 -24.35 -59.39 -3.58 HLE 7.40 7.69 8.57 5.65 IFEval 96.75 93.06 92.00 94.19 IFBench 74.69 64.21 47.44 71.67 Multi-IF 84.38 81.53 82.19 82.34 MATH-500 96.04 96.73 95.66 96.40 SWE-Bench Verified (OpenCode) 51.00 66.20 25.80 53.40 SciCode 32.71 37.35 35.42 27.78 *All the models were evaluated with vLLM, using each benchmark's recommended generation parameters. For your app, the strengths are tool use and instruction following. LFM2.5-24B-A2B leads or matches the competition on five of the eight tool-use and agentic benchmarks (AutomationBench, BFCLv4, ToolSandbox, LiveClaw, and τ³-Bench Banking), and on AutomationBench it scores more than three times the next-best model. It also leads on all three instruction-following benchmarks. Larger models keep an edge on knowledge-heavy benchmarks like GPQA Diamond, HLE, and AA-Omniscience, and on coding benchmarks like SWE-Bench Verified (OpenCode) and SciCode, so pair LFM2.5-24B-A2B with retrieval or web search for knowledge-heavy workloads. These results make LFM2.5-24B-A2B a strong foundation for agents that need to reason, call tools, and run reliably on your device. Inference speed on CPU and GPU LFM2.5-24B-A2B ships with day-one support across the inference ecosystem, including llama.cpp, MLX, vLLM, SGLang, and ONNX. Edge inference. LFM2.5-24B-A2B is the fastest of the compared MoEs, decoding 184 tokens/s on an M5 Max and 114 tokens/s on a Ryzen AI Max+ 395. That is up to 1.7x faster than the next-best model, while using the least memory. GPU inference. LFM2.5-24B-A2B is the fastest model in its size class, reaching over 21K output tokens per second at high concurrency on a single B300. How to use LFM2.5-24B-A2B Reach for LFM2.5-24B-A2B when you need agents that reason, call tools, and run reliably on your device. It thinks before it answers, calls tools, and works through multi-step tasks inside popular agent harnesses. Because only 2B parameters are active per token, each reasoning token is cheap, so you can run agents continuously on your own hardware. Best-in-class agent: Competitive with Qwen3.6-35B-A3B, a model with ~50% more total and active parameters, on agentic and tool-use tasks, scoring 48.09 on LiveClaw versus 38.19. Reasoning at MoE speed: Always thinks before it answers. With only 2B active parameters per token, each reasoning token is cheap. Efficient inference: 184 tok/s on an Apple M5 Max and up to 21K output tok/s on a single NVIDIA B300 GPU. How we built a reasoning agent with 2B active parameters LFM2.5-24B-A2B builds on LFM2-24B-A2B and keeps its architecture: 40 layers, 64 experts per MoE block with top-4 routing, and the same hybrid of gated short convolutions and GQA. The context window grows from 32K to 131K tokens, and an in-place tokenizer expansion doubles the vocabulary from 65K to 128K tokens for better non-Latin tokenization. Unlike its predecessor, it is a reasoning-only model that produces an explicit chain of thought before its final answer. Pre-training was scaled up from ~17T to ~33T tokens. Mid-training then adds 2T tokens at 32K context, weighted toward reasoning, math, code, instruction following, and multilingual text, and 300B tokens at 131K context, weighted toward long-context data. Tool calls and multi-turn trajectories appear throughout both phases. Post-training turns the base model into an agent in five stages: Supervised fine-tuning (SFT) Teacher specialization Multi-domain on-policy distillation (MOPD), non-agentic: distill the specialist teachers on non-agentic tasks. MOPD, agentic: a second distillation stage focused on agentic tasks. Agentic reinforcement learning (Agentic RL): train the model inside agent harnesses, such as OpenClaw , Hermes Agent , Pi , and OpenCode . Benchmark results We evaluated LFM2.5-24B-A2B against Qwen3.6-35B-A3B, Gemma-4-26B-A4B-it, and Nemotron-3.5-Lightning on 16 benchmarks covering tool use and agentic workflows, knowledge, instruction following, math, and coding. It is the smallest model in the group, yet it is competitive with MoEs with ~50% more total and active parameters. items.content: Back to Articles Scaling Indic Pretraining: 2.8 Trillion Tokens and an Open Data Generation Pipeline Enterprise + Article Published October 16, 2026 Upvote 1 Will Jennings WillJenningsDC Follow nvidia Kiran Praveen kipraveen Follow nvidia Sriharsha Niverty sniverty Follow nvidia Raviraj Joshi ravirajoshi Follow nvidia Markus Kliegl mkliegl-nv Follow nvidia Yev Meyer nv-3mei Follow nvidia Utkarsh Vaidya uvaidya Follow nvidia Native-script data for 22 languages, romanized data for twelve, and a reusable GPU-accelerated pipeline for translation, quality assessment, and repair. Authors: AI4Bharat — Mohammed Safi Ur Rahman Khan, Mitesh Khapra, Anoop Kunchukuttan. NVIDIA — Niket Agarwal, Raviraj Joshi, Anusha Kamath, Markus Kliegl, Yev Meyer, Sriharsha Niverty, Kiran Praveen, Utkarsh Vaidya. We're excited to introduce Nemotron-pretraining-Indic-v1 approximately 2.8 trillion tokens across 22 Indian languages , releasing soon alongside the open, GPU-accelerated data generation pipeline used to create it. These are the 22 languages listed in India's Constitution: the first languages for 97% of Indians, or nearly 1.2 billion citizens at the 2011 Census. Developed by NVIDIA with IIT Madras , India's premier engineering institute, and its AI4Bharat lab, this release gives model builders a substantial new resource for Indic pretraining. The pipeline captures the full generation recipe, including prompts, LLM workflows, and quality checks, so developers can adapt it to their own source material and generate more data for their needs. AI4Bharat, IIT Madras' Indian language research lab, builds open-source datasets and models for Indian languages. Its resources, such as Sangraha , an open pretraining corpus for 22 Indian languages, have helped lay the foundation for open Indic language-model research. Our joint open-source release represents a substantial expansion of the open synthetic Indic training data that will be available to the community. It brings a broad mix of curated English material, including mathematics, code, and question-answer content, into Indian languages, giving teams more training material for building models that can explain technical concepts, work through problems, and answer questions in those languages. Every record traces back to a curated source document, and each output is checked against its input, so the synthetic text stays grounded in real information. Mitesh Khapra, who heads AI4Bharat and made the 2025 TIME100 AI list , has named the core problem: Indian language technology trails English because "we do not have enough data for Indian languages." We're answering that call with more data, plus an open recipe for generating more. The corpus also accounts for how people write. It includes native-script data for all 22 languages and romanized text for twelve, spanning 34 language-script configurations. Our workflows combine document-level translation, quality assessment, and targeted repair, with checks to preserve content such as equations, tables, and code. This data complements naturally authored Indic text, which remains essential for local knowledge and cultural context. We're sharing the open generation recipe so the community can not just reproduce the data but take this work further. Teams can use the corpus directly, adapt the prompts and quality checks, or bring their own source documents to the workflow. By opening up both the data and the process, we aim to make large-scale Indic data generation more accessible and enable more developers to contribute to stronger models across Indian languages. Continued pretraining for Nemotron 3.5 Super VL added 10 billion Indic tokens, drawn from a twelve-language subset of this corpus and natural Indic text. Our technical report on the model covers the full story. We plan to build on this corpus in future Nemotron models. What is in the corpus? Figure 1. The corpus contains 2,601.0 billion native-script tokens and 224.6 billion romanized tokens. Counts use the Gemma-4 tokenizer. Document records include translations and script variants of shared sources; they are not counts of unique English documents. The corpus has two groups of language configurations: Native-script and romanized data: Bengali, Gujarati, Hindi, Kannada, Malayalam, Marathi, Nepali, Odia, Punjabi, Tamil, Telugu, and Urdu. Native-script data: Assamese, Bodo, Dogri, Kashmiri, Konkani, Maithili, Manipuri, Sanskrit, Santali, and Sindhi. Here, native-script describes the writing system: the text is still translated from English. Romanized means Indic-language text written in Latin script, not an English translation. For each of the twelve dual-script languages, romanization covers a subset of the accepted native-script translations. This distinction matters when constructing a training mixture. Native and romanized records offer different script exposure, but can express the same underlying content. The token counts describe the retained corpus, including accepted rewrites, rather than a training run's token budget. Counts also depend on the tokenizer used, so corpus inventory and training-token counts should be read separately. From English source documents to Indic training data To build this corpus, we start with documents from 15 Nemotron-CC-v2 subsets, covering web text, question-answer material, mathematics, code, and other specialized content. We use NeMo Data Designer , NVIDIA's open-source framework for generating synthetic data, to run translation, quality checks, and targeted repair. Throughout the workflow, we retain each source identifier so developers can trace an output back to its original document. Clear provenance like this is part of what makes open data practical to audit and build on. Figure 2 shows the workflow for twelve languages. Figure 2. Four-stage Indic synthetic-data pipeline for twelve languages, implemented using NeMo Data Designer and Gemma-4-31B-it. We translate English documents, assess translation quality, repair low-scoring outputs, and convert a subset of accepted translations into Latin script. The other ten languages use the separate Indic Translate workflow described below. The twelve-language workflow For these twelve languages, we translate documents in full so the model can use context across paragraphs, tables, and equations. We selected Gemma-4-31B-it by comparing models on complete documents, checking translation quality and preservation of technical content. Our prompts distinguish prose to translate from content to preserve, including code, equations, URLs, and formatting. After translation, we use the same model to assess each output against its English source. A rubric inspired by Multidimensional Quality Metrics (MQM), an open framework for classifying translation errors by type and severity, covers meaning, fluency, terminology, style, and formatting. We retain only outputs scoring at least 75 out of 100 (a rubric score, not an accuracy percentage). For lower-scoring outputs, we use the assessment feedback to guide repairs, then reassess them against the same threshold. This process recovered 438.4 billion tokens across native-script and romanized data, already included in the corpus total. Sampled human reviews and tests with deliberately introduced errors helped identify omissions and residual English, informing improvements to our prompts and checks. Accepted native-script translations also provide the starting point for romanized data. We convert a subset into Latin script and check each result against its native-script input. This separates translation from script conversion. In our initial human comparison, this two-step approach produced fewer hallucinated additions and less residual English than generating romanized text directly from English. The ten-language workflow For the other ten languages, we adapt the workflow to address long-document quality and script-stability issues observed in our comparisons. We translate with Indic Translate , a document-level translation model for English and 22 Indian languages from Bodhan AI , a nonprofit center for AI in education incubated at IIT Madras. Gemma-4-31B-it then assesses each translation against its English source. For eight languages, we keep the whole-document approach. For longer Santali documents, we translate overlapping windows and reconstruct the document; for Manipuri, we translate into Bengali script before converting to Meitei Mayek, its native script. These workflows retain outputs scoring at least 75 out of 100 and produce native-script data only, without feedback-based rewriting. What changed after Indic continued pretraining? The Nemotron 3.5 Super VL technical report compares the checkpoint immediately before Indic continued pretraining (CPT) with the checkpoint after that stage. The configured budget was 100 billion training tokens, with 10% (10 billion tokens) allocated to a mixture of synthetic and natural Indic text. The remaining 90% maintained the preceding training mixture's relative proportions. Scores increased on all five reported Indic knowledge and reasoning benchmarks: MILU, Indic MMLU-Pro, Indic ARC-Challenge, Indic ARC-Easy, and Indic GSM8K. Figure 3. Nemotron 3.5 Super VL before and after the Indic CPT stage. Gains range from 4.98 to 9.82 percentage points. The comparison reports the change across a training stage that combines synthetic and natural Indic data, rather than isolating the synthetic corpus's contribution. Language coverage differs by benchmark; these are stage-level checkpoints, not a comparison of final model releases. Source: Nemotron 3.5 Super VL technical report, Table 2. GSM8K excludes Odia because evaluation exceeded the serving context limit. These gains support the combined synthetic-and-natural Indic CPT recipe, while leaving the choice of mixture for other models and languages to further study. The companion Indic report examines source mixtures, synthetic-data pool size, and script coverage using first-pass accepted data for the twelve-language group. Evaluating the full corpus, including recovered rewrites and the other ten languages, remains a next step for those controlled studies. Broader Indic capabilities in Nemotron 3.5 Super VL Beyond the CPT-stage results, how does the released model compare with the previous generation? Figure 4 compares Nemotron 3.5 Super VL with Nemotron 3 Super across Indic task performance and language quality. These results reflect the released model's full training pipeline, including Indic CPT and post-training. Nemotron 3.5 Super VL scores higher on five of the six task benchmarks shown, spanning knowledge, reasoning, mathematics, code, and translation. Instruction following on IFEval 1.5 dipped 2.04 points. It also improves across all four IndiVibe dimensions: usefulness, fluency, language and script fidelity, and appropriate verbosity. IndiVibe is Sarvam AI's open benchmark of assistant-style prompts in Indian languages. Together, these evaluations examine both what the model can do and how well it communicates in Indian languages. Figure 4. Indic task performance and language quality across Nemotron Super generations. Left: six task benchmarks. Right: preliminary IndiVibe conditional preference scores, not direct head-to-head win rates. Labels show changes in percentage points, except WMT24++, which uses chrF points. See the companion Indic technical report for benchmark and evaluation details. Start building Load the corpus Start with the languages and scripts your model needs, inspect a sample, and review the dataset card and license before training. Configurations use language, script, and region tags: for example, hi-Deva-IN denotes Hindi in Devanagari, while hi-Latn-IN denotes romanized Hindi. The example below asks for the repository ID from the dataset card, then discovers the available splits and streams a sample. from datasets import get_dataset_split_names, load_dataset dataset_id = input ( "Repository ID from the dataset card: " ).strip() config = "hi-Deva-IN" splits = get_dataset_split_names(dataset_id, config_name=config) print ( "Available splits:" , splits) data = load_dataset( dataset_id, name=config, split=splits[ 0 ], streaming= True ) print ( next ( iter (data))) Hugging Face Datasets supports streaming so readers can inspect records without downloading the entire corpus. Once the release is available, pin a dataset revision for reproducible experiments. For a first training study , compare mixtures at a fixed token budget and record the natural/synthetic and native/romanized shares. Track per-language results alongside English capability retention and language/script quality. When creating held-out splits, account for records derived from the same source across languages and scripts. To build a fuller recipe, pair the corpus with Nemotron post-training data, such as the Chat & Instruction or Post-Training Blends collections. For India-specific synthetic data, seed NeMo Data Designer with Nemotron-Personas-India , synthetic personas in English and Hindi grounded in real-world distributions for India. Adapt the generation recipe The open-source Nemotron Bharat translation plugin for NeMo Data Designer provides translation and evaluation prompts, optional feedback-based rewriting, document windowing, and script-remapping support. Use its configuration reference to choose models and languages, adapt prompts to your domain, and set rewrite parameters. The accompanying developer note explains the workflow and engineering choices. Start with a small sample of your own source documents. Inspect translation quality and preservation of code, mathematics, and formatting, then refine the prompts and checks with native-language reviewers before scaling up. Treat generation and corpus acceptance as separate steps: the plugin returns candidates and scores, while your filtering policy determines which records enter the training corpus. Scope and limitations Translation broadens access to the source material, but does not replace text originally written in Indian languages or guarantee coverage of local knowledge and culture. We recommend combining this corpus with appropriately sourced natural Indic text and evaluating the resulting mixture for the intended use case. Quality assessment is primarily automated, complemented by sampled human review whose coverage varies across languages. For the twelve-language workflow (Figure 2), the translator also serves as the judge. Retained text can still contain errors, and the ten-language workflow needs broader native-speaker validation. Source-ID checks remove processing duplicates; they are not semantic deduplication of similar content. Alongside the corpus, AI4Bharat at IIT Madras, with support from NVIDIA, is building Indic-LLM-Eval-Suite, an open and evolving collection of benchmarks for Indic model capabilities. It helps model builders assess both task performance and language quality. See the companion blog, Better Models Need Better Benchmarks: Introducing Indic-LLM-Eval-Suite . Explore the language configurations, test a training mixture, or adapt the open recipe to a new domain. Sharing per-language results and improvements to the generation workflow can help the community build on this work. Further reading and acknowledgments The companion reports, [*Scaling Synthetic Pre-training Data and Evaluation for Indic LLMs*]( Scaling Synthetic Pre-training Data and Evaluation for Indic LLMs.pdf and the Nemotron 3.5 Super VL and Lightning technical report , provide the corpus accounting, generation methods, experiments, and evaluation details. Evaluation is the other half of this work. For the benchmark side, see the companion blog from AI4Bharat and NVIDIA, Better Models Need Better Benchmarks: Introducing Indic-LLM-Eval-Suite . This work brings together NVIDIA, IIT Madras, AI4Bharat, and Bodhan AI. We also acknowledge the model and tooling contributions used in the pipeline: Google's Gemma, Bodhan AI's Indic Translate, and NeMo Data Designer. Additional NVIDIA data resources are available in the Nemotron Pre-Training Datasets collection . AI4Bharat, IIT Madras' Indian language research lab, builds open-source datasets and models for Indian languages. Its resources, such as Sangraha , an open pretraining corpus for 22 Indian languages, have helped lay the foundation for open Indic language-model research. Our joint open-source release represents a substantial expansion of the open synthetic Indic training data that will be available to the community. It brings a broad mix of curated English material, including mathematics, code, and question-answer content, into Indian languages, giving teams more training material for building models that can explain technical concepts, work through problems, and answer questions in those languages. Every record traces back to a curated source document, and each output is checked against its input, so the synthetic text stays grounded in real information. Mitesh Khapra, who heads AI4Bharat and made the 2025 TIME100 AI list , has named the core problem: Indian language technology trails English because "we do not have enough data for Indian languages." We're answering that call with more data, plus an open recipe for generating more. The corpus also accounts for how people write. It includes native-script data for all 22 languages and romanized text for twelve, spanning 34 language-script configurations. Our workflows combine document-level translation, quality assessment, and targeted repair, with checks to preserve content such as equations, tables, and code. This data complements naturally authored Indic text, which remains essential for local knowledge and cultural context. We're sharing the open generation recipe so the community can not just reproduce the data but take this work further. Teams can use the corpus directly, adapt the prompts and quality checks, or bring their own source documents to the workflow. By opening up both the data and the process, we aim to make large-scale Indic data generation more accessible and enable more developers to contribute to stronger models across Indian languages. Continued pretraining for Nemotron 3.5 Super VL added 10 billion Indic tokens, drawn from a twelve-language subset of this corpus and natural Indic text. Our technical report on the model covers the full story. We plan to build on this corpus in future Nemotron models. What is in the corpus? Figure 1. The corpus contains 2,601.0 billion native-script tokens and 224.6 billion romanized tokens. Counts use the Gemma-4 tokenizer. Document records include translations and script variants of shared sources; they are not counts of unique English documents. The corpus has two groups of language configurations: Native-script and romanized data: Bengali, Gujarati, Hindi, Kannada, Malayalam, Marathi, Nepali, Odia, Punjabi, Tamil, Telugu, and Urdu. Native-script data: Assamese, Bodo, Dogri, Kashmiri, Konkani, Maithili, Manipuri, Sanskrit, Santali, and Sindhi. Here, native-script describes the writing system: the text is still translated from English. Romanized means Indic-language text written in Latin script, not an English translation. For each of the twelve dual-script languages, romanization covers a subset of the accepted native-script translations. This distinction matters when constructing a training mixture. Native and romanized records offer different script exposure, but can express the same underlying content. The token counts describe the retained corpus, including accepted rewrites, rather than a training run's token budget. Counts also depend on the tokenizer used, so corpus inventory and training-token counts should be read separately. From English source documents to Indic training data To build this corpus, we start with documents from 15 Nemotron-CC-v2 subsets, covering web text, question-answer material, mathematics, code, and other specialized content. We use NeMo Data Designer , NVIDIA's open-source framework for generating synthetic data, to run translation, quality checks, and targeted repair. Throughout the workflow, we retain each source identifier so developers can trace an output back to its original document. Clear provenance like this is part of what makes open data practical to audit and build on. Figure 2 shows the workflow for twelve languages. Figure 2. Four-stage Indic synthetic-data pipeline for twelve languages, implemented using NeMo Data Designer and Gemma-4-31B-it. We translate English documents, assess translation quality, repair low-scoring outputs, and convert a subset of accepted translations into Latin script. The other ten languages use the separate Indic Translate workflow described below. The twelve-language workflow For these twelve languages, we translate documents in full so the model can use context across paragraphs, tables, and equations. We selected Gemma-4-31B-it by comparing models on complete documents, checking translation quality and preservation of technical content. Our prompts distinguish prose to translate from content to preserve, including code, equations, URLs, and formatting. After translation, we use the same model to assess each output against its English source. A rubric inspired by Multidimensional Quality Metrics (MQM), an open framework for classifying translation errors by type and severity, covers meaning, fluency, terminology, style, and formatting. We retain only outputs scoring at least 75 out of 100 (a rubric score, not an accuracy percentage). For lower-scoring outputs, we use the assessment feedback to guide repairs, then reassess them against the same threshold. This process recovered 438.4 billion tokens across native-script and romanized data, already included in the corpus total. Sampled human reviews and tests with deliberately introduced errors helped identify omissions and residual English, informing improvements to our prompts and checks. Accepted native-script translations also provide the starting point for romanized data. We convert a subset into Latin script and check each result against its native-script input. This separates translation from script conversion. In our initial human comparison, this two-step approach produced fewer hallucinated additions and less residual English than generating romanized text directly from English. The ten-language workflow For the other ten languages, we adapt the workflow to address long-document quality and script-stability issues observed in our comparisons. We translate with Indic Translate , a document-level translation model for English and 22 Indian languages from Bodhan AI , a nonprofit center for AI in education incubated at IIT Madras. Gemma-4-31B-it then assesses each translation against its English source. For eight languages, we keep the whole-document approach. For longer Santali documents, we translate overlapping windows and reconstruct the document; for Manipuri, we translate into Bengali script before converting to Meitei Mayek, its native script. These workflows retain outputs scoring at least 75 out of 100 and produce native-script data only, without feedback-based rewriting. What changed after Indic continued pretraining? The Nemotron 3.5 Super VL technical report compares the checkpoint immediately before Indic continued pretraining (CPT) with the checkpoint after that stage. The configured budget was 100 billion training tokens, with 10% (10 billion tokens) allocated to a mixture of synthetic and natural Indic text. The remaining 90% maintained the preceding training mixture's relative proportions. Scores increased on all five reported Indic knowledge and reasoning benchmarks: MILU, Indic MMLU-Pro, Indic ARC-Challenge, Indic ARC-Easy, and Indic GSM8K. Figure 3. Nemotron 3.5 Super VL before and after the Indic CPT stage. Gains range from 4.98 to 9.82 percentage points. The comparison reports the change across a training stage that combines synthetic and natural Indic data, rather than isolating the synthetic corpus's contribution. Language coverage differs by benchmark; these are stage-level checkpoints, not a comparison of final model releases. Source: Nemotron 3.5 Super VL technical report, Table 2. GSM8K excludes Odia because evaluation exceeded the serving context limit. These gains support the combined synthetic-and-natural Indic CPT recipe, while leaving the choice of mixture for other models and languages to further study. The companion Indic report examines source mixtures, synthetic-data pool size, and script coverage using first-pass accepted data for the twelve-language group. Evaluating the full corpus, including recovered rewrites and the other ten languages, remains a next step for those controlled studies. Broader Indic capabilities in Nemotron 3.5 Super VL Beyond the CPT-stage results, how does the released model compare with the previous generation? Figure 4 compares Nemotron 3.5 Super VL with Nemotron 3 Super across Indic task performance and language quality. These results reflect the released model's full training pipeline, including Indic CPT and post-training. Nemotron 3.5 Super VL scores higher on five of the six task benchmarks shown, spanning knowledge, reasoning, mathematics, code, and translation. Instruction following on IFEval 1.5 dipped 2.04 points. It also improves across all four IndiVibe dimensions: usefulness, fluency, language and script fidelity, and appropriate verbosity. IndiVibe is Sarvam AI's open benchmark of assistant-style prompts in Indian languages. Together, these evaluations examine both what the model can do and how well it communicates in Indian languages. Figure 4. Indic task performance and language quality across Nemotron Super generations. Left: six task benchmarks. Right: preliminary IndiVibe conditional preference scores, not direct head-to-head win rates. Labels show changes in percentage points, except WMT24++, which uses chrF points. See the companion Indic technical report for benchmark and evaluation details. Start building Load the corpus Start with the languages and scripts your model needs, inspect a sample, and review the dataset card and license before training. Configurations use language, script, and region tags: for example, hi-Deva-IN denotes Hindi in Devanagari, while hi-Latn-IN denotes romanized Hindi. The example below asks for the repository ID from the dataset card, then discovers the available splits and streams a sample. from datasets import get_dataset_split_names, load_dataset dataset_id = input ( "Repository ID from the dataset card: " ).strip() config = "hi-Deva-IN" splits = get_dataset_split_names(dataset_id, config_name=config) print ( "Available splits:" , splits) data = load_dataset( dataset_id, name=config, split=splits[ 0 ], streaming= True ) print ( next ( iter (data))) Hugging Face Datasets supports streaming so readers can inspect records without downloading the entire corpus. Once the release is available, pin a dataset revision for reproducible experiments. For a first training study , compare mixtures at a fixed token budget and record the natural/synthetic and native/romanized shares. Track per-language results alongside English capability retention and language/script quality. When creating held-out splits, account for records derived from the same source across languages and scripts. To build a fuller recipe, pair the corpus with Nemotron post-training data, such as the Chat & Instruction or Post-Training Blends collections. For India-specific synthetic data, seed NeMo Data Designer with Nemotron-Personas-India , synthetic personas in English and Hindi grounded in real-world distributions for India. Adapt the generation recipe The open-source Nemotron Bharat translation plugin for NeMo Data Designer provides translation and evaluation prompts, optional feedback-based rewriting, document windowing, and script-remapping support. Use its configuration reference to choose models and languages, adapt prompts to your domain, and set rewrite parameters. The accompanying developer note explains the workflow and engineering choices. Start with a small sample of your own source documents. Inspect translation quality and preservation of code, mathematics, and formatting, then refine the prompts and checks with native-language reviewers before scaling up. Treat generation and corpus acceptance as separate steps: the plugin returns candidates and scores, while your filtering policy determines which records enter the training corpus. Scope and limitations Translation broadens access to the source material, but does not replace text originally written in Indian languages or guarantee coverage of local knowledge and culture. We recommend combining this corpus with appropriately sourced natural Indic text and evaluating the resulting mixture for the intended use case. Quality assessment is primarily automated, complemented by sampled human review whose coverage varies across languages. For the twelve-language workflow (Figure 2), the translator also serves as the judge. Retained text can still contain errors, and the ten-language workflow needs broader native-speaker validation. Source-ID checks remove processing duplicates; they are not semantic deduplication of similar content. Alongside the corpus, AI4Bharat at IIT Madras, with support from NVIDIA, is building Indic-LLM-Eval-Suite, an open and evolving collection of benchmarks for Indic model capabilities. It helps model builders assess both task performance and language quality. See the companion blog, Better Models Need Better Benchmarks: Introducing Indic-LLM-Eval-Suite . Explore the language configurations, test a training mixture, or adapt the open recipe to a new domain. Sharing per-language results and improvements to the generation workflow can help the community build on this work. Further reading and acknowledgments The companion reports, [*Scaling Synthetic Pre-training Data and Evaluation for Indic LLMs*]( Scaling Synthetic Pre-training Data and Evaluation for Indic LLMs.pdf and the Nemotron 3.5 Super VL and Lightning technical report , provide the corpus accounting, generation methods, experiments, and evaluation details. Evaluation is the other half of this work. For the benchmark side, see the companion blog from AI4Bharat and NVIDIA, Better Models Need Better Benchmarks: Introducing Indic-LLM-Eval-Suite . This work brings together NVIDIA, IIT Madras, AI4Bharat, and Bodhan AI. We also acknowledge the model and tooling contributions used in the pipeline: Google's Gemma, Bodhan AI's Indic Translate, and NeMo Data Designer. Additional NVIDIA data resources are available in the Nemotron Pre-Training Datasets collection .
