items.content: Back to Articles Welcome Muse Spark Open: open-weight frontier multimodal mixture-of-experts model from Meta Published October 15, 2026 Update on GitHub Upvote 26 +20 Pedro Cuenca pcuenq Follow merve merve Follow ben burtenshaw burtenshaw Follow Guarin Flück guarin Follow Quentin Gallouédec qgallouedec Follow Alvaro Bartolome alvarobartt Follow Serveurperso Serveurperso Follow Jun Kim Jundot Follow Muse Spark Open is an open-weight model from Meta. The mixture of experts model brings text, images, audio, and video into a model with approximately 816 billion parameters, around 42 billion active per token, and a context window of up to one million tokens. It generates text, giving developers a common interface for asking questions about different kinds of input. Following Muse Glimmer, Muse Spark Open introduces a mixture-of-experts architecture at a much larger scale, and the most capable US open-weights model to date. Meta trained Muse Spark Open for agentic coding: reading a codebase, writing and debugging code, and calling tools. It also takes images, audio, and video as input, so the same model can read a screenshot, listen to a voice note, or watch a screen recording while it works on your code. This post shows you how to run it, how to fine-tune it, and what we built with it. Find all the models here . Overall Capabilities and Architecture Meta describes Muse Spark Open as a coding-optimized model trained on real developer workflows such as multi-file refactors and long debugging sessions. Muse Spark Open is an agentic focused model that plans, acts, observes, and self-corrects over long tasks, including browsing the web with images. Feature Muse Spark Open Model size ~816B total parameters; ~42B active per token Expert routing 256 experts per MoE layer; 8 selected per token Inputs Text, images, audio, and video Output Text Context window Up to 1M tokens Checkpoint formats BF16 and NVFP4 The checkpoint repositories are Muse-Spark-Open-816B-A42B and Muse-Spark-Open-816B-A42B-NVFP4. Muse Spark Open is the full-size model of the Muse series of models. Muse Glimmer, which Meta released in August, is a small dense model from the same series, ideal for running locally. Both models use the same tokenizer and vocabulary. The chat template follows the Muse Glimmer template, with additions for the new modalities. In Muse Spark Open the input embedding and the output layer are separate matrices of about 1.66B parameters each. Mixture of Experts The language model has 62 layers and a hidden dimension of 8192. Each layer has 128 query heads and 16 key-value heads (grouped-query attention). Each head has 64 dimensions. The attention block has an output gate and an output normalization layer. The model also applies normalization to the queries and the keys (QK-norm). Each block combines its input and its output through a learned residual gate, not through a plain sum. Muse Glimmer uses one dense feed-forward network in each layer. Muse Spark Open replaces this dense network with a Mixture-of-Experts (MoE) block. Each MoE block has 256 experts, and a router selects 8 experts for each token. Each expert is a feed-forward network that projects from 8192 to 4096 dimensions and back to 8192, then applies its own normalization to its output. The experts hold ~97% of the total model parameters. Only 8 experts run per token, so the model computes each token with about 42B parameters. All 256 experts stay in memory, so deployment needs the memory of an 816B-parameter model, but runs at the much faster speed of a 42B model. The BF16 checkpoint is about 1.5 TB in safetensors format. The NVFP4 checkpoint stores the parameters in 4-bit precision with negligible loss in accuracy, specifically for NVIDIA Blackwell GPUs. In transformers, the BF16 checkpoint runs across 4 nodes of 8 H200 GPUs with tensor parallelism (TP=32) and the NVFP4 runs on a single B200 node. If you want to deploy Muse Spark Open, check out the llama.cpp , vLLM, and SGLang recipes below. Perception Encoder A perception encoder converts images and video frames into tokens for the language model, just like Muse Glimmer. The encoder has 1.8B parameters, 50 layers, a hidden dimension of 1536, and 16 attention heads. It splits each image into 14×14 patches and produces features with 4096 dimensions. Position information comes from learned absolute embeddings and 2D RoPE. The feed-forward network in each layer uses LayerNorm and GELU. Every fourth layer and the last layer use full attention, and the other layers use sparse attention. Muse Glimmer 30B uses an encoder with the same architecture. The design follows the Perception Encoder work from Meta. Video input goes through the same encoder as images. Audio Encoder Muse Spark Open accepts audio as input through its audio encoder. An audio tokenizer converts the audio into tokens, and the chat template marks the audio position with <|audio|> tokens. The encoder emits one audio token every 80 ms, which yields 12.5 tokens per second. So let’s say, you have an audio of 10 seconds, the number of input audio tokens would be 125. The encoder itself is a convolutional pyramid where each stage consists of a patch embedder of different patch sizes and 2 convolutional blocks of 1d kernels of size 7 with stride of 1. These stages are repeated for patch sizes of [16, 6, 5, 4]. At the end of the final stage, the temporal frames are fed to a final block of RMSNorm → linear projection → RMSNorm. Long Context The context window is 1M tokens at inference. The configuration sets max_position_embeddings to 1,048,576. This includes image, video, and audio tokens in the same window as text. Grouped-query attention keeps the KV cache small for a model of this size. Each token adds 2 × 16 heads × 64 dimensions × 62 layers = 126,976 values to the cache. In BF16, this is about 250 KB per token and about 266 GB for a full 1M-token context. Inference Support Transformers The Muse Spark Open implementation provides MuseSparkForConditionalGeneration for text generation from multimodal inputs and MuseSparkProcessor for preparing conversations. The processor combines the tokenizer, image and video processors, audio feature extractor, and chat template. Use a DistributedConfig to configure the parallelism settings. tp_size is the number of devices across which the dense layers are sharded, and ep_size is the number of devices across which the experts are distributed. You can initialize the model and processor as follows. import os from transformers import AutoModelForMultimodalLM, AutoTokenizer, DistributedConfig distributed_config = DistributedConfig( tp_size= int (os.environ[ "WORLD_SIZE" ]), ep_size= int (os.environ[ "WORLD_SIZE" ]), ) tokenizer = AutoTokenizer.from_pretrained( "meta-models/Muse-Spark-Open-816B-A42B " ) model = AutoModelForMultimodalLM.from_pretrained( "meta-models/Muse-Spark-Open-816B-A42B" , distributed_config=distributed_config, ) messages = [ { "role" : "user" , "content" : "Explain in one sentence why the sky is usually blue." }, ] inputs = tokenizer.apply_chat_template( messages, reasoning_effort= "medium" , # default: xhigh, options: low/medium/high/xhigh add_generation_prompt= True , tokenize= True , return_dict= True , return_tensors= "pt" , ).to(model.device).to(model.dtype) input_len = inputs[ "input_ids" ].shape[- 1 ] outputs = model.generate(**inputs, max_new_tokens= 2000 ) Text-only Inference Prepare the conversation, then pass the messages to processor.apply_chat_template , enabling add_generation_prompt=True , tokenize=True , return_dict=True , and return_tensors="pt" . Pass the processor output to model.generate and decode the newly generated tokens, excluding the input prefix. The processor has a lever for the reasoning effort, mapping symbolic levels (low/medium/high/xhigh) to the integers the model itself accepts (16, 64, 256, 512). Note that turning off reasoning is not possible with Muse Spark Open, so keep the model reasoning at “low” if you want to consume less tokens to solve an easier task. You can also set a numeric effort by including a line like Reasoning strength: 1 in the system prompt. messages = [ { "role" : "system" , "content" : "You should only answer with a number." }, { "role" : "user" , "content" : "What is 17 * 23?" }, ] inputs = processor.apply_chat_template( messages, add_generation_prompt= True , tokenize= True , return_dict= True , return_tensors= "pt" , reasoning_effort= "high" , # options:low/medium/high/xhigh ).to(model.device).to(model.dtype) output = model.generate(**inputs, max_new_tokens= 2000 ) generated_tokens = output[ 0 ][inputs[ "input_ids" ].shape[ 1 ] :] print (processor.decode(generated_tokens, skip_special_tokens= False )) Images and Text The Muse Spark Open processor expands each image marker into the number of patch tokens required by the processed image, surrounded by image boundary tokens. This expansion keeps the text positions aligned with the visual features passed to the model. The processor also handles multiple images within a single prompt. image_url = ( "https://huggingface.co/datasets/merve/vl-test-suite/" "resolve/main/pills.jpg" ) messages = [ { "role" : "user" , "content" : [ { "type" : "image" , "image" : image_url, }, { "type" : "text" , "text" : "Do any of the components in this supplement interact?" , }, ], }, ] inputs = processor.apply_chat_template( messages, tokenize= True , add_generation_prompt= True , reasoning_effort= "medium" , return_dict= True , return_tensors= "pt" , ).to(model.device).to(model.dtype) input_len = inputs[ "input_ids" ].shape[- 1 ] outputs = model.generate(**inputs, max_new_tokens= 2000 ) response = processor.decode(outputs[ 0 ][input_len:], skip_special_tokens= False ) processor.parse_response(response) Video Inference Video prompts include frame timing as well as visual content. The processor handles videos with audios in them (which is an upgrade from Muse Glimmer thanks to the audio encoder). The processor downsamples video frames and audio to align frames together. By default, videos are sampled to 2 FPS, capped at 96 frames. You can modify this by setting the fps of the video processor: processor.video_processor.fps = 4.0 As a general rule of thumb, videos are frames in temporal sequence, and the more you downsample, the more you will lose frames in between specific events, so you need to keep fps high if you want more accurate generations. However, there’s a trade-off because you will require more memory and increase latency for prefill. The frames are interleaved with text input that states timestamps (e.g. “Time: 3.5s”). To enable passing in videos with audio, pass load_audio_from_video=True to apply_chat_template . Preserve the video's metadata when preparing inputs with return_metadata=True so the processor can assign the correct framerate. import torch messages = [ { "role" : "user" , "content" : [ { "type" : "text" , "text" : ( "Describe what happens in this video. " "Use timestamps and include relevant speech or sounds." ), }, { "type" : "video" , "url" : "https://huggingface.co/datasets/merve/vlm_test_images/resolve/main/ramen.mp4" }, ], } ] inputs = processor.apply_chat_template( messages, add_generation_prompt= True , tokenize= True , return_dict= True , return_tensors= "pt" , load_audio_from_video= True , return_metadata= True , ).to(model.device).to(model.dtype) with torch.inference_mode(): output_ids = model.generate( **inputs, max_new_tokens= 256 , do_sample= False , ) generated_ids = output_ids[:, inputs[ "input_ids" ].shape[ 1 ] :] response = processor.batch_decode( generated_ids, skip_special_tokens= True , )[ 0 ] print (response) Audio Inference The Muse Spark Open audio tower consumes a raw waveform. The processor expects mono audio at 24 kHz and pads the waveform to a multiple of 1,920 samples, corresponding to one audio embedding per 80 milliseconds. Audio supplied directly to the processor at another sample rate must first be resampled. You can do this by using the load_audio util of transformers. load_audio uses torchcodec, librosa or torchaudio backends, so make sure to have one of these installed locally before running inference. If you want to simply use apply_chat_template with messages though, this is all handled for you under the hood: import torch from transformers import AutoProcessor, AutoModelForMultimodalLM model_id = "meta-models/Muse-Spark-Open-816B-A42B" processor = AutoProcessor.from_pretrained(model_id) model = AutoModelForMultimodalLM.from_pretrained(model_id). eval () messages = [ { "role" : "user" , "content" : [ { "type" : "audio" , "url" : "https://huggingface.co/buckets/huggingface/audio-samples/resolve/bbaudio_question_39.mp3" , }, { "type" : "text" , "text" : "Answer the question." , }, ], } ] # Downloads the audio, decodes it as mono, resamples it to 24 kHz, pads it, creates input_values_mask, and expands the audio placeholders. inputs = processor.apply_chat_template( messages, add_generation_prompt= True , tokenize= True , return_dict= True , return_tensors= "pt" , load_audio_backend= "auto" , ).to(model.device).to(model.dtype) with torch.inference_mode(): output_ids = model.generate( **inputs, max_new_tokens= 128 , do_sample= False , ) # Decode only newly generated tokens prompt_length = inputs[ "input_ids" ].shape[ 1 ] generated_text = processor.batch_decode( output_ids[:, prompt_length:], skip_special_tokens= True , ) print (generated_text[ 0 ]) The processor inserts the matching number of audio tokens between audio boundary markers. It also returns a mask identifying real samples, allowing the model to exclude padded audio embeddings. Tool Calling Muse Spark Open can do text-only and multimodal tool calling. You can make the model call tools as follows. from transformers import AutoProcessor, AutoModelForMultimodalLM MODEL_ID = "meta-models/Muse-Spark-Open-816B-A42B" # Load model processor = AutoProcessor.from_pretrained(MODEL_ID) model = AutoModelForMultimodalLM.from_pretrained( MODEL_ID, dtype= "auto" , device_map= "auto" ) tools = [ { "type" : "function" , "function" : { "name" : "weather.get" , "description" : "Get the current weather for a city." , "parameters" : { "type" : "object" , "properties" : { "city" : { "type" : "string" }, }, "required" : [ "city" ], }, }, } ] messages = [ { "role" : "user" , "content" : [ { "type" : "image" , "image" : "https://huggingface.co/datasets/merve/vl-test-suite/resolve/main/SF.png" }, { "type" : "text" , "text" : "I'm going to the city in this picture. What clothes should I wear?" }, ], }, ] inputs = processor.apply_chat_template( messages, tools=tools, tokenize= True , return_dict= True , return_tensors= "pt" , add_generation_prompt= True , reasoning_strength= "high" ).to(model.device).to(model.dtype) input_len = inputs[ "input_ids" ].shape[- 1 ] outputs = model.generate(**inputs) response = processor.parse_response( completion, prefix=inputs[ "input_ids" ][ 0 ], tools=tools, ) print (response) Muse Spark Open uses a channel-based chat template (Harmony, first introduced by gpt-oss). Note that you don’t have to know about the internals, but it’s useful to check the channels the model routes to, in case you get low quality outputs. In the input message below: <|begin_of_text|> <|start|>system<|message|> You are a helpful AI assistant. Knowledge cutoff: 2026-01-04. Current date: ... ... <|eot|> <|start|>user<|message|>... <|eot|> <|start|>assistant <|start|>assistant is intentionally left open, it’s the model that chooses recipient with to= . The model has different recipients, e.g. self asks the model to reason, to=self<|message|>the model reasons here<|eom|> # reasoning <|start|>assistant to=user<|message|>final answer<|eot|> # final answer self is for reasoning, commentary are comments before and between tool calls visible to the end user, user is the final response. Tool-call routing is parsed as follows (assuming you have passed tools to apply_chat_template : <|start|>assistant to=weather.get<|message|> <atem:function_calls> <atem:invoke name="weather.get"> <atem:parameter name="city">San Francisco</atem:parameter> </atem:invoke> </atem:function_calls> <|eot|> Llama.cpp Muse Spark 2-bit running on Llama Server Muse Spark Open is integrated in llama.cpp and comes in the prebuilt binaries. You can install this with following command: curl -LsSf https://llama.app/install.sh | sh You can start the server as follows with quant suffix attached to model ID: llama serve -hf ggml-org/Muse-Spark-Open-816B-A42B-GGUF:Q2_K The repository containing quants is here . Once the server has started, you can head to localhost:9931 to chat with the built-in WebUI. From the web UI you can add audio and images for inference and adjust the reasoning lever. Note that turning off reasoning is not possible with Muse Spark Open, so keep the model reasoning at “low” if you want to consume less tokens to solve an easier task. We tested quants on Mac M3 Ultra (512GB). An imatrix-calibrated 2-bit quant runs at 18 tokens/s, with plenty of room free for the KV cache (304 GB used by the model). You can also query the server as follows. Feel free to check out the API reference for multimodality, tool calls and more. ## Text-only inference curl http://localhost:8080/v1/chat/completions \ -H "Content-Type: application/json" \ -d '{ "messages": [ {"role": "system", "content": "You are a helpful assistant."}, {"role": "user", "content": "Write a limerick about python exceptions"} ] }' ## Image-text inference curl -s http://127.0.0.1:8080/v1/chat/completions \ -H "Content-Type: application/json" -H "Authorization: Bearer <your-key>" \ -d '{"model":"muse-spark-open","messages":[{"role":"user","content":[ {"type":"text","text":"What is in this image?"}, {"type":"image_url","image_url":{"url":"data:image/png;base64,..."}} ]}],"temperature":0}' ## Audio-text inference curl -s http://127.0.0.1:8080/v1/chat/completions \ -H "Content-Type: application/json" -H "Authorization: Bearer <your-key>" \ -d '{"model":"muse-spark-open","messages":[{"role":"user","content":[ {"type":"text","text":"Transcribe this audio."}, {"type":"input_audio","input_audio":{"data":"data:audio/wav;base64,..."}} ]}],"temperature":0}' llama.cpp team ships different quantized versions. We have tested Q2_K, Q4_K_S and Q_8 on Apple Silicon chips. You can run each quant by adding the quant id as suffix, llama serve -hf ggml-org/Muse-Spark-Open-816B-A42B:Q2_K . SGLang The Muse Spark Open integration for SGLang supports text, image, audio, and video inputs. The NVFP4 reference configuration runs across four GB300 GPUs. From the SGLang integration environment, download the checkpoint from the Hugging Face Hub and start the server: export MODEL_ID=meta-models/Muse-Spark-Open-816B-A42B-NVFP4 export CKPT="$(hf download "$MODEL_ID")" SGLANG_FLASHINFER_NVFP4_PER_TOKEN_ACTIVATION=1 \ uv run sglang_meta serve \ --model-path "$CKPT" \ --served-model-name "$MODEL_ID" \ --quantization modelopt_fp4 \ --moe-runner-backend flashinfer_trtllm \ --tp-size 4 \ --ep-size 4 \ --port 30000 The checkpoint includes the chat template, which we pass explicitly. The launcher configures the Muse reasoning and tool-call parsers. Send a request through the OpenAI-compatible API: curl http://localhost:30000/v1/chat/completions \ -H "Content-Type: application/json" \ -d '{ "model": "meta-models/Muse-Spark-Open-816B-A42B-NVFP4", "messages": [{ "role": "user", "content": "Explain how a mixture-of-experts model works." }], "max_tokens": 2048 }' The response separates the reasoning trace in reasoning_content from the final answer in content . vLLM The Muse Spark Open reference integration for vLLM supports text and image inputs with the NVFP4 checkpoint that require blackwell series GPUs. After installing the reference plugin and its dependencies, download the checkpoint from the Hugging Face Hub and launch the server: export MODEL_ID=meta-models/Muse-Spark-Open-816B-A42B-NVFP4 export CKPT="$(hf download "$MODEL_ID")" VLLM_ALLOW_LONG_MAX_MODEL_LEN=1 \ VLLM_PLUGINS=musespark1x_models,ptq_nvfp4 \ vllm serve "$CKPT" \ --served-model-name "$MODEL_ID" \ --tokenizer-mode musespark1x \ --config-format auto \ --load-format internal_safetensor \ --tensor-parallel-size 4 \ --enable-expert-parallel \ --max-model-len 131072 \ --gpu-memory-utilization 0.92 \ --reasoning-parser musespark1x \ --tool-call-parser musespark1x \ --enable-auto-tool-choice \ --port 8000 This configuration sets a 128K-token serving context. The plugin supplies the model implementation, checkpoint loader, and reasoning and tool-call parsers. Send a request using the same Hub model ID: curl http://localhost:8000/v1/chat/completions \ -H "Content-Type: application/json" \ -d '{ "model": "meta-models/Muse-Spark-Open-816B-A42B-NVFP4", "messages": [{ "role": "user", "content": "Explain how a mixture-of-experts model works." }], "max_tokens": 2048 }' MLX Muse Spark Open is available in oMLX and mlx-lm today. oQ quants optimized for oMLX are available in 3-bit and 4-bit , ready to use right away. We tested the oQ3e quant on an M3 Ultra (512 GB). The model takes about 344 GB, leaving room for the KV cache, and runs at about 225 tok/s prefill and 21 tok/s generation with a 1024-token prompt and 128 generated tokens. Once you download the model through the oMLX interface, you can chat with it in the built-in chat UI. From the chat UI you can add images and adjust the reasoning effort on the fly, from low to xhigh. The model’s reasoning shows up as a collapsible thinking block, separate from the final answer. Note that it's not possible to turn reasoning off, and the default (Auto) uses xhigh. Set it to “low” if you want to use fewer tokens on easier tasks. The language model is also available in this PR of the official mlx-lm repository. You can run it on the same high-quality oQ3e quant like this: mlx_lm.generate --model mlx-community/Muse-Spark-Open-816B-A42B-oQ3e \ --prompt "Explain convolutional networks like I am 5" \ --max-tokens 5000 This is a big model, even the 3-bit quantization requires more than 256 GB of RAM, as explained above. You can also run distributed inference across multiple computers, please refer to the documentation for details. Deploying Muse Spark Open with Inference Endpoints You can deploy Muse Spark Open on Inference Endpoints with a pre-validated SGLang recipe for the NVFP4 variant which runs on either 8 × NVIDIA RTX Pro 6000 98 GB with 131072 context length, or with 8 x NVIDIA H200 141GB if you want 1048576 context length instead. To deploy, run one command with the Hugging Face CLI: hf endpoints catalog deploy --repo meta-models/Muse-Spark-Open-816B-A42B-NVFP4 --name muse-spark Or open endpoints.huggingface.co/new/meta-models/Muse-Spark-Open-816B-A42B-NVFP4 and select Create Endpoint. The endpoint exposes an OpenAI-compatible API with both Chat Completions API at /v1/chat/completions and Responses API at /v1/responses . curl "https://<your-endpoint>.endpoints.huggingface.cloud/v1/chat/completions" \ -H "Authorization: Bearer $HF_TOKEN " \ -H "Content-Type: application/json" \ -d '{ "model": "meta-models/Muse-Spark-Open-816B-A42B-NVFP4", "messages": [{ "role": "user", "content": [ {"type": "image_url", "image_url": {"url": "https://huggingface.co/datasets/merve/vl-test-suite/resolve/main/pills.jpg"}}, {"type": "text", "text": "Do any of the components in this supplement interact?"} ] }], "chat_template_kwargs": {"enable_thinking": false} }' Any OpenAI-compatible client works with the same URL and your Hugging Face token as the API key. Fine-tuning with TRL You can fine-tune the 816B checkpoint with the TRL SFTTrainer . This section shows how we fine-tuned it with TRL on 8 nodes of 8 H100 GPUs. The recipe trains LoRA adapters on the attention layers. The experts stay frozen. The full script is in the TRL examples . First, we need to split the model across 64 GPU devices. Given the large size of the model, we need to parallelize it across multiple axes. We shard the model with FSDP
items.raw_text: Back to Articles Welcome Muse Spark Open: open-weight frontier multimodal mixture-of-experts model from Meta Published October 15, 2026 Update on GitHub Upvote 26 +20 Pedro Cuenca pcuenq Follow merve merve Follow ben burtenshaw burtenshaw Follow Guarin Flück guarin Follow Quentin Gallouédec qgallouedec Follow Alvaro Bartolome alvarobartt Follow Serveurperso Serveurperso Follow Jun Kim Jundot Follow Muse Spark Open is an open-weight model from Meta. The mixture of experts model brings text, images, audio, and video into a model with approximately 816 billion parameters, around 42 billion active per token, and a context window of up to one million tokens. It generates text, giving developers a common interface for asking questions about different kinds of input. Following Muse Glimmer, Muse Spark Open introduces a mixture-of-experts architecture at a much larger scale, and the most capable US open-weights model to date. Meta trained Muse Spark Open for agentic coding: reading a codebase, writing and debugging code, and calling tools. It also takes images, audio, and video as input, so the same model can read a screenshot, listen to a voice note, or watch a screen recording while it works on your code. This post shows you how to run it, how to fine-tune it, and what we built with it. Find all the models here . Overall Capabilities and Architecture Meta describes Muse Spark Open as a coding-optimized model trained on real developer workflows such as multi-file refactors and long debugging sessions. Muse Spark Open is an agentic focused model that plans, acts, observes, and self-corrects over long tasks, including browsing the web with images. Feature Muse Spark Open Model size ~816B total parameters; ~42B active per token Expert routing 256 experts per MoE layer; 8 selected per token Inputs Text, images, audio, and video Output Text Context window Up to 1M tokens Checkpoint formats BF16 and NVFP4 The checkpoint repositories are Muse-Spark-Open-816B-A42B and Muse-Spark-Open-816B-A42B-NVFP4. Muse Spark Open is the full-size model of the Muse series of models. Muse Glimmer, which Meta released in August, is a small dense model from the same series, ideal for running locally. Both models use the same tokenizer and vocabulary. The chat template follows the Muse Glimmer template, with additions for the new modalities. In Muse Spark Open the input embedding and the output layer are separate matrices of about 1.66B parameters each. Mixture of Experts The language model has 62 layers and a hidden dimension of 8192. Each layer has 128 query heads and 16 key-value heads (grouped-query attention). Each head has 64 dimensions. The attention block has an output gate and an output normalization layer. The model also applies normalization to the queries and the keys (QK-norm). Each block combines its input and its output through a learned residual gate, not through a plain sum. Muse Glimmer uses one dense feed-forward network in each layer. Muse Spark Open replaces this dense network with a Mixture-of-Experts (MoE) block. Each MoE block has 256 experts, and a router selects 8 experts for each token. Each expert is a feed-forward network that projects from 8192 to 4096 dimensions and back to 8192, then applies its own normalization to its output. The experts hold ~97% of the total model parameters. Only 8 experts run per token, so the model computes each token with about 42B parameters. All 256 experts stay in memory, so deployment needs the memory of an 816B-parameter model, but runs at the much faster speed of a 42B model. The BF16 checkpoint is about 1.5 TB in safetensors format. The NVFP4 checkpoint stores the parameters in 4-bit precision with negligible loss in accuracy, specifically for NVIDIA Blackwell GPUs. In transformers, the BF16 checkpoint runs across 4 nodes of 8 H200 GPUs with tensor parallelism (TP=32) and the NVFP4 runs on a single B200 node. If you want to deploy Muse Spark Open, check out the llama.cpp , vLLM, and SGLang recipes below. Perception Encoder A perception encoder converts images and video frames into tokens for the language model, just like Muse Glimmer. The encoder has 1.8B parameters, 50 layers, a hidden dimension of 1536, and 16 attention heads. It splits each image into 14×14 patches and produces features with 4096 dimensions. Position information comes from learned absolute embeddings and 2D RoPE. The feed-forward network in each layer uses LayerNorm and GELU. Every fourth layer and the last layer use full attention, and the other layers use sparse attention. Muse Glimmer 30B uses an encoder with the same architecture. The design follows the Perception Encoder work from Meta. Video input goes through the same encoder as images. Audio Encoder Muse Spark Open accepts audio as input through its audio encoder. An audio tokenizer converts the audio into tokens, and the chat template marks the audio position with <|audio|> tokens. The encoder emits one audio token every 80 ms, which yields 12.5 tokens per second. So let’s say, you have an audio of 10 seconds, the number of input audio tokens would be 125. The encoder itself is a convolutional pyramid where each stage consists of a patch embedder of different patch sizes and 2 convolutional blocks of 1d kernels of size 7 with stride of 1. These stages are repeated for patch sizes of [16, 6, 5, 4]. At the end of the final stage, the temporal frames are fed to a final block of RMSNorm → linear projection → RMSNorm. Long Context The context window is 1M tokens at inference. The configuration sets max_position_embeddings to 1,048,576. This includes image, video, and audio tokens in the same window as text. Grouped-query attention keeps the KV cache small for a model of this size. Each token adds 2 × 16 heads × 64 dimensions × 62 layers = 126,976 values to the cache. In BF16, this is about 250 KB per token and about 266 GB for a full 1M-token context. Inference Support Transformers The Muse Spark Open implementation provides MuseSparkForConditionalGeneration for text generation from multimodal inputs and MuseSparkProcessor for preparing conversations. The processor combines the tokenizer, image and video processors, audio feature extractor, and chat template. Use a DistributedConfig to configure the parallelism settings. tp_size is the number of devices across which the dense layers are sharded, and ep_size is the number of devices across which the experts are distributed. You can initialize the model and processor as follows. import os from transformers import AutoModelForMultimodalLM, AutoTokenizer, DistributedConfig distributed_config = DistributedConfig( tp_size= int (os.environ[ "WORLD_SIZE" ]), ep_size= int (os.environ[ "WORLD_SIZE" ]), ) tokenizer = AutoTokenizer.from_pretrained( "meta-models/Muse-Spark-Open-816B-A42B " ) model = AutoModelForMultimodalLM.from_pretrained( "meta-models/Muse-Spark-Open-816B-A42B" , distributed_config=distributed_config, ) messages = [ { "role" : "user" , "content" : "Explain in one sentence why the sky is usually blue." }, ] inputs = tokenizer.apply_chat_template( messages, reasoning_effort= "medium" , # default: xhigh, options: low/medium/high/xhigh add_generation_prompt= True , tokenize= True , return_dict= True , return_tensors= "pt" , ).to(model.device).to(model.dtype) input_len = inputs[ "input_ids" ].shape[- 1 ] outputs = model.generate(**inputs, max_new_tokens= 2000 ) Text-only Inference Prepare the conversation, then pass the messages to processor.apply_chat_template , enabling add_generation_prompt=True , tokenize=True , return_dict=True , and return_tensors="pt" . Pass the processor output to model.generate and decode the newly generated tokens, excluding the input prefix. The processor has a lever for the reasoning effort, mapping symbolic levels (low/medium/high/xhigh) to the integers the model itself accepts (16, 64, 256, 512). Note that turning off reasoning is not possible with Muse Spark Open, so keep the model reasoning at “low” if you want to consume less tokens to solve an easier task. You can also set a numeric effort by including a line like Reasoning strength: 1 in the system prompt. messages = [ { "role" : "system" , "content" : "You should only answer with a number." }, { "role" : "user" , "content" : "What is 17 * 23?" }, ] inputs = processor.apply_chat_template( messages, add_generation_prompt= True , tokenize= True , return_dict= True , return_tensors= "pt" , reasoning_effort= "high" , # options:low/medium/high/xhigh ).to(model.device).to(model.dtype) output = model.generate(**inputs, max_new_tokens= 2000 ) generated_tokens = output[ 0 ][inputs[ "input_ids" ].shape[ 1 ] :] print (processor.decode(generated_tokens, skip_special_tokens= False )) Images and Text The Muse Spark Open processor expands each image marker into the number of patch tokens required by the processed image, surrounded by image boundary tokens. This expansion keeps the text positions aligned with the visual features passed to the model. The processor also handles multiple images within a single prompt. image_url = ( "https://huggingface.co/datasets/merve/vl-test-suite/" "resolve/main/pills.jpg" ) messages = [ { "role" : "user" , "content" : [ { "type" : "image" , "image" : image_url, }, { "type" : "text" , "text" : "Do any of the components in this supplement interact?" , }, ], }, ] inputs = processor.apply_chat_template( messages, tokenize= True , add_generation_prompt= True , reasoning_effort= "medium" , return_dict= True , return_tensors= "pt" , ).to(model.device).to(model.dtype) input_len = inputs[ "input_ids" ].shape[- 1 ] outputs = model.generate(**inputs, max_new_tokens= 2000 ) response = processor.decode(outputs[ 0 ][input_len:], skip_special_tokens= False ) processor.parse_response(response) Video Inference Video prompts include frame timing as well as visual content. The processor handles videos with audios in them (which is an upgrade from Muse Glimmer thanks to the audio encoder). The processor downsamples video frames and audio to align frames together. By default, videos are sampled to 2 FPS, capped at 96 frames. You can modify this by setting the fps of the video processor: processor.video_processor.fps = 4.0 As a general rule of thumb, videos are frames in temporal sequence, and the more you downsample, the more you will lose frames in between specific events, so you need to keep fps high if you want more accurate generations. However, there’s a trade-off because you will require more memory and increase latency for prefill. The frames are interleaved with text input that states timestamps (e.g. “Time: 3.5s”). To enable passing in videos with audio, pass load_audio_from_video=True to apply_chat_template . Preserve the video's metadata when preparing inputs with return_metadata=True so the processor can assign the correct framerate. import torch messages = [ { "role" : "user" , "content" : [ { "type" : "text" , "text" : ( "Describe what happens in this video. " "Use timestamps and include relevant speech or sounds." ), }, { "type" : "video" , "url" : "https://huggingface.co/datasets/merve/vlm_test_images/resolve/main/ramen.mp4" }, ], } ] inputs = processor.apply_chat_template( messages, add_generation_prompt= True , tokenize= True , return_dict= True , return_tensors= "pt" , load_audio_from_video= True , return_metadata= True , ).to(model.device).to(model.dtype) with torch.inference_mode(): output_ids = model.generate( **inputs, max_new_tokens= 256 , do_sample= False , ) generated_ids = output_ids[:, inputs[ "input_ids" ].shape[ 1 ] :] response = processor.batch_decode( generated_ids, skip_special_tokens= True , )[ 0 ] print (response) Audio Inference The Muse Spark Open audio tower consumes a raw waveform. The processor expects mono audio at 24 kHz and pads the waveform to a multiple of 1,920 samples, corresponding to one audio embedding per 80 milliseconds. Audio supplied directly to the processor at another sample rate must first be resampled. You can do this by using the load_audio util of transformers. load_audio uses torchcodec, librosa or torchaudio backends, so make sure to have one of these installed locally before running inference. If you want to simply use apply_chat_template with messages though, this is all handled for you under the hood: import torch from transformers import AutoProcessor, AutoModelForMultimodalLM model_id = "meta-models/Muse-Spark-Open-816B-A42B" processor = AutoProcessor.from_pretrained(model_id) model = AutoModelForMultimodalLM.from_pretrained(model_id). eval () messages = [ { "role" : "user" , "content" : [ { "type" : "audio" , "url" : "https://huggingface.co/buckets/huggingface/audio-samples/resolve/bbaudio_question_39.mp3" , }, { "type" : "text" , "text" : "Answer the question." , }, ], } ] # Downloads the audio, decodes it as mono, resamples it to 24 kHz, pads it, creates input_values_mask, and expands the audio placeholders. inputs = processor.apply_chat_template( messages, add_generation_prompt= True , tokenize= True , return_dict= True , return_tensors= "pt" , load_audio_backend= "auto" , ).to(model.device).to(model.dtype) with torch.inference_mode(): output_ids = model.generate( **inputs, max_new_tokens= 128 , do_sample= False , ) # Decode only newly generated tokens prompt_length = inputs[ "input_ids" ].shape[ 1 ] generated_text = processor.batch_decode( output_ids[:, prompt_length:], skip_special_tokens= True , ) print (generated_text[ 0 ]) The processor inserts the matching number of audio tokens between audio boundary markers. Send a request using the same Hub model ID: curl http://localhost:8000/v1/chat/completions \ -H "Content-Type: application/json" \ -d '{ "model": "meta-models/Muse-Spark-Open-816B-A42B-NVFP4", "messages": [{ "role": "user", "content": "Explain how a mixture-of-experts model works." }], "max_tokens": 2048 }' MLX Muse Spark Open is available in oMLX and mlx-lm today. oQ quants optimized for oMLX are available in 3-bit and 4-bit , ready to use right away. We tested the oQ3e quant on an M3 Ultra (512 GB). The model takes about 344 GB, leaving room for the KV cache, and runs at about 225 tok/s prefill and 21 tok/s generation with a 1024-token prompt and 128 generated tokens. Once you download the model through the oMLX interface, you can chat with it in the built-in chat UI. From the chat UI you can add images and adjust the reasoning effort on the fly, from low to xhigh. The model’s reasoning shows up as a collapsible thinking block, separate from the final answer. Note that it's not possible to turn reasoning off, and the default (Auto) uses xhigh. Set it to “low” if you want to use fewer tokens on easier tasks. The language model is also available in this PR of the official mlx-lm repository. You can run it on the same high-quality oQ3e quant like this: mlx_lm.generate --model mlx-community/Muse-Spark-Open-816B-A42B-oQ3e \ --prompt "Explain convolutional networks like I am 5" \ --max-tokens 5000 This is a big model, even the 3-bit quantization requires more than 256 GB of RAM, as explained above. You can also run distributed inference across multiple computers, please refer to the documentation for details. Deploying Muse Spark Open with Inference Endpoints You can deploy Muse Spark Open on Inference Endpoints with a pre-validated SGLang recipe for the NVFP4 variant which runs on either 8 × NVIDIA RTX Pro 6000 98 GB with 131072 context length, or with 8 x NVIDIA H200 141GB if you want 1048576 context length instead. To deploy, run one command with the Hugging Face CLI: hf endpoints catalog deploy --repo meta-models/Muse-Spark-Open-816B-A42B-NVFP4 --name muse-spark Or open endpoints.huggingface.co/new/meta-models/Muse-Spark-Open-816B-A42B-NVFP4 and select Create Endpoint. The endpoint exposes an OpenAI-compatible API with both Chat Completions API at /v1/chat/completions and Responses API at /v1/responses . curl "https://<your-endpoint>.endpoints.huggingface.cloud/v1/chat/completions" \ -H "Authorization: Bearer $HF_TOKEN " \ -H "Content-Type: application/json" \ -d '{ "model": "meta-models/Muse-Spark-Open-816B-A42B-NVFP4", "messages": [{ "role": "user", "content": [ {"type": "image_url", "image_url": {"url": "https://huggingface.co/datasets/merve/vl-test-suite/resolve/main/pills.jpg"}}, {"type": "text", "text": "Do any of the components in this supplement interact?"} ] }], "chat_template_kwargs": {"enable_thinking": false} }' Any OpenAI-compatible client works with the same URL and your Hugging Face token as the API key. Fine-tuning with TRL You can fine-tune the 816B checkpoint with the TRL SFTTrainer . This section shows how we fine-tuned it with TRL on 8 nodes of 8 H100 GPUs. The recipe trains LoRA adapters on the attention layers. The experts stay frozen. The full script is in the TRL examples . First, we need to split the model across 64 GPU devices. Given the large size of the model, we need to parallelize it across multiple axes. We shard the model with FSDP

items.content: Computer Science > Machine Learning arXiv:2610.22358 (cs) [Submitted on 15 Oct 2026] Title: PathFM: Fast Generative Forecasting of Multivariate Trajectories Authors: Jiachen Yao , Xiyuan Zhang , Annan Yu , Boran Han , Abdul Fatir Ansari , Shuai Zhang , Michael Bohlke-Schneider , Bernie Wang View a PDF of the paper titled PathFM: Fast Generative Forecasting of Multivariate Trajectories, by Jiachen Yao and 7 other authors View PDF HTML (experimental) Abstract: Time series foundation models are becoming increasingly popular for general-purpose forecasting. However, most leading models predict marginal quantiles, leaving the dependence structure of future trajectories unspecified. This distinction matters for trajectory-dependent quantities such as cumulative demand, peak load, and event timing, yet point and marginal scores do not reveal it. To model this dependence, we introduce PathFM, a trajectory-based forecasting model that uses flow matching to generate complete future paths. We further distill the model to one or two steps and share history attention cache across draws. Together, these enable PathFM to generate multiple paths for a single series in roughly the time needed for one query to a quantile model. The distilled sampler also makes it practical to optimize a calibration loss directly. PathFM achieves competitive marginal accuracy on the established forecasting benchmarks fev-bench and TIME. To complement these evaluations, we introduce Forecast Path Score Bench (fps-bench), which augments fev-bench tasks with energy and variogram scores and downstream metrics. PathFM achieves a higher aggregate path score on fps-bench than all evaluated external baselines. Experiments on chaotic systems further show that our flow model sustains long-run variability, while strong baselines rapidly collapse. PathFM makes generative time series forecasting both competitive and practical, enabling diverse downstream applications. items.content: Rethinking Routing Exploration in Modern Mixture-of-Experts Bingcong Li 1,2 Hao Ma 2 Michael Muehlebach 3,4 Niao He 1 Yi Ma 2 Abstract Mixture-of-experts (MoE) models have become an important approach for scaling model parameters. Modern MoE architectures increasingly combine two design choices: fine-grained expert segmentation and shared experts. The former increases expressiveness by enabling more expert combinations at a fixed activation ratio, and the latter introduces experts that are active for every token. We identify an exploration dilemma between these designs: shared experts can make routing less exploratory by reducing the variability of token representations. This conflicts with the greater need for exploration induced by fine-grained expert segmentation due to the combinatorially enlarged routing space. Consequently, the additional expressiveness offered by fine-grained segmentation may not be fully realized in practice. MirrorMoE is proposed to reconcile this exploration dilemma by shrinking the exploration space through token-adaptive suppression of unnecessary experts. MirrorMoE consistently improves performance across model scales. Code is available here . 1 ETH Zurich 2 The University of Hong Kong 3 Max Planck Institute for Intelligent Systems 4 WU Vienna {bingcong.li, niao.he}@inf.ethz.ch, {haoma, mayi}@hku.hk, michael.muehlebach@tuebingen.mpg.de 1 Introduction Mixture-of-experts (MoE) models have been instrumental in scaling large language models (LLMs) to trillions of parameters and beyond ( Lepikhin et al., 2020 ; Fedus et al., 2022 ) . MoEs adopt a sparse conditional-computation paradigm, where each token activates only a subset of experts, or subnetworks. During pretraining, recent work has shown that MoEs can outperform their dense counterparts under matched total parameter counts, compute, and data budgets ( Li et al., 2026 ) . At inference, sparse activation allows computational cost to grow sublinearly with total parameters. Thanks to these advantages, MoEs have become a core architecture underlying model families such as DeepSeek ( Dai et al., 2024 ; Liu et al., 2024 ) , Kimi ( Team-Kimi, 2025 ; Team-Kimi, 2026 ) , and Qwen ( Team-Qwen, 2024b ; Yang et al., 2025 ) , among many others ( Jiang et al., 2024 ; Abdin et al., 2024 ) . At the core of MoEs is the MoE layer, which consists of a router and E E experts, each implemented as a feedforward network (FFN). For each input token, the router selects K K experts ( K < E K<E ) for sparse activation ( Lepikhin et al., 2020 ; Fedus et al., 2022 ) . Building on this basic design, recent MoEs have increasingly adopted two notable architectural advances. The first is fine-grained expert segmentation ( Team-Kimi, 2026 ; Liu et al., 2024 ) . Recent MoEs tend to use larger numbers of both total and activated experts, i.e., larger E E and K K . For example, at the same activation ratio K / E K/E , ( E , K ) = ( 64 , 8 ) (E,K)=(64,8) is often preferred over ( E , K ) = ( 8 , 1 ) (E,K)=(8,1) . Since there are ( E K ) \binom{E}{K} expert combinations, the latter yields richer routing space for more expressive token representations ( Elango et al., 2026 ) . The second advance is shared experts . Activated for every token, shared experts capture common knowledge that would otherwise be learned redundantly by routed experts. This allows routed ones to devote more capacity to specialization. The combination of the above architectural choices have become standard in modern MoEs ( Dai et al., 2024 ; Liu et al., 2024 ; Team-Qwen, 2024b ) . This work reexamines the interaction between these two trends from the angle of routing exploration . The goal of exploration is to search for alternative expert combinations during pretraining to identify (near-)optimal routes for each token. On the one hand, realizing the expressive potential of fine-grained expert segmentation requires exploring a combinatorially larger routing space within each MoE layer. For example, the number of expert subsets increases from 8 8 when ( E , K ) = ( 8 , 1 ) (E,K)=(8,1) to ( 64 8 ) ≈ 4.4 × 10 9 {64\choose 8}\approx 4.4\times 10^{9} with ( E , K ) = ( 64 , 8 ) (E,K)=(64,8) , i.e., several orders of magnitude increase. On the other hand, our analysis reveals an asymmetry during pretraining: shared experts dominate the learned token representations, leaving routed experts with less influence on the layer output. Consequently, even activating different routed experts only leads to limited variation in the learned features, making alternative routes harder to distinguish and thereby undermining the goal of exploration. This exploration dilemma has tangible consequences for shared-expert MoEs. To see this, we train matched MoE models with and without shared experts at 4 scales, ranging from 100M to 2.4B total parameters. At each scale, we fix the total number of experts E E and vary the number of (total) activated experts K K over { 6 , 8 , 10 } \{6,8,10\} . A larger K K simultaneously increases model expressiveness and demands more strategic exploration due to enlarged routing space. As shown in Fig. 1 , shared experts no longer provide benefits over their non-shared counterparts as K K increases. More strikingly, the performance of shared-expert MoEs can even degrade as K K increases in Figs. 1(b) and 1(d) , suggesting that the inefficient exploration hinders realization of the additional expressiveness from larger K K . MirrorMoE is proposed to reconcile the conflicting architecture designs above. It adaptively suppresses routed experts on a token basis, reducing the exploration space to better match the model’s exploration capability. Technically, MirrorMoE is derived by mirroring the routing logits via sign negation, hence its name. As shown in Fig. 1 , MirrorMoE improves the performance of shared-expert MoEs and attains expressiveness gains from larger K K . In summary, our contributions are as follows: ❖ We identify an exploration dilemma in modern MoEs: the enlarged routing space induced by fine-grained expert segmentation demands greater exploration, while shared experts make routing less explorative. As a result, the benefits of shared experts diminish as the routing space grows. ❖ We propose MirrorMoE , which adaptively shrinks the exploration space to reconcile competing demands above. MirrorMoE is conceptually simple, and its adaptivity is theoretically characterized. ❖ We demonstrate that MirrorMoE addresses the exploration dilemma across MoEs of different scales. On the 2.4B model, MirrorMoE improves pretraining and downstream performance by 0.67 and 1.64 points, respectively. Moreover, it enables shared-expert MoEs to consistently outperform their non-shared counterparts and restores the performance gains from increasing K K ; see Fig. 1 . (a) 100M (b) 498M (c) 625M (d) 2.4B Figure 1: Comparison of MoEs with and without shared experts (SE) and the proposed MirrorMoE. MirrorMoE consistently i) achieves the best performance, ii) realizes the expressiveness gains from larger K K , and iii) enables shared-expert MoEs to outperform their non-shared counterparts. 1.1 Related work MoEs. Modern sparse MoEs originated with the sparsely gated MoE layer of Shazeer et al. (2017) and were extended to large-scale Transformers in e.g., Lepikhin et al. (2020) ; Fedus et al. (2022) . Later work focused on improving scalability, stability, and expert specialization. GLaM ( Du et al., 2022 ) demonstrated that sparse language models could scale beyond one trillion parameters, while ST-MoE ( Zoph et al., 2022 ) improved training stability. MoEs have since become widely adopted. Beyond those mentioned earlier, other representative examples include Gemma4, OLMoE and gpt-oss ( Team-Gemma, 2026 ; Muennighoff et al., 2025 ; Agarwal et al., 2025 ) . Across this development trajectory, two trends have clearly emerged: fine-grained expert segmentation and shared experts. Tension between expressiveness and pretraining. A growing line of work shows that a model’s expressive capacity may not be readily realized without carefully designed training procedures ( Lion et al., 2025 ; Zhang et al., 2026 ; Jha and Reagen, 2026 ; Wei et al., 2025a ) . Within the context of MoEs, related evidence is provided by Jin et al. (2024) , which augments learnable experts with fixed zero, copy, and constant experts. Although standard FFN experts can, in principle, learn these operations, explicitly incorporating them still improves empirical performance. The benefit of directly defining these operations, rather than learning them through training, suggests that the available expressiveness may not be fully realized in practice. Our work further shows that the additional expressiveness provided by fine-grained expert segmentation is not naturally attained in shared-expert MoEs. Additional related work on MoE routing and systems is deferred to App. A due to limited space. 2 The Exploration Dilemma in Shared-Expert MoEs This section first reviews MoEs and then examines the effect of shared experts on exploration. 2.1 MoE recap MoEs replace the FFN in each Transformer layer with a collection of FFNs, each referred to as an expert . Among E E experts at layer l l , there are two types: S S shared experts { 𝒮ℰ l , s } s \{{\cal SE}_{l,s}\}_{s} , activated for every token ( Liu et al., 2024 ) , and R := E − S R\!:=\!E\!-\!S routed experts { ℛℰ l , e } e \{{\cal RE}_{l,e}\}_{e} , activated in a token-driven manner. We use K K to denote the total number of activated experts, including the shared ones. For 𝐡 l n ∈ ℝ d \mathbf{h}_{l}^{n}\in\mathbb{R}^{d} , the representation of the n n -th token entering the l l -th MoE layer, the routed experts to be activated are selected by a linear projection 𝐆 l ∈ ℝ R × d \mathbf{G}_{l}\in\mathbb{R}^{R\times d} , known as the router . The router produces a probability distribution over the routed experts, and those with the highest probabilities are activated. The activated routed experts are collected in 𝒜 l ​ ( 𝐡 l n ) {\cal A}_{l}(\mathbf{h}_{l}^{n}) : p l , e ( 𝐡 l n ) = exp ( 𝐆 l [ e , : ] 𝐡 l n ) ∑ j = 1 R exp ( 𝐆 l [ j , : ] 𝐡 l n ) , 𝒜 l ( 𝐡 l n ) = 𝖳𝗈𝗉 K − S ( { p l , e ( 𝐡 l n ) } , e ∈ [ R ] ) . \displaystyle p_{l,e}(\mathbf{h}_{l}^{n})=\frac{\exp(\mathbf{G}_{l}[e,:]\mathbf{h}_{l}^{n})}{\sum_{j=1}^{R}\exp(\mathbf{G}_{l}[j,:]\mathbf{h}_{l}^{n})},~~~{\cal A}_{l}(\mathbf{h}_{l}^{n})=\mathsf{Top}_{K-S}\big(\{p_{l,e}(\mathbf{h}_{l}^{n})\},e\in[R]\big). (1) Here, 𝖳𝗈𝗉 K − S ​ ( ⋅ ) \mathsf{Top}_{K-S}(\cdot) deterministically selects K − S K-S experts with the largest probabilities and [ R ] := { 1 , … , R } [R]:=\{1,\ldots,R\} denotes all the routed experts. The learned token representation of this layer combines the outputs of both shared and routed experts, where shared experts capture common features and routed experts learn specialized ones, i.e., 𝐡 l + 1 n = ∑ s = 1 S 𝒮ℰ l , s ​ ( 𝐡 l n ) + ∑ e ∈ 𝒜 l ​ ( 𝐡 l n ) p l , e ​ ( 𝐡 l n ) Z ⁡ ( 𝐡 l n ) ⋅ ℛℰ l , e ​ ( 𝐡 l n ) \displaystyle\mathbf{h}_{l+1}^{n}=\sum_{s=1}^{S}{\cal SE}_{l,s}(\mathbf{h}_{l}^{n})+\sum_{e\in{\cal A}_{l}(\mathbf{h}_{l}^{n})}\frac{p_{l,e}(\mathbf{h}_{l}^{n})}{Z(\mathbf{h}_{l}^{n})}\cdot{\cal RE}_{l,e}(\mathbf{h}_{l}^{n}) (2) where Z ⁡ ( 𝐡 l n ) = ∑ j ∈ 𝒜 l ​ ( 𝐡 l n ) p l , j ​ ( 𝐡 l n ) Z(\mathbf{h}_{l}^{n})=\sum_{j\in{\cal A}_{l}(\mathbf{h}_{l}^{n})}p_{l,j}(\mathbf{h}_{l}^{n}) renormalizes the weights of the activated experts, as in ( Yang et al., 2025 ) or Z ⁡ ( 𝐡 l n ) = 1 Z(\mathbf{h}_{l}^{n})=1 as in DeepSeek-MoE and Qwen1.5-MoE ( Dai et al., 2024 ; Muennighoff et al., 2025 ; Team-Qwen, 2024a ) . We follow the latter in this paper. Vanilla MoEs without shared experts are recovered when S = 0 S=0 . For convenience, we omit the dependence of p l , e p_{l,e} and 𝒜 l {\cal A}_{l} on 𝐡 l n \mathbf{h}_{l}^{n} , as well as the token index n n whenever clear from context. Beyond shared experts, recent MoEs have also shifted toward fine-grained expert segmentation ( Liu et al., 2024 ; Yang et al., 2025 ; Elango et al., 2026 ) . For the same activation ratio, this trend favors configurations such as R = 64 , K − S = 8 R=64,K-S=8 over R = 8 , K − S = 1 R=8,K-S=1 , enabling a combinatorially richer set of expert compositions and, hence, more expressive token representations. However, realizing such expressiveness through pretraining is far from straightforward, where the challenge also stems from the combinatorial expansion of the routing space. Identifying optimal expert combinations therefore requires more exploration. This motivates us to revisit exploration in MoE training. 2.2 Shared experts weaken routing exploration This subsection reexamines the roles of shared and routed experts, reveals an asymmetry in their learning dynamics, and shows how shared-expert dominance can hinder exploration. To isolate the impact of shared experts, we compare MoEs with and without them using matching datasets, tokenizers, and configurations. The models in this subsection have 121M activated and 498M total parameters, with E = 66 E=66 and K = 8 K=8 . We set S = 2 S\!=\!2 for shared-expert MoEs, while MoEs without shared experts amount to S = 0 S\!=\!0 . Details are deferred to App. B.1 . We select checkpoints at 20 % 20\% , 50 % 50\% , and 100 % 100\% of pretraining to represent the early, middle, and final stages, respectively. Asymmetric training dynamics in shared-expert MoEs. We first ablate individual experts to assess their importance. Specifically, we zero out each expert’s output and measure the resulting perplexity change, Δ ​ 𝖯𝖯𝖫 = 𝖯𝖯𝖫 after − 𝖯𝖯𝖫 base \Delta\mathsf{PPL}=\mathsf{PPL}_{\mathrm{after}}-\mathsf{PPL}_{\mathrm{base}} . In Fig. 2 , the two rightmost columns in the right-hand plots correspond to shared experts. Across all three checkpoints, ablating a shared expert leads to a substantially larger perplexity increase than ablating a routed expert. This shows that shared experts play a disproportionately important role in model performance. (a) 20% of training (b) 50% of training (c) 100% of training Figure 2: Perplexity increase after ablating individual experts. In the right subplot, the two rightmost columns, separated by a solid line, correspond to shared experts. Another means to quantify the asymmetric roles of experts is through the so-termed routing criticality , which replaces the learned router with uniform random routing and measures the resulting performance change. We apply this intervention one layer at a time and report the relative perplexity increase, 𝖯𝖯𝖫 after − 𝖯𝖯𝖫 base 𝖯𝖯𝖫 base \frac{\mathsf{PPL}_{\mathrm{after}}-\mathsf{PPL}_{\mathrm{base}}}{\mathsf{PPL}_{\mathrm{base}}} . Larger values indicate greater dependence on the learned router. As shown in Fig. 3(a) , uniform routing in the early and middle layers of the shared-expert MoE leads to a much smaller perplexity increase than in standard MoEs. In other words, shared experts in these layers capture such a large fraction of the learned representation that the layers are robust to random routing. Next, we examine how this asymmetry in expert roles shapes exploration. Exploration aims to discover alternative routes that produce diverse token representations. We therefore quantify exploration by measuring how much the learned representation changes under different routing decisions. Even before this analysis, the asymmetry between shared and routed experts suggests that exploration may be ineffective: if a highly exploratory routing policy, such as uniform routing, barely changes the output of a shared-expert layer, other routing is also unlikely to produce substantially different representations. We next confirm this intuition using two complementary variance metrics, one induced by experts and the other by routers. Shared experts suppress expert-induced variance. We first quantify how much an MoE layer’s output can vary when different experts are activated. To this end, we introduce the notion of expert variance . items.raw_text: Rethinking Routing Exploration in Modern Mixture-of-Experts Bingcong Li 1,2 Hao Ma 2 Michael Muehlebach 3,4 Niao He 1 Yi Ma 2 Abstract Mixture-of-experts (MoE) models have become an important approach for scaling model parameters. Modern MoE architectures increasingly combine two design choices: fine-grained expert segmentation and shared experts. The former increases expressiveness by enabling more expert combinations at a fixed activation ratio, and the latter introduces experts that are active for every token. We identify an exploration dilemma between these designs: shared experts can make routing less exploratory by reducing the variability of token representations. This conflicts with the greater need for exploration induced by fine-grained expert segmentation due to the combinatorially enlarged routing space. Consequently, the additional expressiveness offered by fine-grained segmentation may not be fully realized in practice. MirrorMoE is proposed to reconcile this exploration dilemma by shrinking the exploration space through token-adaptive suppression of unnecessary experts. MirrorMoE consistently improves performance across model scales. Code is available here . 1 ETH Zurich 2 The University of Hong Kong 3 Max Planck Institute for Intelligent Systems 4 WU Vienna {bingcong.li, niao.he}@inf.ethz.ch, {haoma, mayi}@hku.hk, michael.muehlebach@tuebingen.mpg.de 1 Introduction Mixture-of-experts (MoE) models have been instrumental in scaling large language models (LLMs) to trillions of parameters and beyond ( Lepikhin et al., 2020 ; Fedus et al., 2022 ) . MoEs adopt a sparse conditional-computation paradigm, where each token activates only a subset of experts, or subnetworks. During pretraining, recent work has shown that MoEs can outperform their dense counterparts under matched total parameter counts, compute, and data budgets ( Li et al., 2026 ) . At inference, sparse activation allows computational cost to grow sublinearly with total parameters. Thanks to these advantages, MoEs have become a core architecture underlying model families such as DeepSeek ( Dai et al., 2024 ; Liu et al., 2024 ) , Kimi ( Team-Kimi, 2025 ; Team-Kimi, 2026 ) , and Qwen ( Team-Qwen, 2024b ; Yang et al., 2025 ) , among many others ( Jiang et al., 2024 ; Abdin et al., 2024 ) . At the core of MoEs is the MoE layer, which consists of a router and E E experts, each implemented as a feedforward network (FFN). For each input token, the router selects K K experts ( K < E K<E ) for sparse activation ( Lepikhin et al., 2020 ; Fedus et al., 2022 ) . Building on this basic design, recent MoEs have increasingly adopted two notable architectural advances. The first is fine-grained expert segmentation ( Team-Kimi, 2026 ; Liu et al., 2024 ) . Recent MoEs tend to use larger numbers of both total and activated experts, i.e., larger E E and K K . For example, at the same activation ratio K / E K/E , ( E , K ) = ( 64 , 8 ) (E,K)=(64,8) is often preferred over ( E , K ) = ( 8 , 1 ) (E,K)=(8,1) . Since there are ( E K ) \binom{E}{K} expert combinations, the latter yields richer routing space for more expressive token representations ( Elango et al., 2026 ) . The second advance is shared experts . Activated for every token, shared experts capture common knowledge that would otherwise be learned redundantly by routed experts. This allows routed ones to devote more capacity to specialization. The combination of the above architectural choices have become standard in modern MoEs ( Dai et al., 2024 ; Liu et al., 2024 ; Team-Qwen, 2024b ) . This work reexamines the interaction between these two trends from the angle of routing exploration . The goal of exploration is to search for alternative expert combinations during pretraining to identify (near-)optimal routes for each token. On the one hand, realizing the expressive potential of fine-grained expert segmentation requires exploring a combinatorially larger routing space within each MoE layer. For example, the number of expert subsets increases from 8 8 when ( E , K ) = ( 8 , 1 ) (E,K)=(8,1) to ( 64 8 ) ≈ 4.4 × 10 9 {64\choose 8}\approx 4.4\times 10^{9} with ( E , K ) = ( 64 , 8 ) (E,K)=(64,8) , i.e., several orders of magnitude increase. On the other hand, our analysis reveals an asymmetry during pretraining: shared experts dominate the learned token representations, leaving routed experts with less influence on the layer output. Consequently, even activating different routed experts only leads to limited variation in the learned features, making alternative routes harder to distinguish and thereby undermining the goal of exploration. This exploration dilemma has tangible consequences for shared-expert MoEs. To see this, we train matched MoE models with and without shared experts at 4 scales, ranging from 100M to 2.4B total parameters. At each scale, we fix the total number of experts E E and vary the number of (total) activated experts K K over { 6 , 8 , 10 } \{6,8,10\} . A larger K K simultaneously increases model expressiveness and demands more strategic exploration due to enlarged routing space. As shown in Fig. 1 , shared experts no longer provide benefits over their non-shared counterparts as K K increases. More strikingly, the performance of shared-expert MoEs can even degrade as K K increases in Figs. 1(b) and 1(d) , suggesting that the inefficient exploration hinders realization of the additional expressiveness from larger K K . MirrorMoE is proposed to reconcile the conflicting architecture designs above. It adaptively suppresses routed experts on a token basis, reducing the exploration space to better match the model’s exploration capability. Technically, MirrorMoE is derived by mirroring the routing logits via sign negation, hence its name. As shown in Fig. 1 , MirrorMoE improves the performance of shared-expert MoEs and attains expressiveness gains from larger K K . In summary, our contributions are as follows: ❖ We identify an exploration dilemma in modern MoEs: the enlarged routing space induced by fine-grained expert segmentation demands greater exploration, while shared experts make routing less explorative. As a result, the benefits of shared experts diminish as the routing space grows. ❖ We propose MirrorMoE , which adaptively shrinks the exploration space to reconcile competing demands above. MirrorMoE is conceptually simple, and its adaptivity is theoretically characterized. ❖ We demonstrate that MirrorMoE addresses the exploration dilemma across MoEs of different scales. On the 2.4B model, MirrorMoE improves pretraining and downstream performance by 0.67 and 1.64 points, respectively. Moreover, it enables shared-expert MoEs to consistently outperform their non-shared counterparts and restores the performance gains from increasing K K ; see Fig. 1 . MirrorMoE consistently i) achieves the best performance, ii) realizes the expressiveness gains from larger K K , and iii) enables shared-expert MoEs to outperform their non-shared counterparts. 1.1 Related work MoEs. Modern sparse MoEs originated with the sparsely gated MoE layer of Shazeer et al. (2017) and were extended to large-scale Transformers in e.g., Lepikhin et al. (2020) ; Fedus et al. (2022) . Later work focused on improving scalability, stability, and expert specialization. GLaM ( Du et al., 2022 ) demonstrated that sparse language models could scale beyond one trillion parameters, while ST-MoE ( Zoph et al., 2022 ) improved training stability. MoEs have since become widely adopted. Beyond those mentioned earlier, other representative examples include Gemma4, OLMoE and gpt-oss ( Team-Gemma, 2026 ; Muennighoff et al., 2025 ; Agarwal et al., 2025 ) . Across this development trajectory, two trends have clearly emerged: fine-grained expert segmentation and shared experts. Tension between expressiveness and pretraining. A growing line of work shows that a model’s expressive capacity may not be readily realized without carefully designed training procedures ( Lion et al., 2025 ; Zhang et al., 2026 ; Jha and Reagen, 2026 ; Wei et al., 2025a ) . Within the context of MoEs, related evidence is provided by Jin et al. (2024) , which augments learnable experts with fixed zero, copy, and constant experts. Although standard FFN experts can, in principle, learn these operations, explicitly incorporating them still improves empirical performance. The benefit of directly defining these operations, rather than learning them through training, suggests that the available expressiveness may not be fully realized in practice. Our work further shows that the additional expressiveness provided by fine-grained expert segmentation is not naturally attained in shared-expert MoEs. Additional related work on MoE routing and systems is deferred to App. A due to limited space. 2 The Exploration Dilemma in Shared-Expert MoEs This section first reviews MoEs and then examines the effect of shared experts on exploration. 2.1 MoE recap MoEs replace the FFN in each Transformer layer with a collection of FFNs, each referred to as an expert . items.content: Computer Science > Machine Learning arXiv:2610.22339 (cs) [Submitted on 15 Oct 2026] Title: Lean Graph Search for Formal Theorem Proving Authors: Yihan Xu , Jia-Chen Gu , Junyi Zhang , Di Wu , Haikang Deng , Po-Nien Kung , Kai-Wei Chang , Amit Sahai , Wei Wang , Nanyun Peng View a PDF of the paper titled Lean Graph Search for Formal Theorem Proving, by Yihan Xu and 9 other authors View PDF HTML (experimental) Abstract: Retrieving relevant lemmas is crucial for formal theorem proving, enabling provers to build machine-checkable proofs from established mathematical results. Recent retrieval systems match library declarations to a target theorem or its intermediate proof steps, but make limited use of multi-hop dependencies among declarations. These dependencies can reveal supporting lemmas that are not necessarily lexically similar to the target theorem but recur in proofs of related problems. To this end, we propose LeanGraphSearch, a graph-based retrieval method for Lean 4 that constructs a graph from Mathlib's forward dependencies and traverses it to uncover supporting lemmas through multi-hop dependency chains. Specifically, LeanGraphSearch links each declaration to the premises it depends on, uses a graph-based ranking algorithm to propagate relevance from semantically matched declarations to their dependencies, and reranks the expanded candidates against the original query. Across two mathematical retrieval benchmarks, LeanGraphSearch improves recall by up to 12% over the strongest baseline, LeanSearch v2, on MathlibQR and increases coverage of complete annotated proof routes on MathlibMPR, covering up to 3.7% of extra groups. More importantly, we evaluate whether these retrieval gains translate into improved end-to-end theorem proving by integrating LeanGraphSearch into an iterative proving loop guided by Lean feedback. Across three theorem proving benchmarks, LeanGraphSearch improves pass rate at {8, 16, 32} reflection turns by as much as 40% compared to vanilla prover and at most 10% compared to LeanSearch v2, showing higher accuracy-cost efficiency. These findings highlight the value of dependency graph search for theorem proving and motivate further research on structure-aware search for proof discovery.
