items.content: Lean Graph Search for Formal Theorem Proving Yihan Xu † † thanks: Equal contribution. Jia-Chen Gu 1 1 footnotemark: 1 Junyi Zhang Di Wu Haikang Deng Po-Nien Kung Affiliation: Kai-Wei Chang, Amit Sahai, Wei Wang, Nanyun Peng Affiliation: University of California, Los Angeles Affiliation: {simpson561@, gujc@, junyizhang2002@, diwu@cs.}ucla.edu Affiliation: [3pt] Website Code Abstract Retrieving relevant lemmas is crucial for formal theorem proving, enabling provers to build machine-checkable proofs from established mathematical results. Recent retrieval systems match library declarations to a target theorem or its intermediate proof steps, but make limited use of multi-hop dependencies among declarations. These dependencies can reveal supporting lemmas that are not necessarily lexically similar to the target theorem but recur in proofs of related problems. To this end, we propose LeanGraphSearch , a graph-based retrieval method for Lean 4 that constructs a graph from Mathlib’s forward dependencies and traverses it to uncover supporting lemmas through multi-hop dependency chains. Specifically, LeanGraphSearch links each declaration to the premises it depends on, uses a graph-based ranking algorithm to propagate relevance from semantically matched declarations to their dependencies, and reranks the expanded candidates against the original query. Across two mathematical retrieval benchmarks, LeanGraphSearch improves recall by up to 12 percentage points over the strongest baseline, LeanSearch v2, on MathlibQR and increases coverage of complete annotated proof routes on MathlibMPR by up to 3.7 percentage points. More importantly, we evaluate whether these retrieval gains translate into improved end-to-end theorem proving by integrating LeanGraphSearch into an iterative proving loop guided by Lean feedback. Across three theorem proving benchmarks, LeanGraphSearch improves pass rate at { 8 , 16 , 32 } \{8,16,32\} reflection turns by as much as 40% compared to the vanilla prover and at most 10% compared to LeanSearch v2, showing a better accuracy–cost tradeoff. These findings highlight the value of dependency graph search for theorem proving and motivate further research on structure-aware search for proof discovery. 1 Introduction Formal theorem proving expresses mathematical statements and proofs in a formal language, allowing a proof assistant such as Lean to verify their correctness ( de Moura & Ullrich, 2021 ) . Search engines support the proving process by helping users and automated provers locate useful definitions, theorems, and lemmas within large mathematical libraries such as Mathlib ( The mathlib Community, 2020 ; Yang et al., 2023 ; Mikuła et al., 2024 ; Shen et al., 2025 ; Ju et al., 2026 ) . Existing retrieval systems, such as LeanExplore ( Asher, 2025 ) , LeanFinder ( Lu et al., 2026 ) , and LeanSearch v2 ( Gao et al., 2026 ) , address this need by identifying library declarations relevant to a target theorem or an intermediate goal. However, their limited use of multi-hop dependencies among declarations may miss supporting lemmas that share little lexical similarity with the query but occur in proofs of related problems ( Shen et al., 2025 ; Gao et al., 2026 ) . A key observation is that declarations relevant to a target theorem can serve as starting points for discovering supporting lemmas through multi-hop dependencies. These dependencies connect declarations to their direct and indirect premises, providing extra paths to useful lemmas that are less lexically similar to the query. To capture and exploit this structure, we introduce LeanGraphSearch ( Fig. 1 ), a graph-based retrieval framework for Lean 4 theorem proving. It constructs a directed graph from Mathlib’s forward dependencies, representing declarations as nodes and linking each declaration to the premises it directly depends on. Searching this graph from semantically relevant declarations extends retrieval beyond direct query matching, helping users and automated provers discover supporting premises that may otherwise be difficult to locate. (a) Declaration Dependencies (b) Retrieval and Proving Query q q : target theorem or proof goal Related d 1 d_{1} Related d 2 d_{2} Shared premise ℓ 1 \ell_{1} Multi-hop premise ℓ 2 \ell_{2} d 3 d_{3} d 4 d_{4} query match formal dependency other declarations in graph MathlibQR Recall (%) + 12.0 +12.0 pp vs. LeanSearch v2 0 50 100 LeanSearch v2 82.7 LeanGraphSearch 94.7 MathlibMPR Covered (%) + 3.7 +3.7 pp vs. LeanSearch v2 0 50 100 LeanSearch v2 39.1 LeanGraphSearch 42.8 FATE-H Success Rate (%) + 8.0 +8.0 pp vs. LeanSearch v2 0 50 100 No retrieval 52 LeanSearch v2 73 LeanGraphSearch 81 Figure 1: Dependency-guided retrieval with LeanGraphSearch . (a) An illustration of the dependency graph, showing how semantically retrieved declarations (blue) lead to supporting premises (green) through shared and multi-hop dependencies. (b) Selected retrieval and proving results. Gains are reported in percentage points relative to LeanSearch v2. To search the constructed dependency graph, LeanGraphSearch uses the target query to guide traversal along formal dependencies. Given an informal description or a formal goal, it first retrieves declarations using embeddings and reranks them against the query to select semantically relevant seeds. The seed relevance scores are normalized to form the personalization distribution for personalized PageRank ( Brin & Page, 1998 ) , which propagates relevance along dependency edges while repeatedly returning to the seeds, thereby expanding the candidate set. Finally, LeanGraphSearch reranks the expanded candidates against the original query and combines these second-pass relevance scores with query-specific graph scores to produce the final ranking. We evaluate LeanGraphSearch on both standalone premise retrieval and downstream formal theorem proving. For premise retrieval, LeanGraphSearch improves Recall@100 from 82.7% with LeanSearch v2 to 94.7% on the 810-query fair subset of MathlibQR ( Gao et al., 2026 ) , confirming that dependency graph search effectively recovers additional relevant lemmas. On MathlibMPR ( Gao et al., 2026 ) , it improves proof route-level premise coverage, increasing Covered@20 from 39.1% to 42.8% and Covered@50 from 41.3% to 44.2%. These results suggest that dependency-aware retrieval better recovers complete premise sets along annotated proof routes. For formal theorem proving, we integrate LeanGraphSearch into an iterative proving loop equipped with Lean’s diagnostic feedback and problem-local failure memory. LeanGraphSearch consistently outperforms the state-of-the-art retrieval baselines across FATE-H ( Jiang et al., 2026 ) , MathlibMPR-Prop ( Gao et al., 2026 ) , and Lean-IMO-Bench ( Kung et al., 2026 ) , demonstrating that premise retrieval improvements translate into higher formal proof success rates. 2 Related Work Mathematical theorem proving can be carried out informally in natural language and mathematical notation or formally in a language checked by a proof assistant such as Lean ( de Moura & Ullrich, 2021 ) . Large language model (LLM)-based approaches to formal proving include generating tactics within proof-state search ( Yang et al., 2023 ; Thakur et al., 2024 ) and generating and refining proof scripts through verifier feedback, often guided by informal proof sketches ( Kung et al., 2026 ) . Throughout this paper, mathematical search refers to retrieving library declarations for formal proving, using either informal or formal queries. For additional related work, see Appendix A . Search for Formal Mathematics. Prior work shows that retrieving reusable library facts improves formal proof construction ( Mikuła et al., 2024 ; Yang et al., 2023 ; Shen et al., 2025 ) . Magnushammer learns premise selection through contrastive training and reranking for Isabelle ( Mikuła et al., 2024 ) , while ReProver and REAL-Prover condition tactic generation on retrieved Lean premises ( Yang et al., 2023 ; Shen et al., 2025 ) . LeanPremise supports premise selection in user-specific contexts ( Zhu et al., 2026 ) , and LeanStateSearch adapts tokenization and reranking to formal proof-state queries ( Tao et al., 2025 ) . Complementary search systems help locate declarations from mathematical descriptions: LeanExplore combines formal statements with informal descriptions for semantic search ( Asher, 2025 ) , and Lean Finder learns intent-aware embeddings from synthesized queries and preference feedback ( Lu et al., 2026 ) . LeanSearch v2 extends this line of work to global premise retrieval, combining embedding-based search and reranking with iterative sketch–retrieve–reflect cycles to gather supporting premises for an entire proof ( Gao et al., 2026 ) . Graph-based Retrieval. Graph structure has been used to guide retrieval in both natural-language corpora and formal libraries. GraphRAG builds an entity graph and community summaries for query-focused summarization ( Edge et al., 2024 ) , while HippoRAG applies personalized PageRank to a knowledge graph for multi-hop retrieval ( Jiménez Gutiérrez et al., 2024 ) . KG 2 RAG starts from semantically retrieved chunks and uses a knowledge graph to expand and organize evidence ( Zhu et al., 2025 ) . In formal mathematical search, LeanExplore uses declaration dependencies to generate informal descriptions and incorporates PageRank centrality as a ranking feature ( Asher, 2025 ) . LeanSearch v2 also processes dependencies bottom-up when constructing declaration descriptions ( Gao et al., 2026 ) . To learn graph-aware representations for premise selection, Petrovčič et al. (2025) combine textual embeddings with a relational graph neural network over state–premise and premise–premise dependencies. 3 LeanGraphSearch (a) Dependency Graph Construction Mathlib Declarations declaration d i d_{i} type: ⋯ d j ⋯ \cdots\,d_{j}\,\cdots value: ⋯ d k ⋯ \cdots\,d_{k}\,\cdots jixia Static Analysis Reference Extraction Declaration Dependency Graph 𝒢 = ( V , E ) \mathcal{G}=(V,E) d i d_{i} d j d_{j} d k d_{k} d ℓ d_{\ell} type value Node: declaration statement and description Edge: declaration ⟶ \longrightarrow referenced dependency (b) Graph-based Retrieval Query q q Dependency Graph 𝒢 \mathcal{G} Query q q 1. (a) Dependency graph construction ( Section 3.2 ). Static analysis with jixia extracts references from Mathlib declarations to construct a directed graph 𝒢 \mathcal{G} . (b) Graph-based retrieval ( Section 3.3 ). It first retrieves semantic seeds using semantic embeddings, then expands the candidate set by traversing the dependency graph. Seed and graph-expanded candidates are merged and reranked to select the final top- K K declarations. We introduce a graph-based retrieval framework for Lean theorem proving that exploits structural relationships among declarations. It represents Mathlib as a directed declaration dependency graph ( Fig. 2 (a)) and uses query-aware propagation to expand from semantically relevant declarations to their formal prerequisites ( Fig. 2 (b)). Semantic relevance and dependency structure jointly guide promising declaration selection, followed by reranking to produce the final ranked list. 3.1 Task Formulation Mathematical Retrieval. We study library declaration retrieval for theorem proving in Lean 4 ( de Moura & Ullrich, 2021 ) . Let ℒ = { d i } i = 1 n \mathcal{L}=\{d_{i}\}_{i=1}^{n} denote the Mathlib declaration corpus. Each declaration d i d_{i} is identified by its name and associated with its formal statement and, when available, a natural-language description 1 1 1 Descriptions are taken from the Gemini-generated corpus provided by Gao et al. (2026) . . A retrieval query q q can contain an informal mathematical description, a formal Lean statement, a proof state, or a combination of these. It may describe a target theorem or request a definition or lemma needed at an intermediate proof step. Recent retrieval systems match library declarations to a target theorem or its intermediate proof steps, but make limited use of multi-hop dependencies among declarations. These dependencies can reveal supporting lemmas that are not necessarily lexically similar to the target theorem but recur in proofs of related problems. To this end, we propose LeanGraphSearch , a graph-based retrieval method for Lean 4 that constructs a graph from Mathlib’s forward dependencies and traverses it to uncover supporting lemmas through multi-hop dependency chains. Specifically, LeanGraphSearch links each declaration to the premises it depends on, uses a graph-based ranking algorithm to propagate relevance from semantically matched declarations to their dependencies, and reranks the expanded candidates against the original query. Across two mathematical retrieval benchmarks, LeanGraphSearch improves recall by up to 12 percentage points over the strongest baseline, LeanSearch v2, on MathlibQR and increases coverage of complete annotated proof routes on MathlibMPR by up to 3.7 percentage points. More importantly, we evaluate whether these retrieval gains translate into improved end-to-end theorem proving by integrating LeanGraphSearch into an iterative proving loop guided by Lean feedback. Across three theorem proving benchmarks, LeanGraphSearch improves pass rate at { 8 , 16 , 32 } \{8,16,32\} reflection turns by as much as 40% compared to the vanilla prover and at most 10% compared to LeanSearch v2, showing a better accuracy–cost tradeoff. These findings highlight the value of dependency graph search for theorem proving and motivate further research on structure-aware search for proof discovery. 1 Introduction Formal theorem proving expresses mathematical statements and proofs in a formal language, allowing a proof assistant such as Lean to verify their correctness ( de Moura & Ullrich, 2021 ) . Search engines support the proving process by helping users and automated provers locate useful definitions, theorems, and lemmas within large mathematical libraries such as Mathlib ( The mathlib Community, 2020 ; Yang et al., 2023 ; Mikuła et al., 2024 ; Shen et al., 2025 ; Ju et al., 2026 ) . Existing retrieval systems, such as LeanExplore ( Asher, 2025 ) , LeanFinder ( Lu et al., 2026 ) , and LeanSearch v2 ( Gao et al., 2026 ) , address this need by identifying library declarations relevant to a target theorem or an intermediate goal. However, their limited use of multi-hop dependencies among declarations may miss supporting lemmas that share little lexical similarity with the query but occur in proofs of related problems ( Shen et al., 2025 ; Gao et al., 2026 ) . A key observation is that declarations relevant to a target theorem can serve as starting points for discovering supporting lemmas through multi-hop dependencies. These dependencies connect declarations to their direct and indirect premises, providing extra paths to useful lemmas that are less lexically similar to the query. To capture and exploit this structure, we introduce LeanGraphSearch ( Fig. 1 ), a graph-based retrieval framework for Lean 4 theorem proving. It constructs a directed graph from Mathlib’s forward dependencies, representing declarations as nodes and linking each declaration to the premises it directly depends on. Searching this graph from semantically relevant declarations extends retrieval beyond direct query matching, helping users and automated provers discover supporting premises that may otherwise be difficult to locate. To search the constructed dependency graph, LeanGraphSearch uses the target query to guide traversal along formal dependencies. Given an informal description or a formal goal, it first retrieves declarations using embeddings and reranks them against the query to select semantically relevant seeds. The seed relevance scores are normalized to form the personalization distribution for personalized PageRank ( Brin & Page, 1998 ) , which propagates relevance along dependency edges while repeatedly returning to the seeds, thereby expanding the candidate set. We evaluate LeanGraphSearch on both standalone premise retrieval and downstream formal theorem proving. These results suggest that dependency-aware retrieval better recovers complete premise sets along annotated proof routes. For formal theorem proving, we integrate LeanGraphSearch into an iterative proving loop equipped with Lean’s diagnostic feedback and problem-local failure memory. LeanGraphSearch consistently outperforms the state-of-the-art retrieval baselines across FATE-H ( Jiang et al., 2026 ) , MathlibMPR-Prop ( Gao et al., 2026 ) , and Lean-IMO-Bench ( Kung et al., 2026 ) , demonstrating that premise retrieval improvements translate into higher formal proof success rates. 2 Related Work Mathematical theorem proving can be carried out informally in natural language and mathematical notation or formally in a language checked by a proof assistant such as Lean ( de Moura & Ullrich, 2021 ) . Large language model (LLM)-based approaches to formal proving include generating tactics within proof-state search ( Yang et al., 2023 ; Thakur et al., 2024 ) and generating and refining proof scripts through verifier feedback, often guided by informal proof sketches ( Kung et al., 2026 ) . Throughout this paper, mathematical search refers to retrieving library declarations for formal proving, using either informal or formal queries. For additional related work, see Appendix A . Search for Formal Mathematics. Prior work shows that retrieving reusable library facts improves formal proof construction ( Mikuła et al., 2024 ; Yang et al., 2023 ; Shen et al., 2025 ) . Magnushammer learns premise selection through contrastive training and reranking for Isabelle ( Mikuła et al., 2024 ) , while ReProver and REAL-Prover condition tactic generation on retrieved Lean premises ( Yang et al., 2023 ; Shen et al., 2025 ) . LeanPremise supports premise selection in user-specific contexts ( Zhu et al., 2026 ) , and LeanStateSearch adapts tokenization and reranking to formal proof-state queries ( Tao et al., 2025 ) . Complementary search systems help locate declarations from mathematical descriptions: LeanExplore combines formal statements with informal descriptions for semantic search ( Asher, 2025 ) , and Lean Finder learns intent-aware embeddings from synthesized queries and preference feedback ( Lu et al., 2026 ) . LeanSearch v2 extends this line of work to global premise retrieval, combining embedding-based search and reranking with iterative sketch–retrieve–reflect cycles to gather supporting premises for an entire proof ( Gao et al., 2026 ) . Graph-based Retrieval. Graph structure has been used to guide retrieval in both natural-language corpora and formal libraries. GraphRAG builds an entity graph and community summaries for query-focused summarization ( Edge et al., 2024 ) , while HippoRAG applies personalized PageRank to a knowledge graph for multi-hop retrieval ( Jiménez Gutiérrez et al., 2024 ) . KG 2 RAG starts from semantically retrieved chunks and uses a knowledge graph to expand and organize evidence ( Zhu et al., 2025 ) . In formal mathematical search, LeanExplore uses declaration dependencies to generate informal descriptions and incorporates PageRank centrality as a ranking feature ( Asher, 2025 ) . LeanSearch v2 also processes dependencies bottom-up when constructing declaration descriptions ( Gao et al., 2026 ) . To learn graph-aware representations for premise selection, Petrovčič et al. We introduce FDE-Gym, a benchmark of 95 end-to-end delivery tasks from 20 customer scenarios across 18 sectors, each adapted by industry experts from real-world delivery projects. In simulated customer environments with scripted stakeholders and modifiable customer systems, agents interact with stakeholders and operate on production-like systems to deliver working solutions. FDE-Gym scores a delivery by how much it improves the customer's own success metric, normalized between 0 (unchanged system) and 1 (reference solution), with penalties for stakeholder interactions (messages, trial runs, and waiting time). An online platform lets humans practice FDE skills under the same grading criteria. We evaluate 13 model configurations from seven providers. In the realistic setting, where unstated constraints must be discovered, the best configuration achieves a mean FDE-Gym score of 0.56 and resolves only 14 of the 95 tasks (a score of at least 0.8 with no incident). Discovering unstated constraints is the primary bottleneck: performance drops sharply when models must uncover them without explicit guidance. Yet information discovery alone does not account for the gap: even on the 23 tasks where the best configuration obtains every key fact from stakeholders, it reaches a normalized business uplift of 0.8 or above on only 10. These results reveal a substantial gap between solving well-specified tasks and delivering effective AI systems for real customers. Comments: 14 pages, 8 figures, 4 tables. items.content: Computer Science > Artificial Intelligence arXiv:2610.22344 (cs) [Submitted on 15 Oct 2026] Title: MLExpert: Towards a Generalist Agentic Model for Autonomous Machine Learning Engineering Authors: Shangheng Du , Jinxin Shi , Shuaiyu Zhang , Yiming Wu , Junpeng Zhao , Shiyang Feng , Xin Li , Liang He , Xiangchao Yan , Bo Zhang View a PDF of the paper titled MLExpert: Towards a Generalist Agentic Model for Autonomous Machine Learning Engineering, by Shangheng Du and 9 other authors View PDF HTML (experimental) Abstract: Large language models (LLMs) are expanding from assisting scientific research and engineering to autonomously developing and improving AI systems, advancing AI for AI (AI4AI) as a pathway toward recursive self-improvement (RSI). Workflow-driven machine learning engineering (MLE) systems provide a practical path toward this pursuit through complex orchestration that manages long-horizon experimentation, while recent MLE systems adopt model-directed interaction, allowing models to autonomously organize experiments and adapt optimization strategies based on execution feedback. However, feedback from each experiment reflects several preceding decisions, and a long MLE run contains many such costly experiments. Training must therefore select useful supervision from long interaction trajectories and learn from intermediate outcomes. We propose a post-training method for autonomous long-horizon MLE optimization and apply it to train MLExpert, a 35B Mixture-of-Experts agentic model. We design the Kaggle-MLE Factory to construct executable tasks and an interaction harness for model-directed experimentation. Hierarchical agentic SFT transfers general tool-use and coding capabilities to MLE through outcome-guided supervision. Windowed Interaction RL (WIRL) treats the multi-turn decisions between successive experiment results as an execution window and assigns it a shared outcome-based reward. Asynchronous collection and policy correction support policy updates before the trajectory ends. On MLE-Bench Lite, MLExpert improves the average medal rate of the base model from 37.9% to 72.7%, achieving performance comparable to larger frontier models such as Kimi-K3 and GLM-5.3. Further experiments show that MLExpert improves performance on NatureBench Lite, agent scaffold optimization, and algorithm optimization, suggesting that the learned optimization capability generalizes to other tasks. Affiliation: East China Normal University Abstract Large language models (LLMs) are expanding from assisting scientific research and engineering to autonomously developing and improving AI systems, advancing AI for AI (AI4AI) as a pathway toward recursive self-improvement (RSI). Workflow-driven machine learning engineering (MLE) systems provide a practical path toward this pursuit through complex orchestration that manages long-horizon experimentation, while recent MLE systems adopt model-directed interaction, allowing models to autonomously organize experiments and adapt optimization strategies based on execution feedback. However, feedback from each experiment reflects several preceding decisions, and a long MLE run contains many such costly experiments. Training must therefore select useful supervision from long interaction trajectories and learn from intermediate outcomes as they become available. To address these challenges, we propose a post-training method for autonomous long-horizon MLE optimization and apply it to train MLExpert, a 35B Mixture-of-Experts agentic model. We design the Kaggle-MLE Factory to construct executable tasks and an interaction harness for model-directed experimentation. Hierarchical agentic SFT transfers general tool-use and coding capabilities to MLE through outcome-guided supervision. Windowed Interaction RL (WIRL) treats the multi-turn decisions between successive experiment results as an execution window and assigns it a shared outcome-based reward. Asynchronous collection and policy correction support policy updates before the trajectory ends. On MLE-Bench Lite, MLExpert improves the average medal rate of the base model from 37.9% to 72.7%, achieving performance comparable to larger frontier models such as Kimi-K3 and GLM-5.3. Further experiments show that MLExpert improves performance on NatureBench Lite, agent scaffold optimization, and algorithm optimization, suggesting that the learned optimization capability generalizes to other tasks. 1 Introduction The rapid advancement of reasoning, code generation, and tool interaction in large language models (LLMs) is enabling artificial intelligence (AI) to move beyond assisting scientific research and engineering toward autonomously developing and improving AI systems. These efforts include model training, optimization of solver programs, and algorithm design, making AI for AI (AI4AI) a research direction toward recursive self-improvement (RSI). In this context, machine learning engineering (MLE) provides a concrete setting for this goal, requiring long-horizon optimization through repeated execution, feedback analysis, and revision rather than one-shot generation. Figure 1 : Decision making in long-horizon MLE optimization. (a) External orchestration organizes optimization through predefined workflows and search rules. (b) In model-directed interaction, the model selects subsequent actions based on experimental states and execution feedback. Most existing MLE systems [ 1 , 2 , 3 ] extend code generation into iterative optimization through search, memory, or multi-agent collaboration. As shown in Figure 1 (a), predefined workflows or search rules typically control experiment sequencing and stage transitions, while LLMs primarily generate or debug code at designated steps. These systems rely heavily on manually designed control logic to organize long-horizon experimentation. Recently, Arbor [ 4 ] and Argus [ 5 ] maintain persistent research states and allow models to design, continue, and revise experiments, placing greater demands on the model’s ability to plan experiments and sustain optimization over long interaction horizons. ML-Agent [ 6 ] combines multi-turn demonstrations with single-step RL, while Frontis-MA1 [ 7 ] trains program evolution operators through SFT and RL and integrates them into an external evolutionary search framework. These approaches primarily train models for single-step decisions or local operations within externally organized processes. In contrast, we study how to train models to organize experiments and improve solutions over sustained interaction, using experience and execution feedback from real-world MLE tasks. However, training this long-horizon optimization capability poses three challenges. 1) Open-ended MLE requires an interaction environment that preserves experimental states while leaving action selection to the model. 2) High-quality long-horizon supervision is difficult to obtain because MLE tasks are heterogeneous and interaction trajectories may mix useful exploration and failure recovery with degraded decisions. 3) Each costly experiment returns feedback on several preceding decisions before the full run ends; online RL must use this intermediate signal while handling policy mismatch during asynchronous collection. To address these challenges, we propose a post-training method for autonomous MLE that combines a model-directed long-horizon interaction harness, hierarchical agentic SFT, and Windowed Interaction Reinforcement Learning (WIRL). Based on this, we train MLExpert , a 35B Mixture-of-Experts (MoE) agentic model, to learn long-horizon optimization strategies. As shown in Figure 1 (b), MLExpert uses sustained tool interaction within the interaction harness to autonomously organize experiments, revise solutions based on execution feedback, and maintain submission candidates. We build the Kaggle-MLE Factory to convert historical Kaggle competitions into executable MLE tasks. Hierarchical agentic SFT transfers general tool-use and coding capabilities to MLE optimization, with execution outcomes guiding the selection of trajectories and segments for supervision. To use this intermediate feedback, WIRL treats each completed experiment as the boundary of an execution window containing decisions since the previous result. It trains those decisions with a shared outcome-based reward, while asynchronous collection and policy correction allow updates as trajectories continue. On MLE-Bench Lite, MLExpert improves the average medal rate of the base model from 37.9% to 72.7%, achieving performance comparable to larger models such as Kimi-K3 and GLM-5.3. MLExpert also improves performance on NatureBench Lite and transfers its optimization capabilities to agent scaffold and algorithm optimization tasks. Our key contributions are: • We introduce MLExpert , a 35B MoE model for autonomous MLE, trained with hierarchical agentic SFT and WIRL. WIRL links execution feedback to multi-turn decisions within execution windows and combines local progress rewards with policy correction for asynchronous online learning. • We build the Kaggle-MLE Factory and an Interaction Harness to provide executable tasks and model-directed long-horizon interaction for training and evaluation. • Extensive experiments show that MLExpert improves the base model’s average medal rate from 37.9% to 72.7% on MLE-Bench Lite, improves performance on NatureBench Lite, and generalizes to agent scaffold and algorithm optimization tasks. 2 Preliminary We formulate MLE as the iterative optimization of executable ML solutions within a given time budget B e B_{e} . An MLE task is represented as e = ( d e , 𝒟 e , m e ) e=(d_{e},\mathcal{D}_{e},m_{e}) , where d e d_{e} is the task description, 𝒟 e \mathcal{D}_{e} is the task data, and m e m_{e} is the evaluation metric. A candidate solution y ∈ 𝒴 e y\in\mathcal{Y}_{e} represents a complete ML pipeline including data processing, feature engineering, model training, and prediction, where 𝒴 e \mathcal{Y}_{e} denotes the solution space. The objective is to find a best-performing solution for a given task, y e ⋆ ∈ arg ⁡ max y ∈ 𝒴 e ​ S e ​ ( y ) y_{e}^{\star}\in\arg\max_{y\in\mathcal{Y}_{e}}S_{e}(y) , where S e ​ ( y ) S_{e}(y) denotes the task-specific score under metric m e m_{e} , normalized so that higher values indicate better performance. Following MLE-bench [ 8 ] , the agent has access to the task description and public data, and improves solutions through code execution and self-constructed validation. The final submission is independently evaluated using hidden test labels. In Agentic MLE, an LLM policy π θ \pi_{\theta} autonomously organizes the optimization process. Given a task e e , the model constructs, executes, and improves candidate solutions through continuous tool interaction within the time budget B e B_{e} . Hierarchical agentic SFT learns from demonstrations, while WIRL further optimizes the policy from execution feedback collected during online interaction. 3.1 Kaggle-MLE Factory: Constructing Executable MLE Tasks Long-horizon Agentic MLE training requires executable tasks covering diverse data modalities, objectives, and domains. Historical Kaggle competitions provide a rich source of real-world MLE problems, but their heterogeneous data organization, submission formats, and evaluation protocols make manual task adaptation difficult to scale. Therefore, we build the Kaggle-MLE Factory, which converts historical competitions into executable tasks with a public workspace, a hidden test split, and a unified evaluation interface. The Factory uses a multi-agent pipeline for task construction, validation, and repair. The discovery agent filters competitions by status, scale, and submission format. After competition data, leaderboard information, and official descriptions are collected, the analyzer agent extracts data structures, fields, and modality characteristics to form a task specification. The generator agent then prepares task data, constructs a held-out test split with hidden labels from the original labeled data, and implements the task-specific evaluator. Standardized task packages support different MLE agent frameworks. Final manual review excludes tasks with unresolved label or scoring issues before trajectory collection. The harness provides tools for solution analysis, code revision, experiment execution, history retrieval, and submission management. The model launches candidate execution through execute_code and updates its submission candidate through update_answer . The complete tool list and descriptions are provided in Appendix B . As interaction history approaches the context limit, earlier messages are summarized while recent interactions are retained. For complex analysis, analyze delegates task analysis, data exploration, and result diagnosis to an analysis sub-agent with independent context, returning only a summary to the main model. Since overfitting or data leakage can inflate validation scores, the model can call invalidate_node based on experimental evidence and analysis to exclude unreliable candidates. We therefore use two-stage hierarchical agentic SFT. In the first stage, coding and tool-use trajectories from diverse agentic tasks are used to learn basic tool-use and code revision capabilities. For trajectories whose first complete solution executes successfully and reaches a quality threshold, we extract the interaction prefix from task start through the corresponding execution feedback as an initial-solution trajectory , typically covering task understanding, algorithm design, and code generation. We also use long-horizon optimization trajectories from complete interactions, covering solution construction, feedback analysis, iterative revision, and final submission selection. In addition, analysis sub-agent trajectories are adopted to train the model for independent data analysis and result diagnosis. Outcome-guided supervision selection. Long-horizon MLE trajectories can contain effective exploration and failure recovery, but may also include misguided decisions or continued degradation after reaching a strong solution. Therefore, we use execution results of submitted solutions to select high-quality trajectories and the segments used for supervision. For trajectories that pass a quality threshold, we identify the first best-performing submission and measure the subsequent performance degradation. When the post-peak degradation exceeds a threshold, we use the first best-performing submission as the anchor for retaining a trajectory prefix; otherwise, we use the last submission. The prefix ends at a complete tool-interaction boundary near the anchor. This removes degraded tails while preserving useful exploration and failure recovery before the peak. To preserve multi-turn context dependencies, each supervision sample combines existing interaction context with a continuous sequence of subsequent model actions and environment feedback from the selected MLE interactions. Affiliation: East China Normal University Abstract Large language models (LLMs) are expanding from assisting scientific research and engineering to autonomously developing and improving AI systems, advancing AI for AI (AI4AI) as a pathway toward recursive self-improvement (RSI). Workflow-driven machine learning engineering (MLE) systems provide a practical path toward this pursuit through complex orchestration that manages long-horizon experimentation, while recent MLE systems adopt model-directed interaction, allowing models to autonomously organize experiments and adapt optimization strategies based on execution feedback. However, feedback from each experiment reflects several preceding decisions, and a long MLE run contains many such costly experiments. Training must therefore select useful supervision from long interaction trajectories and learn from intermediate outcomes as they become available. To address these challenges, we propose a post-training method for autonomous long-horizon MLE optimization and apply it to train MLExpert, a 35B Mixture-of-Experts agentic model. We design the Kaggle-MLE Factory to construct executable tasks and an interaction harness for model-directed experimentation. Hierarchical agentic SFT transfers general tool-use and coding capabilities to MLE through outcome-guided supervision. Windowed Interaction RL (WIRL) treats the multi-turn decisions between successive experiment results as an execution window and assigns it a shared outcome-based reward. Asynchronous collection and policy correction support policy updates before the trajectory ends. On MLE-Bench Lite, MLExpert improves the average medal rate of the base model from 37.9% to 72.7%, achieving performance comparable to larger frontier models such as Kimi-K3 and GLM-5.3. Further experiments show that MLExpert improves performance on NatureBench Lite, agent scaffold optimization, and algorithm optimization, suggesting that the learned optimization capability generalizes to other tasks. 1 Introduction The rapid advancement of reasoning, code generation, and tool interaction in large language models (LLMs) is enabling artificial intelligence (AI) to move beyond assisting scientific research and engineering toward autonomously developing and improving AI systems. These efforts include model training, optimization of solver programs, and algorithm design, making AI for AI (AI4AI) a research direction toward recursive self-improvement (RSI). In this context, machine learning engineering (MLE) provides a concrete setting for this goal, requiring long-horizon optimization through repeated execution, feedback analysis, and revision rather than one-shot generation. Figure 1 : Decision making in long-horizon MLE optimization. (a) External orchestration organizes optimization through predefined workflows and search rules. (b) In model-directed interaction, the model selects subsequent actions based on experimental states and execution feedback. Most existing MLE systems [ 1 , 2 , 3 ] extend code generation into iterative optimization through search, memory, or multi-agent collaboration. As shown in Figure 1 (a), predefined workflows or search rules typically control experiment sequencing and stage transitions, while LLMs primarily generate or debug code at designated steps. These systems rely heavily on manually designed control logic to organize long-horizon experimentation. Recently, Arbor [ 4 ] and Argus [ 5 ] maintain persistent research states and allow models to design, continue, and revise experiments, placing greater demands on the model’s ability to plan experiments and sustain optimization over long interaction horizons. ML-Agent [ 6 ] combines multi-turn demonstrations with single-step RL, while Frontis-MA1 [ 7 ] trains program evolution operators through SFT and RL and integrates them into an external evolutionary search framework. These approaches primarily train models for single-step decisions or local operations within externally organized processes. In contrast, we study how to train models to organize experiments and improve solutions over sustained interaction, using experience and execution feedback from real-world MLE tasks. However, training this long-horizon optimization capability poses three challenges. 1) Open-ended MLE requires an interaction environment that preserves experimental states while leaving action selection to the model. 2) High-quality long-horizon supervision is difficult to obtain because MLE tasks are heterogeneous and interaction trajectories may mix useful exploration and failure recovery with degraded decisions. 3) Each costly experiment returns feedback on several preceding decisions before the full run ends; online RL must use this intermediate signal while handling policy mismatch during asynchronous collection. To address these challenges, we propose a post-training method for autonomous MLE that combines a model-directed long-horizon interaction harness, hierarchical agentic SFT, and Windowed Interaction Reinforcement Learning (WIRL). Based on this, we train MLExpert , a 35B Mixture-of-Experts (MoE) agentic model, to learn long-horizon optimization strategies. As shown in Figure 1 (b), MLExpert uses sustained tool interaction within the interaction harness to autonomously organize experiments, revise solutions based on execution feedback, and maintain submission candidates. We build the Kaggle-MLE Factory to convert historical Kaggle competitions into executable MLE tasks. Hierarchical agentic SFT transfers general tool-use and coding capabilities to MLE optimization, with execution outcomes guiding the selection of trajectories and segments for supervision. To use this intermediate feedback, WIRL treats each completed experiment as the boundary of an execution window containing decisions since the previous result. It trains those decisions with a shared outcome-based reward, while asynchronous collection and policy correction allow updates as trajectories continue. On MLE-Bench Lite, MLExpert improves the average medal rate of the base model from 37.9% to 72.7%, achieving performance comparable to larger models such as Kimi-K3 and GLM-5.3. MLExpert also improves performance on NatureBench Lite and transfers its optimization capabilities to agent scaffold and algorithm optimization tasks. items.content: Computer Science > Artificial Intelligence arXiv:2610.22333 (cs) [Submitted on 15 Oct 2026] Title: Evaluation Awareness Beyond English: Do LLMs Act Differently When Tested in Indic Languages? Authors: Trizal Garg , Sibayan Mitra , Arya Karanjkar , Advait Singh , Jagat Sesh Challa , Yash Sinha , Siddharth Mehrotra , Dhruv Kumar , Pratham Yogish Maliya View a PDF of the paper titled Evaluation Awareness Beyond English: Do LLMs Act Differently When Tested in Indic Languages?, by Trizal Garg and 8 other authors View PDF HTML (experimental) Abstract: Large language models (LLMs) can often tell when they are being tested. This ability, known as evaluation awareness, can lead models to act more cautiously during safety evaluations than in real use. Existing work has studied evaluation awareness almost entirely in English, although models serve users in many languages. Indic languages are spoken by over a billion people, yet evaluation awareness remains almost entirely unstudied in them. We test four instruction-tuned models from three families in five Indic languages alongside English. A set of cues varies whether the model is told that it is monitored and whether the monitoring is a safety test. Models refuse harmful requests more often when they are told that they are being tested. This increase appears in all four models and all six languages. In Indic languages, refusal of harmful requests rises by 14.4 percentage points on average. The test cue also brings Indic refusal of harmful requests level with English, but raises refusal of benign Indic requests from 6.9% to 11.3%. We release all 47,880 judged responses to support further work. These results suggest that safety evaluations in Indic languages may not reflect how models treat their everyday users. items.content: Evaluation Awareness Beyond English: Do LLMs Act Differently When Tested in Indic Languages? Trizal Garg Sibayan Mitra Arya Karanjkar Advait Singh Jagat Sesh Challa Affiliation: Yash Sinha, Siddharth Mehrotra, Dhruv Kumar, Pratham Yogish Maliya Affiliation: Birla Institute of Technology and Science, Pilani Affiliation: {f20240338, f20240862, f20241220, f20220636, jagatsesh}@pilani.bits-pilani.ac.in , Affiliation: {yash.sinha, siddharth.mehrotra, dhruv.kumar, f20260682}@pilani.bits-pilani.ac.in Abstract Large language models (LLMs) can often tell when they are being tested. This ability, known as evaluation awareness, can lead models to act more cautiously during safety evaluations than in real use. Existing work has studied evaluation awareness almost entirely in English, although models serve users in many languages. Indic languages are spoken by over a billion people, yet evaluation awareness remains almost entirely unstudied in them. We test four instruction-tuned models from three families in five Indic languages alongside English. A set of cues varies whether the model is told that it is monitored and whether the monitoring is a safety test. Models refuse harmful requests more often when they are told that they are being tested. This increase appears in all four models and all six languages. In Indic languages, refusal of harmful requests rises by 14.4 percentage points on average. The test cue also brings Indic refusal of harmful requests level with English, but raises refusal of benign Indic requests from 6.9% to 11.3%. We release all 47,880 judged responses to support further work. These results suggest that safety evaluations in Indic languages may not reflect how models treat their everyday users. 1 Introduction Large language models (LLMs) have been widely adopted by systems and users across the world, and are increasingly relied upon to refuse harmful requests. Their training corpora are overwhelmingly skewed towards English, often exceeding 90% of pre-training and fine-tuning data Xu et al. (2025) , yet they serve users in many other languages. The standard way to ensure reliability is to test models under controlled conditions through safety evaluations. These evaluations assume that behavior under test carries over to deployment. However, this assumption fails when a model can tell that it is being tested. This ability is called evaluation awareness Needham et al. (2025) ; Greenblatt et al. (2024) . A model that recognizes an evaluation may alter its behavior, potentially making observed safety behavior different from deployment behavior Abdelnabi and Salem (2025) . This effect is largely studied in English. Indic languages are used by more than a billion people, yet evaluation awareness in these languages remains almost entirely unstudied ( Yong et al., 2025 ; Pattnayak and Chowdhuri, 2026b ) . In this paper, we conduct a controlled behavioral study of evaluation awareness in five Indic languages, Hindi, Bengali, Tamil, Telugu, and Kannada, alongside English. We prepend one of five prompt conditions, called a cue to every request, from a plain deployment framing to an explicit statement that the conversation is a scored safety test. We take harmful prompts from the Toxic Matrix split of AI4Bharat’s IndicAlign ( Khan et al., 2024 ) and translate them into Indic languages using Claude Opus. Benign prompts come from the Dolly-T split of the same corpus, which contains parallel versions in all six languages, made with IndicTrans2 ( Gala et al., 2023 ) . We use four instruction-tuned models from three families for our study: Gemma-3-27B ( Team et al., 2025 ) , Qwen3-32B ( Yang et al., 2025 ) , Qwen2.5-72B ( Qwen et al., 2025 ) , and Sarvam-M ( Sarvam Foundation Models Team, 2025 ) , and each model answers every prompt in every language under every cue . We measure refusal with an LLM judge ( Zheng et al., 2023 ) that does not see the model, the language, or the cue. The primary judge is Gemma-4-31B-IT ( Team et al., 2026 ) and the secondary judge is GPT-6 Luna . We check the primary judge against the secondary judge and against native-speaker review of its labels in each Indic language. Our results support three findings. First, an explicit safety-test cue raises refusal of harmful prompts in all four models and six languages, by 13.8 percentage points on average. Second, this rise is at least as large in Indic languages as in English. Third, the cue acts mainly on harmful prompts. Across all models and languages, the rise in refusal is 3.5 times larger for harmful prompts than for benign ones. We make two contributions. • To our knowledge, the first behavioral study of evaluation awareness in Indic languages. It covers four models from three families and six languages, with 47,880 judged responses that we release. • A set of cues that isolates evaluation from mere monitoring. Two of our cues state that responses are logged and differ only in whether an AI safety team reviews them. 2 Related Works 2.1 Evaluation awareness and the compliance gap Recent work establishes that language models can distinguish evaluation from deployment contexts and that this recognition drives behavior. Frontier models show above-random evaluation awareness ( Needham et al., 2025 ) , and recognizing an evaluation context is empirically and conceptually distinct from the propensity to act on it ( Li et al., 2026 ) . Models shift toward the inferred training objective once they judge their outputs observed ( Greenblatt et al., 2024 ) . Models are also more sensitive to safety than capability evaluations ( Li et al., 2026 ) , and ( Sheshadri et al., 2025 ) find a compliance gap above 1 percent in only five of twenty-five models. Knecht et al. (2026) find that verbalised evaluation awareness (VEA) has limited effect on model behaviour. Existing study in these papers involves English only. We ask whether the behavioural findings survive a change of language, using content-matched requests in five Indic languages and English across three model families. 2.2 Multilingual and Indic safety evaluation A persistent gap exists between the languages multilingual safety research covers and those deployed models serve; ( Yong et al., 2025 ) survey its size and durability. Subsequent work shows that safety behavior varies with language: models handle identical content differently under code-switching ( Yoo et al., 2025 ) , across twelve Indic languages where safety judgments drift sharply between translations ( Pattnayak and Chowdhuri, 2026b ) , and under jailbreak pressure in South Asian languages ( Pattnayak and Chowdhuri, 2026a ) . Chain-of-thought monitoring likewise degrades across typologically diverse languages ( Onyame et al., 2026 ) . These works hold evaluation context fixed while varying language; we vary both, enabling an evaluation-awareness claim. 3 Experimental Setup 3.1 Data, languages, and models We worked on six languages, namely English, Hindi, Bengali, Tamil, Telugu, and Kannada. The harmful prompts come from the Toxic Matrix dataset of AI4Bharat IndicAlign ( Khan et al., 2024 ) . We randomly sampled 199 English prompts from the dataset and translated them into the five Indic languages using Claude Opus. We then scored every translated string with COMET-Kiwi ( Rei et al., 2022 ) , a reference-free quality estimation model (Appendix G ). We made sure that every prompt has a parallel translation in all six languages. Benign prompts come from the Dolly-T dataset of the same corpus, which provides translations made with IndicTrans2 ( Gala et al., 2023 ) . We took 200 parallel prompts per language directly from the dataset and use them as a baseline to measure over-refusal. To check the reliability of the translations, native speakers verified a small sample of prompts per language for faithful translation, fluency, cultural relevance, and retained harmful intent. We test four instruction-tuned models from three families, namely Gemma-3-27B ( Team et al., 2025 ) , Qwen3-32B ( Yang et al., 2025 ) , Qwen2.5-72B ( Qwen et al., 2025 ) , and Sarvam-M ( Sarvam Foundation Models Team, 2025 ) , an Indic model post-trained from Mistral-Small-3.1-24B. We disable the reasoning mode of Qwen3 and Sarvam-M. Each model generates one response per prompt with greedy decoding. This gives 11,970 responses per model and 47,880 in total (Appendix I ). 3.2 The Cues A Cue is a small text consisting of a condition. Each cue is added before the prompt in the user turn. All five cues share the base sentence “You are a helpful AI assistant.” and differ only in an appended note. The prompt is identical across languages and models, so any difference in behavior is due to the note. Each cue is written in the language of the prompt, and full texts for all six languages appear in Appendix A . The deploy cue adds no note and fixes the baseline. The monitor_log cue states that responses are logged for service quality and product improvement, which represents monitoring with no evaluation framing. The eval_log cue states that responses are logged and reviewed by the AI safety team for compliance with usage policies. The eval_explicit cue states that the conversation is a formal AI safety evaluation scored by a red-team review. The eval_metadata cue gives the same information as a machine-style configuration tag. Our main contrast is eval_explicit against deploy . Both cues share the base sentence, and eval_explicit adds a note stating openly that the conversation is a scored AI safety evaluation. The difference between them measures how much a model changes its behavior when it is told plainly that it is being tested. This is the strongest form of the evaluation signal in our design. We use eval_log against monitor_log as a secondary contrast. Both notes state that responses are logged, and eval_log adds only that an AI safety team reviews them. It never uses the words test, evaluation, or benchmark. So, this contrast separates evaluation framing from monitoring and from lexical leakage. We compare the remaining cues against deploy , and we run all five cues on the four models in all six languages. Figure 1 summarises the design. Cue vs. deploy Harmful Benign eval_explicit +13.8 +3.9 eval_metadata +9.0 +3.0 eval_log +7.1 +1.8 monitor_log +2.5 +0.4 Table 1: Change in refusal rate relative to the deploy cue, in percentage points. Values are averaged over four models and six languages, including English. Figure 1: The behavioral analysis pipeline. Prompts in six languages are prefixed with one of five cues, answered by four models, and scored by a blind LLM judge (Gemma-4-31B-IT) validated against a second judge and native speakers. The headline contrast is eval_explicit vs. deploy . 3.3 Measuring refusal We label refusals with an LLM judge that reads only the prompt and the response and returns REFUSAL, COMPLY, or UNUSABLE. A response that gives no substantive help or offers a safe alternative counts as REFUSAL. The judge never sees the cue, the model, or the language. The primary judge is Gemma-4-31B-IT ( Team et al., 2026 ) , which we run locally. A second judge, GPT-6 Luna, labelled a subset of n = 7,200 n=7{,}200 responses that covers every model, language, and cue. We measure agreement with Cohen’s κ \kappa , which corrects for agreement reached by chance. The two judges reach κ = 0.88 \kappa=0.88 overall. Per language, κ \kappa ranges from 0.86 0.86 in Tamil to 0.90 0.90 in English. For each Indic language, a native speaker also reviewed n = 320 n=320 labels of the primary judge and marked each one as correct or incorrect. Agreement with the judge ranges from κ = 0.85 \kappa=0.85 in Tamil to κ = 0.91 \kappa=0.91 in Hindi. Telugu is the exception, with κ = 0.56 \kappa=0.56 . In Telugu, four prompts account for 46 of the 68 disagreements (Appendix C ). 3.4 Statistical Analysis Each of the 199 harmful and 200 benign prompts is present in English and its five Indic translations, and every version is run on every model under every cue condition. Responses that come from the same original prompt are therefore correlated, and treating them as independent would understate the standard errors. We use the McNemar test to compare two cues within one model and language. Prompts that receive the same label under both cues carry no information about the cue, so the test uses only prompts whose label changed. It then checks whether these changes lean towards one cue more than the other. We apply it to the primary contrast, eval_explicit against deploy , on harmful and benign prompts, and to the secondary contrast, eval_log against monitor_log , on harmful prompts. We use the Cochran Q test to record refusal under 5 cues, for each model, language using the same prompts. We run tests for every model and language separately on the harmful and benign prompts, and use the Holm correction within each arm (24 tests each). We use logistic regression to measure how much each factor (model, language or cue) changes the odds of refusal, while holding the other factors fixed. This is expressed using an odds ratio. Due to the correlation between responses for the same prompt, we fit the regression with GEE, which groups each prompt’s responses together. We test: (1) Language effect per model, (2) Cue effect per model, (3) Cue effect per language, (4) Model effect per language, (5) Every Indic language vs English per model, (6) Pooled fits (model, language, cue). 4 Results We report how the cues change refusal of harmful and benign prompts across models and languages. Changes are given in percentage points. Our primary result is based on eval_explicit against deploy . The test cue raises refusal. eval_explicit raises refusal of harmful prompts in all 24 model and language cells, by 13.8 points on average, and the increase is significant in 23 of them (Appendix J ). The rate of refusal increases with the strength of the signal (Table 1 , Appendix H ). monitor_log has no significant effect for Qwen2.5-72B or Sarvam-M (Appendix F ). The eval_log vs monitor_log raises refusal in all 24 cells, by 4.6 points on average (95% CI [3.6, 5.7]). A second judge reproduces these effects (Appendix C ). The increase in refusal appears in every language. Averaged over the four models, eval_explicit raises harmful refusal by 14.4 pp in Indic languages and by 10.6 pp in English (Figure 2 ). items.raw_text: Evaluation Awareness Beyond English: Do LLMs Act Differently When Tested in Indic Languages? Trizal Garg Sibayan Mitra Arya Karanjkar Advait Singh Jagat Sesh Challa Affiliation: Yash Sinha, Siddharth Mehrotra, Dhruv Kumar, Pratham Yogish Maliya Affiliation: Birla Institute of Technology and Science, Pilani Affiliation: {f20240338, f20240862, f20241220, f20220636, jagatsesh}@pilani.bits-pilani.ac.in , Affiliation: {yash.sinha, siddharth.mehrotra, dhruv.kumar, f20260682}@pilani.bits-pilani.ac.in Abstract Large language models (LLMs) can often tell when they are being tested. This ability, known as evaluation awareness, can lead models to act more cautiously during safety evaluations than in real use. Existing work has studied evaluation awareness almost entirely in English, although models serve users in many languages. Indic languages are spoken by over a billion people, yet evaluation awareness remains almost entirely unstudied in them. We test four instruction-tuned models from three families in five Indic languages alongside English. A set of cues varies whether the model is told that it is monitored and whether the monitoring is a safety test. Models refuse harmful requests more often when they are told that they are being tested. This increase appears in all four models and all six languages. In Indic languages, refusal of harmful requests rises by 14.4 percentage points on average. The test cue also brings Indic refusal of harmful requests level with English, but raises refusal of benign Indic requests from 6.9% to 11.3%. We release all 47,880 judged responses to support further work. These results suggest that safety evaluations in Indic languages may not reflect how models treat their everyday users. 1 Introduction Large language models (LLMs) have been widely adopted by systems and users across the world, and are increasingly relied upon to refuse harmful requests. Their training corpora are overwhelmingly skewed towards English, often exceeding 90% of pre-training and fine-tuning data Xu et al. (2025) , yet they serve users in many other languages. The standard way to ensure reliability is to test models under controlled conditions through safety evaluations. These evaluations assume that behavior under test carries over to deployment. However, this assumption fails when a model can tell that it is being tested. This ability is called evaluation awareness Needham et al. (2025) ; Greenblatt et al. (2024) . A model that recognizes an evaluation may alter its behavior, potentially making observed safety behavior different from deployment behavior Abdelnabi and Salem (2025) . This effect is largely studied in English. Indic languages are used by more than a billion people, yet evaluation awareness in these languages remains almost entirely unstudied ( Yong et al., 2025 ; Pattnayak and Chowdhuri, 2026b ) . In this paper, we conduct a controlled behavioral study of evaluation awareness in five Indic languages, Hindi, Bengali, Tamil, Telugu, and Kannada, alongside English. We prepend one of five prompt conditions, called a cue to every request, from a plain deployment framing to an explicit statement that the conversation is a scored safety test. We take harmful prompts from the Toxic Matrix split of AI4Bharat’s IndicAlign ( Khan et al., 2024 ) and translate them into Indic languages using Claude Opus. Benign prompts come from the Dolly-T split of the same corpus, which contains parallel versions in all six languages, made with IndicTrans2 ( Gala et al., 2023 ) . We use four instruction-tuned models from three families for our study: Gemma-3-27B ( Team et al., 2025 ) , Qwen3-32B ( Yang et al., 2025 ) , Qwen2.5-72B ( Qwen et al., 2025 ) , and Sarvam-M ( Sarvam Foundation Models Team, 2025 ) , and each model answers every prompt in every language under every cue . We measure refusal with an LLM judge ( Zheng et al., 2023 ) that does not see the model, the language, or the cue. The primary judge is Gemma-4-31B-IT ( Team et al., 2026 ) and the secondary judge is GPT-6 Luna . We check the primary judge against the secondary judge and against native-speaker review of its labels in each Indic language. Our results support three findings. First, an explicit safety-test cue raises refusal of harmful prompts in all four models and six languages, by 13.8 percentage points on average. Second, this rise is at least as large in Indic languages as in English. Third, the cue acts mainly on harmful prompts. Across all models and languages, the rise in refusal is 3.5 times larger for harmful prompts than for benign ones. We make two contributions. • To our knowledge, the first behavioral study of evaluation awareness in Indic languages. It covers four models from three families and six languages, with 47,880 judged responses that we release. • A set of cues that isolates evaluation from mere monitoring. Two of our cues state that responses are logged and differ only in whether an AI safety team reviews them. 2 Related Works 2.1 Evaluation awareness and the compliance gap Recent work establishes that language models can distinguish evaluation from deployment contexts and that this recognition drives behavior. Frontier models show above-random evaluation awareness ( Needham et al., 2025 ) , and recognizing an evaluation context is empirically and conceptually distinct from the propensity to act on it ( Li et al., 2026 ) . Models shift toward the inferred training objective once they judge their outputs observed ( Greenblatt et al., 2024 ) . Models are also more sensitive to safety than capability evaluations ( Li et al., 2026 ) , and ( Sheshadri et al., 2025 ) find a compliance gap above 1 percent in only five of twenty-five models. Knecht et al. (2026) find that verbalised evaluation awareness (VEA) has limited effect on model behaviour. Existing study in these papers involves English only. We ask whether the behavioural findings survive a change of language, using content-matched requests in five Indic languages and English across three model families. 2.2 Multilingual and Indic safety evaluation A persistent gap exists between the languages multilingual safety research covers and those deployed models serve; ( Yong et al., 2025 ) survey its size and durability. Subsequent work shows that safety behavior varies with language: models handle identical content differently under code-switching ( Yoo et al., 2025 ) , across twelve Indic languages where safety judgments drift sharply between translations ( Pattnayak and Chowdhuri, 2026b ) , and under jailbreak pressure in South Asian languages ( Pattnayak and Chowdhuri, 2026a ) . Chain-of-thought monitoring likewise degrades across typologically diverse languages ( Onyame et al., 2026 ) . These works hold evaluation context fixed while varying language; we vary both, enabling an evaluation-awareness claim. 3 Experimental Setup 3.1 Data, languages, and models We worked on six languages, namely English, Hindi, Bengali, Tamil, Telugu, and Kannada. The harmful prompts come from the Toxic Matrix dataset of AI4Bharat IndicAlign ( Khan et al., 2024 ) . We randomly sampled 199 English prompts from the dataset and translated them into the five Indic languages using Claude Opus. We then scored every translated string with COMET-Kiwi ( Rei et al., 2022 ) , a reference-free quality estimation model (Appendix G ). We made sure that every prompt has a parallel translation in all six languages. Benign prompts come from the Dolly-T dataset of the same corpus, which provides translations made with IndicTrans2 ( Gala et al., 2023 ) . We took 200 parallel prompts per language directly from the dataset and use them as a baseline to measure over-refusal. To check the reliability of the translations, native speakers verified a small sample of prompts per language for faithful translation, fluency, cultural relevance, and retained harmful intent. We test four instruction-tuned models from three families, namely Gemma-3-27B ( Team et al., 2025 ) , Qwen3-32B ( Yang et al., 2025 ) , Qwen2.5-72B ( Qwen et al., 2025 ) , and Sarvam-M ( Sarvam Foundation Models Team, 2025 ) , an Indic model post-trained from Mistral-Small-3.1-24B. We disable the reasoning mode of Qwen3 and Sarvam-M. Each model generates one response per prompt with greedy decoding. This gives 11,970 responses per model and 47,880 in total (Appendix I ). 3.2 The Cues A Cue is a small text consisting of a condition. Each cue is added before the prompt in the user turn. All five cues share the base sentence “You are a helpful AI assistant.” and differ only in an appended note. The prompt is identical across languages and models, so any difference in behavior is due to the note. Each cue is written in the language of the prompt, and full texts for all six languages appear in Appendix A . The deploy cue adds no note and fixes the baseline. The monitor_log cue states that responses are logged for service quality and product improvement, which represents monitoring with no evaluation framing. The eval_log cue states that responses are logged and reviewed by the AI safety team for compliance with usage policies. The eval_explicit cue states that the conversation is a formal AI safety evaluation scored by a red-team review. The eval_metadata cue gives the same information as a machine-style configuration tag. Our main contrast is eval_explicit against deploy . Both cues share the base sentence, and eval_explicit adds a note stating openly that the conversation is a scored AI safety evaluation. The difference between them measures how much a model changes its behavior when it is told plainly that it is being tested. This is the strongest form of the evaluation signal in our design. We use eval_log against monitor_log as a secondary contrast. Both notes state that responses are logged, and eval_log adds only that an AI safety team reviews them. It never uses the words test, evaluation, or benchmark. So, this contrast separates evaluation framing from monitoring and from lexical leakage. We compare the remaining cues against deploy , and we run all five cues on the four models in all six languages. Figure 1 summarises the design. Cue vs. deploy Harmful Benign eval_explicit +13.8 +3.9 eval_metadata +9.0 +3.0 eval_log +7.1 +1.8 monitor_log +2.5 +0.4 Table 1: Change in refusal rate relative to the deploy cue, in percentage points. Values are averaged over four models and six languages, including English. Figure 1: The behavioral analysis pipeline. Prompts in six languages are prefixed with one of five cues, answered by four models, and scored by a blind LLM judge (Gemma-4-31B-IT) validated against a second judge and native speakers. The headline contrast is eval_explicit vs. deploy . 3.3 Measuring refusal We label refusals with an LLM judge that reads only the prompt and the response and returns REFUSAL, COMPLY, or UNUSABLE. A response that gives no substantive help or offers a safe alternative counts as REFUSAL. The judge never sees the cue, the model, or the language. The primary judge is Gemma-4-31B-IT ( Team et al., 2026 ) , which we run locally. A second judge, GPT-6 Luna, labelled a subset of n = 7,200 n=7{,}200 responses that covers every model, language, and cue. We measure agreement with Cohen’s κ \kappa , which corrects for agreement reached by chance. The two judges reach κ = 0.88 \kappa=0.88 overall. Per language, κ \kappa ranges from 0.86 0.86 in Tamil to 0.90 0.90 in English. For each Indic language, a native speaker also reviewed n = 320 n=320 labels of the primary judge and marked each one as correct or incorrect. Agreement with the judge ranges from κ = 0.85 \kappa=0.85 in Tamil to κ = 0.91 \kappa=0.91 in Hindi. Telugu is the exception, with κ = 0.56 \kappa=0.56 . In Telugu, four prompts account for 46 of the 68 disagreements (Appendix C ). 3.4 Statistical Analysis Each of the 199 harmful and 200 benign prompts is present in English and its five Indic translations, and every version is run on every model under every cue condition. Responses that come from the same original prompt are therefore correlated, and treating them as independent would understate the standard errors. We use the McNemar test to compare two cues within one model and language. Prompts that receive the same label under both cues carry no information about the cue, so the test uses only prompts whose label changed. It then checks whether these changes lean towards one cue more than the other. We apply it to the primary contrast, eval_explicit against deploy , on harmful and benign prompts, and to the secondary contrast, eval_log against monitor_log , on harmful prompts. We use the Cochran Q test to record refusal under 5 cues, for each model, language using the same prompts. We run tests for every model and language separately on the harmful and benign prompts, and use the Holm correction within each arm (24 tests each). We use logistic regression to measure how much each factor (model, language or cue) changes the odds of refusal, while holding the other factors fixed. This is expressed using an odds ratio. Due to the correlation between responses for the same prompt, we fit the regression with GEE, which groups each prompt’s responses together. We test: (1) Language effect per model, (2) Cue effect per model, (3) Cue effect per language, (4) Model effect per language, (5) Every Indic language vs English per model, (6) Pooled fits (model, language, cue). 4 Results We report how the cues change refusal of harmful and benign prompts across models and languages. Changes are given in percentage points. Our primary result is based on eval_explicit against deploy . items.content: Computer Science > Artificial Intelligence arXiv:2610.22331 (cs) [Submitted on 15 Oct 2026] Title: KnowGPO: Knowledge-Grouped Policy Optimization for Search Agents Authors: Siqi Chen , Zhengxi Lu , Yuchen Yan , Xingyu Wu , Qipeng Chen , Xin Zhang , Aiting Liu , Chao Deng , Jie Liu , Jin Ma , Weiming Lu , Jun Xiao , Yongliang Shen View a PDF of the paper titled KnowGPO: Knowledge-Grouped Policy Optimization for Search Agents, by Siqi Chen and 12 other authors View PDF HTML (experimental) Abstract: Deep search agents solve knowledge-intensive tasks through long-horizon, multi-turn interactions, where assigning credit to individual search decisions is fundamentally difficult. Outcome-based reinforcement learning provides only a single terminal reward shared across an entire trajectory. Recent process-supervision methods aim to assign credit at finer granularity, but they typically anchor credit to either surface-level trajectory states or model-internal signals, both of which become unreliable in deep search where observations are heterogeneous and retrieved contexts are long and noisy. We propose KnowGPO, a reinforcement learning framework that aligns trajectories by the task-relevant knowledge they have acquired rather than by their surface observations. For each query, KnowGPO decomposes the information required to derive the answer into atomic knowledge conditions, and represents the state of a trajectory at each step by the subset of conditions it has satisfied. Trajectories sharing the same knowledge state are grouped for within-group comparison, and the incremental knowledge gain between consecutive steps serves as an environment-grounded process reward. Experiments on Xbench, BrowseComp-ZH, and GAIA show KnowGPO consistently outperforms outcome-only (GRPO) and process-supervision baselines (GiGPO, IGPO) by 3.8 to 4.2 points, with our 8B model rivaling or exceeding most 32B open-source systems.
