items.content: KnowGPO: Knowledge-Grouped Policy Optimization for Search Agents Siqi Chen Affiliation: Zhejiang University Affiliation: Tencent. {siqichen,syl}@zju.edu.cn, daniellwang@tencent.com Zhengxi Lu Affiliation: Zhejiang University Yuchen Yan Affiliation: Zhejiang University Xingyu Wu Affiliation: Zhejiang University Affiliation: Tencent. {siqichen,syl}@zju.edu.cn, daniellwang@tencent.com Qipeng Chen Affiliation: Zhejiang University Xin Zhang Affiliation: Tencent. {siqichen,syl}@zju.edu.cn, daniellwang@tencent.com Aiting Liu Affiliation: Tencent. {siqichen,syl}@zju.edu.cn, daniellwang@tencent.com Chao Deng Affiliation: Tencent. {siqichen,syl}@zju.edu.cn, daniellwang@tencent.com Jie Liu Affiliation: Tencent. {siqichen,syl}@zju.edu.cn, daniellwang@tencent.com Jin Ma Affiliation: Tencent. {siqichen,syl}@zju.edu.cn, daniellwang@tencent.com Weiming Lu Affiliation: Zhejiang University Jun Xiao Affiliation: Zhejiang University Yongliang Shen † † thanks: Corresponding author Affiliation: Zhejiang University Abstract Deep search agents solve knowledge-intensive tasks through long-horizon, multi-turn interactions, where assigning credit to individual search decisions is fundamentally difficult. Outcome-based reinforcement learning provides only a single terminal reward shared across an entire trajectory. Recent process-supervision methods aim to assign credit at finer granularity, but they typically anchor credit to either surface-level trajectory states or model-internal signals, both of which become unreliable in deep search where observations are heterogeneous and retrieved contexts are long and noisy. We propose KnowGPO , a reinforcement learning framework that aligns trajectories by the task-relevant knowledge they have acquired rather than by their surface observations. For each query, KnowGPO decomposes the information required to derive the answer into atomic knowledge conditions, and represents the state of a trajectory at each step by the subset of conditions it has satisfied. Trajectories sharing the same knowledge state are grouped for within-group comparison, and the incremental knowledge gain between consecutive steps serves as an environment-grounded process reward. Experiments on Xbench, BrowseComp-ZH, and GAIA show KnowGPO consistently outperforms outcome-only (GRPO) and process-supervision baselines (GiGPO, IGPO) by 3.8 to 4.2 points, with our 8B model rivaling or exceeding most 32B open-source systems. Our code is available at https://github.com/ZJU-REAL/KnowGPO . Figure 1: Comparison of credit assignment in deep search agents. Left: GRPO uses episode-level advantages from terminal rewards ( R 1 R_{1} , R 2 R_{2} , R 3 R_{3} ) without intermediate feedback. Middle: GiGPO matches environment states ( 𝐬 ~ \tilde{\mathbf{s}} ) but suffers from severe fragmentation under heterogeneous observations. Right: KnowGPO abstracts heterogeneous states into knowledge states ( 𝐬 i , t \mathbf{s}_{i,t} ) and computes step-level advantages from incremental knowledge gains ( r i , t r_{i,t} ). 1 Introduction LLM-based deep search agents have become a powerful paradigm for knowledge-intensive problem solving, coordinating multi-turn search, evidence inspection, query reformulation, and termination decisions through language-model reasoning ( Yao et al., 2022 ; Zhang et al., 2026a ) . Unlike conventional retrieval-augmented generation (RAG), which typically follows a one-pass retrieve-then-read pipeline ( Lewis et al., 2021 ; Gao et al., 2024 ; Zhao et al., 2024 ) , deep search agents iteratively formulate queries, inspect evidence, update beliefs, and decide when to stop ( Nakano et al., 2021 ; Li et al., 2025c ) . This makes deep search a long-horizon sequential decision problem, where success depends on adaptive decisions about what to search, what evidence to keep, and when to terminate . Because supervised fine-tuning mainly imitates surface behavior ( Nakano et al., 2021 ; Schick et al., 2023 ) and cannot optimize such strategic decisions, reinforcement learning has become central to training competitive deep search agents ( Guo et al., 2025 ; Jin et al., 2025 ; Song et al., 2025 ) . However, applying reinforcement learning to deep search agents encounters three coupled difficulties in credit assignment (Figure 1 ). First, terminal outcome rewards used by group-relative methods such as GRPO ( Shao et al., 2024 ; Jin et al., 2025 ; Song et al., 2025 ; Lu et al., 2025 ; Li et al., 2025b ; Liu et al., 2025 ) are uniformly broadcast to every action, so a single final reward cannot reveal which intermediate decisions were useful, redundant, or harmful. Second, recent process-supervision methods such as GiGPO ( Feng et al., 2025 ) that align trajectories by their intermediate states require state recurrence across trajectories, yet deep search rollouts seldom revisit the same observable state even when they acquire the same evidence. Third, dense process rewards derived from changes in the model’s predicted answer probability, as in IGPO ( Wang et al., 2026 ) , or from learned critics and rubric-based reward models ( Shi et al., 2025 ; Lee et al., 2025 ; Zhang et al., 2025 ; Zhang et al., 2026b ; Lu et al., 2026 ) , provide denser signals but are driven by model-internal beliefs or learned proxies rather than by externally verified knowledge. Deep search trajectories vary widely at the level of queries, pages, and reasoning traces, but converge on the same underlying quantity: the task-relevant knowledge they have accumulated toward the correct answer. This knowledge, not observations or model confidence, provides the natural signal for credit assignment in long-horizon search. We propose Knowledge-Grouped Policy Optimization (KnowGPO) , a RL framework that aligns trajectories by the task-relevant knowledge they have acquired rather than by their surface observations. For each query, we decompose the information required to derive the correct answer into a set of atomic knowledge conditions. At every step of a trajectory, we represent its state by the subset of conditions it has satisfied, called its knowledge state . We further define incremental knowledge gain , the increase in satisfied conditions between consecutive steps, as a process reward that scores each action’s immediate contribution. While knowledge-state grouping ensures only semantically comparable steps are contrasted, incremental gain provides the dense signal within each group, enabling fine-grained credit assignment without a learned critic. Trajectories sharing the same knowledge state are grouped for within-group comparison, yielding step-level advantages that combine with episode-level outcome advantages through a single mixing coefficient. The result is fine-grained credit assignment for long-horizon deep search without observation matching, without dependence on the model’s own confidence, and without a learned reward model. We train Qwen3-8B with KnowGPO on three challenging deep search benchmarks: Xbench, BrowseComp-ZH, and GAIA. KnowGPO improves over outcome-only GRPO by 2.0% to 5.9% and consistently outperforms recent process-supervision baselines including GiGPO and IGPO, with the resulting 8B agent matching or surpassing open-source systems of up to 32B parameters. In summary, our contributions are threefold: • We propose KnowGPO, a reinforcement learning framework that performs credit assignment in a query-specific knowledge state space rather than over surface observations, enabling within-group comparison across semantically equivalent trajectories. • We introduce incremental knowledge gain as a process reward grounded in the environment, providing dense step-level supervision without observation matching, learned critics, or reliance on model-internal probabilities. • We demonstrate that KnowGPO outperforms outcome-based and recent process-supervision baselines by 3.8% to 4.2% across three deep search benchmarks, with an 8B agent matching or surpassing open-source systems of up to 32B parameters. 2 Related Work 2.1 Reinforcement Learning for Search Agent Reinforcement learning with verifiable outcome rewards has become the dominant paradigm for post-training deep search agents. Early systems train models to interleave search and reasoning through outcome-based optimization on multi-hop QA ( Jin et al., 2025 ; Chen et al., 2025 ; Wang et al., 2025 ; Zheng et al., 2025 ; Wu et al., 2025 ) , showing that group-relative methods such as GRPO scale to multi-turn tool use without learned value functions. Subsequent work scales this paradigm along two axes: harder data through knowledge graphs, web exploration, and synthetic multi-hop generation ( Lu et al., 2025 ; Li et al., 2025b ; Liu et al., 2025 ; Li et al., 2025a ; Du et al., 2026 ; Gao et al., 2025 ; Chu et al., 2026 ; Team et al., 2026e ; Team et al., 2026d ) , and refined reward shaping and policy gradient stability for long-horizon rollouts ( Wu et al., 2026 ; Dong et al., 2025 ; Luo et al., 2025 ; Tang et al., 2025 ) . Despite these advances, the supervisory signal in most systems remains a binary reward at the end of each trajectory, leaving the contribution of search decisions inside long rollouts unidentified. 2.2 Credit Assignment for Search Agents A growing line of work aims to address long-horizon credit assignment through process-level supervision. GiGPO ( Feng et al., 2025 ) extends GRPO with anchor-state grouping, computing step-level advantages by matching trajectories that revisit the same environment state; this mechanism requires reliable state recurrence, which is rare in deep search where retrieved contents and reasoning histories are open-ended. IGPO ( Wang et al., 2026 ) instead derives dense step rewards from the model’s own probability of producing the correct answer, sidestepping state matching but anchoring the signal to internal confidence that can be biased by long, noisy retrieved contexts. A parallel direction introduces externally grounded supervision through learned reward models or rubric decompositions ( Zhang et al., 2026b ; Zhang et al., 2025 ; Lee et al., 2025 ; Shi et al., 2025 ) , providing denser feedback than outcome rewards but relying on learned proxies whose calibration is itself a research question, and without producing step groupings that make semantically equivalent decisions directly comparable across trajectories. KnowGPO instead anchors credit assignment to an externally verifiable representation of progress, the set of satisfied atomic knowledge conditions, and uses this representation as both the grouping criterion for within-group comparison and the basis of a process reward grounded in the environment. 3 Method 3.1 Problem Formulation We formulate deep search as a multi-turn sequential decision process. Given a query Q Q and a reference answer y ∗ y^{*} , an agent interacts with a retrieval environment over time steps t ∈ { 1 , … , T } t\in\{1,\dots,T\} . At each step the agent produces a reasoning trace and an action a t ∈ { search , answer } a_{t}\in\{\texttt{search},\texttt{answer}\} from its policy π θ ( ⋅ ∣ h t , Q ) \pi_{\theta}(\cdot\mid h_{t},Q) , where h t = ( a 1 , o 1 , … , a t − 1 , o t − 1 ) h_{t}=(a_{1},o_{1},\dots,a_{t-1},o_{t-1}) is the interaction history and o t o_{t} is the observation returned by the environment (e.g., retrieved documents for search , or a terminal signal for answer ). A complete trajectory is denoted τ = ( a 1 , o 1 , … , a T , o T ) \tau=(a_{1},o_{1},\dots,a_{T},o_{T}) and terminates with a binary outcome reward R ⁡ ( τ ) = 𝕀 ⁡ ( ans ​ ( τ ) = y ∗ ) R(\tau)=\mathbb{I}(\text{ans}(\tau)=y^{*}) . We build on group-relative policy optimization, which estimates advantages from a group of N N trajectories sampled for the same Q Q and avoids learning a separate value network. The challenge addressed throughout this section is that R ⁡ ( τ ) R(\tau) alone provides no signal for distinguishing useful, redundant, or harmful steps inside a long-horizon trajectory. Figure 2: Overview of the KnowGPO framework. Left: Knowledge condition construction via a two-stage pipeline, illustrated with an example. Right: Rollout trajectories are grouped by matched knowledge states; step-level advantages are computed from incremental knowledge gains via group-relative comparisons. 3.2 Knowledge State A central design choice in KnowGPO is to abstract the progress of a search trajectory through the task-relevant knowledge it has acquired, rather than through its surface observations. We realize this abstraction in two steps: constructing a query-specific set of atomic knowledge conditions, and representing each trajectory step by the subset of conditions it has satisfied. Knowledge conditions. For each query Q Q with reference answer y ∗ y^{*} , we construct a finite set of atomic knowledge conditions 𝒦 ⁡ ( Q ) = { k 1 , … , k K } , \mathcal{K}(Q)=\{k_{1},\dots,k_{K}\}, (1) where each k j k_{j} is a single-hop factual constraint needed to derive y ∗ y^{*} . Intuitively, 𝒦 ⁡ ( Q ) \mathcal{K}(Q) encodes the answer’s logical skeleton: a trajectory cannot reliably produce y ∗ y^{*} without acquiring every k j k_{j} . We construct 𝒦 ⁡ ( Q ) \mathcal{K}(Q) through a two-stage pipeline that first identifies the reasoning skeleton implied by Q Q (with placeholders for unknown entities) and then grounds each placeholder using y ∗ y^{*} and a successful reference trajectory. This decoupling produces a trajectory-agnostic knowledge space and ensures three properties: each condition encodes a single fact (atomicity), the conditions jointly support the full reasoning chain to y ∗ y^{*} (completeness), and entity references remain consistent across the query, the answer, and the search trajectories (grounding consistency). Construction details and the prompts used at each stage are deferred to Appendix B . Knowledge state. Given 𝒦 ⁡ ( Q ) \mathcal{K}(Q) , we represent the state of a trajectory τ i \tau_{i} at step t t by the subset of conditions it has satisfied so far. At each step, an LLM-based verifier inspects the new observation o i , t o_{i,t} and outputs a binary vector Δ ​ 𝐬 i , t ∈ { 0 , 1 } K \Delta\mathbf{s}_{i,t}\in\{0,1\}^{K} indicating the set of conditions newly verifiable from o i , t o_{i,t} : [ Δ ​ 𝐬 i , t ] j = 𝕀 ⁡ ( h i , t ⊧ k j ) . [\Delta\mathbf{s}_{i,t}]_{j}=\mathbb{I}\!\left(h_{i,t}\models k_{j}\right). We evaluate KnowGPO on three challenging deep search benchmarks that cover diverse question distributions and difficulty levels: Xbench ( Xbench-Team, 2025 ) (covering the 2505 and 2510 splits), BrowseComp-ZH ( Zhou et al., 2025 ) , and the text-only subset of GAIA ( Mialon et al., 2023 ) . We compare KnowGPO against three representative reinforcement learning approaches, all trained from the same SFT checkpoint with identical data and tool environments. Unlike conventional retrieval-augmented generation (RAG), which typically follows a one-pass retrieve-then-read pipeline ( Lewis et al., 2021 ; Gao et al., 2024 ; Zhao et al., 2024 ) , deep search agents iteratively formulate queries, inspect evidence, update beliefs, and decide when to stop ( Nakano et al., 2021 ; Li et al., 2025c ) . This makes deep search a long-horizon sequential decision problem, where success depends on adaptive decisions about what to search, what evidence to keep, and when to terminate . Because supervised fine-tuning mainly imitates surface behavior ( Nakano et al., 2021 ; Schick et al., 2023 ) and cannot optimize such strategic decisions, reinforcement learning has become central to training competitive deep search agents ( Guo et al., 2025 ; Jin et al., 2025 ; Song et al., 2025 ) . However, applying reinforcement learning to deep search agents encounters three coupled difficulties in credit assignment (Figure 1 ). First, terminal outcome rewards used by group-relative methods such as GRPO ( Shao et al., 2024 ; Jin et al., 2025 ; Song et al., 2025 ; Lu et al., 2025 ; Li et al., 2025b ; Liu et al., 2025 ) are uniformly broadcast to every action, so a single final reward cannot reveal which intermediate decisions were useful, redundant, or harmful. Second, recent process-supervision methods such as GiGPO ( Feng et al., 2025 ) that align trajectories by their intermediate states require state recurrence across trajectories, yet deep search rollouts seldom revisit the same observable state even when they acquire the same evidence. Third, dense process rewards derived from changes in the model’s predicted answer probability, as in IGPO ( Wang et al., 2026 ) , or from learned critics and rubric-based reward models ( Shi et al., 2025 ; Lee et al., 2025 ; Zhang et al., 2025 ; Zhang et al., 2026b ; Lu et al., 2026 ) , provide denser signals but are driven by model-internal beliefs or learned proxies rather than by externally verified knowledge. Deep search trajectories vary widely at the level of queries, pages, and reasoning traces, but converge on the same underlying quantity: the task-relevant knowledge they have accumulated toward the correct answer. This knowledge, not observations or model confidence, provides the natural signal for credit assignment in long-horizon search. We propose Knowledge-Grouped Policy Optimization (KnowGPO) , a RL framework that aligns trajectories by the task-relevant knowledge they have acquired rather than by their surface observations. For each query, we decompose the information required to derive the correct answer into a set of atomic knowledge conditions. At every step of a trajectory, we represent its state by the subset of conditions it has satisfied, called its knowledge state . We further define incremental knowledge gain , the increase in satisfied conditions between consecutive steps, as a process reward that scores each action’s immediate contribution. While knowledge-state grouping ensures only semantically comparable steps are contrasted, incremental gain provides the dense signal within each group, enabling fine-grained credit assignment without a learned critic. Trajectories sharing the same knowledge state are grouped for within-group comparison, yielding step-level advantages that combine with episode-level outcome advantages through a single mixing coefficient. The result is fine-grained credit assignment for long-horizon deep search without observation matching, without dependence on the model’s own confidence, and without a learned reward model. We train Qwen3-8B with KnowGPO on three challenging deep search benchmarks: Xbench, BrowseComp-ZH, and GAIA. KnowGPO improves over outcome-only GRPO by 2.0% to 5.9% and consistently outperforms recent process-supervision baselines including GiGPO and IGPO, with the resulting 8B agent matching or surpassing open-source systems of up to 32B parameters. In summary, our contributions are threefold: • We propose KnowGPO, a reinforcement learning framework that performs credit assignment in a query-specific knowledge state space rather than over surface observations, enabling within-group comparison across semantically equivalent trajectories. • We introduce incremental knowledge gain as a process reward grounded in the environment, providing dense step-level supervision without observation matching, learned critics, or reliance on model-internal probabilities. • We demonstrate that KnowGPO outperforms outcome-based and recent process-supervision baselines by 3.8% to 4.2% across three deep search benchmarks, with an 8B agent matching or surpassing open-source systems of up to 32B parameters. 2 Related Work 2.1 Reinforcement Learning for Search Agent Reinforcement learning with verifiable outcome rewards has become the dominant paradigm for post-training deep search agents. Early systems train models to interleave search and reasoning through outcome-based optimization on multi-hop QA ( Jin et al., 2025 ; Chen et al., 2025 ; Wang et al., 2025 ; Zheng et al., 2025 ; Wu et al., 2025 ) , showing that group-relative methods such as GRPO scale to multi-turn tool use without learned value functions. Subsequent work scales this paradigm along two axes: harder data through knowledge graphs, web exploration, and synthetic multi-hop generation ( Lu et al., 2025 ; Li et al., 2025b ; Liu et al., 2025 ; Li et al., 2025a ; Du et al., 2026 ; Gao et al., 2025 ; Chu et al., 2026 ; Team et al., 2026e ; Team et al., 2026d ) , and refined reward shaping and policy gradient stability for long-horizon rollouts ( Wu et al., 2026 ; Dong et al., 2025 ; Luo et al., 2025 ; Tang et al., 2025 ) . Despite these advances, the supervisory signal in most systems remains a binary reward at the end of each trajectory, leaving the contribution of search decisions inside long rollouts unidentified. 2.2 Credit Assignment for Search Agents A growing line of work aims to address long-horizon credit assignment through process-level supervision. GiGPO ( Feng et al., 2025 ) extends GRPO with anchor-state grouping, computing step-level advantages by matching trajectories that revisit the same environment state; this mechanism requires reliable state recurrence, which is rare in deep search where retrieved contents and reasoning histories are open-ended. IGPO ( Wang et al., 2026 ) instead derives dense step rewards from the model’s own probability of producing the correct answer, sidestepping state matching but anchoring the signal to internal confidence that can be biased by long, noisy retrieved contexts. A parallel direction introduces externally grounded supervision through learned reward models or rubric decompositions ( Zhang et al., 2026b ; Zhang et al., 2025 ; Lee et al., 2025 ; Shi et al., 2025 ) , providing denser feedback than outcome rewards but relying on learned proxies whose calibration is itself a research question, and without producing step groupings that make semantically equivalent decisions directly comparable across trajectories. KnowGPO instead anchors credit assignment to an externally verifiable representation of progress, the set of satisfied atomic knowledge conditions, and uses this representation as both the grouping criterion for within-group comparison and the basis of a process reward grounded in the environment. 3 Method 3.1 Problem Formulation We formulate deep search as a multi-turn sequential decision process. items.content: At a glance End-to-end forecasting: A machine learning pipeline uses forecast-time solar-wind information to generate location-specific risk estimates for 66,935 substations in the continental United States. Physics and place: The system combines Auroral Electrojet (AE) and Disturbance Storm Time (Dst) forecasts with local latitude, geology, and ground conductivity. Advance warning: The pipeline detected nearly 80% of major space-weather events during the evaluation period and can warn grid operators 30 to 60 minutes before a specific risk appears. Forecasting a threat to critical infrastructure During the May 2024 geomagnetic storm, utilities across North America prepared for possible impacts as auroras extended far beyond their usual range. The storm would degrade GPS accuracy and satellite operations, impacting farm operations in North America and Europe. Modern society depends on reliable electric power, yet extreme space-weather events can induce currents in transmission networks that damage equipment and increase operational risk. The challenge is not only knowing that a storm is approaching, but estimating when and where its effects could be most severe with enough warning for grid operators to respond. During my summer internship at Microsoft Research, I developed a machine learning system that forecasts space-weather risk across 66,935 substations in the continental United States. The system measures how the sun’s activity can affect the earth’s magnetic field and, ultimately, the power grid. It combines solar-wind observations, forecasts of the Auroral Electrojet (AE) and Disturbance Storm Time (Dst) indices, physics-informed constraints, local geological conductivity, and grid-infrastructure data to produce location-specific risk estimates 30-60 minutes ahead of potential impact. Building an end-to-end prediction pipeline Space-weather prediction is difficult because it spans several coupled systems. The solar wind changes rapidly, its interaction with Earth’s magnetosphere is irregular, and the resulting ground effects depend on local conditions. Regions with resistive bedrock can experience stronger geomagnetically induced currents (GICs) than regions with more conductive geology. Transmission-line orientation, latitude, and other power-system characteristics further influence the exposure of individual assets. video series On Second Thought A video series with Sinead Bovell built around the questions everyone’s asking about AI. With expert voices from across Microsoft, we break down the tension and promise of this rapidly changing technology, exploring what’s evolving and what’s possible. Explore the series Opens in a new tab The pipeline addresses this complexity in three stages, shown in Figure 1. First, solar-wind measurements from the L1 Lagrange point are used to generate forecasts of the AE and Dst indices, while geological conductivity and location features are assembled for each substation. Second, a gradient-boosting model combines these forecasted and location-specific inputs to estimate dB/dt, the rate of magnetic-field change associated with GIC risk. Finally, the resulting predictions are converted into location-specific risk estimates and aggregated into a continental risk assessment. A system of 50 AI agents helped explore features, validation strategies, and model configurations across the pipeline. Only public data sources were used, included NASA OMNI and NASA-aggregated Kyoto World Data Center data, INTERMAGNET and U.S. Geological Survey magnetometer observations, and GridSFM-derived grid data. Figure 1. End-to-end forecasting pipeline from L1 solar-wind measurements to location-specific risk estimates across 66,935 U.S. substations. Evaluating geomagnetic forecasts and infrastructure risk The AE predictor was designed to forecast rare, high-intensity geomagnetic activity that drives infrastructure risk. In the 2020-2026 evaluation period, the model produced forecasts spanning nearly the full observed range of AE activity and outperformed several empirical solar-wind-based approaches. The Dst predictor provided an additional signal describing large-scale geomagnetic storm strength. During the most geomagnetically active periods of the 2020-2026 evaluation period, the machine-learning model outperformed the Burton equation on 62.2% of individual hours. The model also produced a substantially wider prediction range than Burton-style approaches and improved severe-event detection in the end-to-end forecasting system by 1.2 percentage points when combined with AE forecasts. Predictor Result Baseline comparison Impact AE 410.2 nT RMSE Lower RMSE than empirical and solar-wind-only baselines Captures extreme-event activity used by the GIC forecasting system Dst 7.2 nT RMSE Outperformed Burton on 62.2% of peak-activity hours and provided wider prediction range +1.2pp severe storm detection when integrated into final GIC system The GIC risk stage was evaluated differently. There is no equivalent widely deployed operational system that provides a direct industry benchmark for this calculation, so the machine learning model was compared with simple linear regression. As Figure 2 shows, the system achieved detection rates of 76.5% for major events (≥10 nT/min), 81.2% for severe events (≥20 nT/min), and 64.1% for extreme events (≥50 nT/min). False-alarm rates increased with storm severity, reflecting the trade-off between missed events and cautious alerts. Performance varied by latitude, with the highest detection rates at northern stations where geomagnetic activity is strongest. Figure 2. Detection rates across storm-severity thresholds for regionally different substations, with a comparison between the average POD for each severity tier. Translating predictions into continental risk assessments The final stage translates predicted geomagnetic activity into location-specific estimates of dB/dt, the rate of magnetic-field change associated with GIC exposure. Rather than issuing a single alert for the continental United States, the system combines storm conditions with each substation’s latitude and geological factor. This produces continuous risk estimates that can distinguish lower-risk locations from areas where resistive geology can amplify ground-level effects. Figure 3 illustrates the output for a representative major-storm scenario. The map is a demonstration of the model’s continental-scale output, not a record of a live operational event. It shows how a grid operator or planner could move from a broad space-weather warning toward a more targeted view of which locations may warrant closer analysis. The current pipeline produced estimates for all 66,935 substations in approximately 333 milliseconds during measured inference, allowing many scenarios to be evaluated quickly. Figure 3. Demonstration of a continental GIC risk assessment under a representative major-storm scenario. Colors indicate modeled risk levels across 66,935 substations. Implications and looking forward This work demonstrates how physics-grounded machine learning could support more specific and timely assessment of space-weather exposure. Earlier, location-specific information could help utilities prioritize engineering review and consider targeted protective actions, such as adjusting reactive-power reserves or temporarily reconfiguring parts of the network. Further validation with utilities and operational data would be needed before the system could be used in grid operations. The project also connects with broader Microsoft Research work on AI for power systems. The open grid-data pipeline provided realistic U.S. transmission models, while GridSFM applies deep learning to AC optimal power flow for fast scenario analysis. Together, these efforts point toward richer planning and resilience workflows that combine hazard forecasts, grid topology, and power-flow analysis. Extend forecast horizons: Explore temporal-transformer approaches that capture longer-range patterns in solar-wind data and move beyond the current 30-60-minute window. Scale internationally: Adapt the system to additional regions while accounting for different geological conditions and grid topologies. Integrate with grid operations: Evaluate how forecasts could support existing decision-making and engineering-review workflows before considering higher levels of automation. Provide transformer-level risk: Add asset-specific characteristics to move from substation-level estimates toward more granular assessments of critical equipment. items.raw_text: At a glance End-to-end forecasting: A machine learning pipeline uses forecast-time solar-wind information to generate location-specific risk estimates for 66,935 substations in the continental United States. Physics and place: The system combines Auroral Electrojet (AE) and Disturbance Storm Time (Dst) forecasts with local latitude, geology, and ground conductivity. Advance warning: The pipeline detected nearly 80% of major space-weather events during the evaluation period and can warn grid operators 30 to 60 minutes before a specific risk appears. Forecasting a threat to critical infrastructure During the May 2024 geomagnetic storm, utilities across North America prepared for possible impacts as auroras extended far beyond their usual range. The storm would degrade GPS accuracy and satellite operations, impacting farm operations in North America and Europe. Modern society depends on reliable electric power, yet extreme space-weather events can induce currents in transmission networks that damage equipment and increase operational risk. The challenge is not only knowing that a storm is approaching, but estimating when and where its effects could be most severe with enough warning for grid operators to respond. The solar wind changes rapidly, its interaction with Earth’s magnetosphere is irregular, and the resulting ground effects depend on local conditions. Regions with resistive bedrock can experience stronger geomagnetically induced currents (GICs) than regions with more conductive geology. Transmission-line orientation, latitude, and other power-system characteristics further influence the exposure of individual assets. video series On Second Thought A video series with Sinead Bovell built around the questions everyone’s asking about AI. Description of the Treasury Nominal and Inflation-Indexed Constant Maturity Series Yields on Treasury nominal securities at “constant maturity” are interpolated by the U.S. Treasury from the daily yield curve for non-inflation-indexed Treasury securities. This curve, which relates the yield on a security to its time to maturity, is based on the closing market bid yields on actively traded Treasury securities in the over-the-counter market. These market yields are calculated from composites of quotations obtained by the Federal Reserve Bank of New York. The constant maturity yield values are read from the yield curve at fixed maturities, currently 1, 3, and 6 months and 1, 2, 3, 5, 7, 10, 20, and 30 years. This method provides a yield for a 10-year maturity, for example, even if no outstanding security has exactly 10 years remaining to maturity. Similarly, yields on inflation-indexed securities at “constant maturity” are interpolated from the daily yield curve for Treasury inflation protected securities in the over-the-counter market. The inflation-indexed constant maturity yields are read from this yield curve at fixed maturities, currently 5, 7, 10, 20, and 30 years. Back to Top Last Update: October 15, 2026 Back to Top
